mem.t: I will set no vile thing before my eyes. I hate the deeds of faithless men. They will not cling to me.

sat.t: Family Day: A Screen-Free Half Day
sat.d: Choose a half day and put all the phones and tablets into a “rest basket,” keeping back just one phone on silent for emergencies. Go together to a park, a wet market or the seaside, and give everyone a “five senses list”: see three colors, hear two sounds, touch one texture, smell one scent, taste one small snack. Back home, sit together and share: “What did I notice when there were no screens?” Finish by thanking God that the world he made is bigger and more real than any screen.

sun: This week, at what moments did you find yourself picking up your phone most often? What were you really looking for in your heart at those times?
In your home, has the screen quietly become a “third parent”? What has it been teaching your children lately?
Next week, which phone boundary will you set for yourself first, and which group member or family member will you invite to remind you?

lessons.title: No Vile Thing Before My Eyes
lessons.theme: Watching over a family begins with watching over my own eyes

v: I will be careful to live a blameless life. When will you come to me? I will walk within my house with a blameless heart.
I will set no vile thing before my eyes. I hate the deeds of faithless men. They will not cling to me.

lessons.still: Turn your phone face down and set it aside, or put it in another room. Be quiet for a minute and notice whether there is an urge in you to go and look. Don’t criticize it. Just say to the Lord, “Lord, right now I will look at you first.”
teach: When David wrote Psalm 101, he was a newly crowned king. The first thing he resolved was not to expand his territory but this: “I will walk within my house with a blameless heart.” Right after that he said, “I will set no vile thing before my eyes.” Three thousand years ago, there was only so much that could be put before your eyes. Today one glowing screen can put the whole world in front of us and our children, good and bad, day and night.

Some people describe the screen as the “third parent” in many homes. The child cries, so we give him a video. Mealtime is boring, so we scroll a little. He can’t sleep, so we put on one more episode. The screen may spend more time with a child than his parents do, and he may hear more from it than from us. What we should also notice is that many platforms run on an algorithm: it remembers where you linger and serves up more of the same. It doesn’t care what kind of person your child becomes, only how long he stays.

To watch over a home in the digital age, the starting point is not the child’s phone but the parents’ own eyes. David begins with “I”: I will walk, I will set, I hate. When parents can put down the screen and look their children in the eye as they talk, children learn that real people are worth more of our gaze than a glowing screen. This week we do not begin by forbidding the children, but by parents returning to God first.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The order of relationships is God first, then myself, then others, then tasks. Screens upset this order most easily: waking up and checking messages before looking to God, looking at the phone at the table before looking at the family. Letting Jesus reign includes letting him be Lord of my phone.
q: Who is God? — David asked, “When will you come to me?” What kind of home is God willing to dwell in?
Who am I? — If you laid out all the time I spend on screens in a day, what would it say my heart is pursuing?
How should I respond? — What is one thing that is “set before my eyes” that I am willing to move away today, for God and for my family?
lessons.jesus: When Jesus was on earth he was often surrounded by crowds, everyone looking for him, yet he “withdrew himself into the desert and prayed.” His attention was never held hostage by the crowd, because he first had fellowship with the Father. So when he looked at a person, he truly saw him: Zacchaeus in the tree, the widow with her two small coins, the little children brought to him. His eyes are the best example for parents.
lessons.pray: Lord, I confess that my phone often gets my attention before you do, and before my family does. Today I give my eyes to you. Help me not to set any vile thing before my eyes, and not to let useless things steal the time I have with my children. Be Lord over every screen in our home, and let me walk within my house with a blameless heart. Amen.
acts: Open your phone’s screen-time record and look honestly at where you spent the most time this week. Don’t defend it; just note it
For the first hour after you get home today, leave your phone at a fixed charging spot and don’t carry it with you
Write a line on your phone’s lock screen: “I will walk within my house with a blameless heart.”
lessons.noon: “I will set no vile thing before my eyes.” — Lord, right now I turn my eyes to you. Please watch over my heart and watch over my home.

fam.key: My eyes will look at good things.

lamb.do: Put down your phone, crouch to your baby’s eye level and play “peekaboo”: cover your face with your hands, then open them and give a big smile so he sees your face.
lamb.say: Mommy and Daddy are looking at you, and God is always watching over you too.

sprout.story: Xiaoen’s mommy loved looking at her phone. One day Xiaoen ran over with a drawing and said, “Mommy, look!” Mommy didn’t even look up: “Wait a moment.” Xiaoen waited and waited until the drawing was all crumpled. Then Mommy noticed. She quickly put down her phone, hugged Xiaoen and said, “I’m sorry. You are much more important than my phone!” They looked at the drawing together, and Xiaoen smiled and smiled.
sprout.ask: What do you like Mommy and Daddy to look at you doing?
sprout.do: Play “eye parking lot”: everyone “parks” their phones in a box, then pairs look into each other’s eyes. Whoever laughs first has to say “I love you” to the other.

soldier.story: After David became king he wrote a psalm saying he would live honestly at home and would not set bad things before his eyes. Today a screen can put anything in front of us: fun videos, exciting games, and also things that are not good. Many apps are very clever: whatever you watch, they send you more of the same, like a salesman who can read your mind. It doesn’t care what kind of person you become, only how long you watch. So who decides what gets put before your eyes? The salesman, or you and God?
ask: What do you think the videos or games you watch most are teaching you?
If you could give an app an instruction, what would you tell it to send you more of and less of?
soldier.do: Be “screen detectives” as a family: each person writes down three things they did on screens yesterday, guesses roughly how long each took, and shares at dinner. Mom and Dad write too, and go first.

youth.talk: I want to admit something first. Lately I’ve often told you to use your phone less, yet I scroll at meals and while we talk, and that isn’t fair. I’ve been reading Psalm 101, where David says that at home he will first take charge of his own eyes. I’ve realized that instead of keeping on managing you, I need to manage myself first. I’m also curious: what do you make of what the algorithm pushes at you every day?
ask: How do our habits with our phones feel to you? You can be honest.
Have you noticed that what apps push at you has slowly changed how you think or feel?
youth.do: Ask your child to be a one-week “phone coach”: when a parent picks up a phone at a meal or during a conversation, the child may give a reminder, and the parent puts it down at once without defending themselves.

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for always watching over us. Please protect our eyes so that we look at good things, and help us look at each other more and at screens less. In Jesus’ name, amen.

lessons.title: What Kind of Phone Parent Am I?
lessons.theme: The eye is the lamp of the body: where do my eyes rest most?

v: for where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.
“The lamp of the body is the eye. If therefore your eye is sound, your whole body will be full of light.
But if your eye is evil, your whole body will be full of darkness. If therefore the light that is in you is darkness, how great is the darkness!

lessons.still: Close your eyes and recall the first thing you did when you woke this morning. Ask the Holy Spirit to shine his light gently: “Lord, where do my eyes rest most? And what is my heart chasing?” Don’t rush to change; first, just see.
teach: Jesus said, “The lamp of the body is the eye.” The eye is like a window: whatever we look at, we invite into the heart. In the line before, Jesus said, “where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.” Today we might put it this way: where your attention is, there your heart will be also. Our screen-time records often say more honestly than our prayers where our hearts are.

Ask the Holy Spirit to hold up a mirror. There is the “escape” parent: tired and fed up, he hides in his phone, and the child has to call three times before he looks up. There is the “work” parent: messages must be answered at any moment, and home is just another office. There is the “comparison” parent: scrolling through other people’s children’s award photos, growing more anxious. And there is the “babysitter” parent: using the screen as a babysitter in exchange for a moment of quiet. We may be a little of each. Knowing which we are tells us which need we should bring to God.

One day Mrs. Su in Kuala Lumpur noticed her three-year-old daughter playing house, holding a building block to her ear and frowning, saying, “Wait a moment, Mommy’s busy.” She couldn’t laugh. Children are the most honest mirror. We look not to be condemned but to turn back; God shines his light on us because he wants to heal us, so that our eyes may become clear again.
lessons.light: 321 Light: A self-ruled parent uses the phone to fill his own emptiness, anxiety or tiredness while demanding self-control from the children; a self-emptied parent first admits his own needs and brings his emptiness to God. The focus is on Jesus, not on other people’s lives in the screen, and not on our own shortcomings.
q: Who is God? — Jesus said the eye is the lamp of the body. What kind of light does he want to shine into my heart?
Who am I? — Escape, work, comparison or babysitter: which kind of parent am I most like? When is it most obvious?
How should I respond? — What “phone language” do my children learn from me? What do I want them to learn?
lessons.jesus: When Jesus met the Samaritan woman at the well, he was tired and thirsty, yet he gave her his whole attention and saw her years of thirst. He never put off those who came to him with “wait a moment.” That focused gaze came from his unbroken connection with the Father. When our hearts are satisfied in him, we no longer need to look for comfort in a screen.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, shine your light on me. I confess that I often hide in my phone to escape weariness, and I compare myself with other people’s lives, so the more I scroll the more confused my heart becomes. Heal the emptiness inside me, make my eyes clear again, and let both my treasure and my heart be with you. When my child calls me, help me to lift my head and see him. Amen.
acts: Write down the three moments you pick up your phone most, and next to each write the real need in your heart then (tired, bored, anxious, afraid of missing out)
Move the one app that most easily makes you compare or feel anxious off your phone’s home screen today
When your child calls you, practice putting down the phone first, turning around and looking into his eyes before you answer
lessons.noon: “The lamp of the body is the eye. If therefore your eye is sound, your whole body will be full of light.” — Lord, cleanse my eyes, so that I see you first and see my children.

fam.key: What I look at fills my heart.

lamb.do: Hold your baby by a window or beside a lamp, point to the light and say “bright”, then gently touch beside his eyelids and say “bright”.
lamb.say: Your eyes are so bright, and God loves it when you look at beautiful things.

sprout.story: Xiaojie had a clear glass cup. When he poured in orange juice, the cup turned orange. When he poured in milk, it turned white. When someone poured in muddy water, the cup turned dirty. Mommy said, “Our hearts are like this cup. Whatever our eyes look at fills our hearts.” Xiaojie thought for a while and said, “Then I’ll look at lots of good things, so my heart is sparkling!”
sprout.ask: What good thing did you see today and put into your heart?
sprout.do: Fill a clear glass with water, add a drop of soy sauce or paint, and watch the water change together. Then say together: “Whatever my eyes look at fills my heart.”

soldier.story: Jesus said, “The lamp of the body is the eye.” Imagine a house with only one window. If sunlight comes in through that window, the whole house is bright; if the window is painted black, the house is dark. Our eyes are like that window. If we often watch videos that frighten us, laugh at others or are very violent, the window in our heart slowly darkens; if we often watch things that make us thankful, brave and loving, our heart becomes bright. This isn’t only for children. Mom and Dad need to check their windows too.
ask: Is there a video or game that left you feeling uncomfortable, upset or scared after watching it?
What do you think Mom and Dad look at on their phones most? What would you like to say to us?
soldier.do: Do a “window check” as a family: each person names one thing that makes their heart bright and one that might make it dark, and then pray for one another.

youth.talk: Sometimes after scrolling my phone I feel worse: other people seem to be living more exciting lives and I seem like a failure. I think you may feel this too, maybe even more strongly, because your generation is compared every day. Jesus said the eye is the lamp of the body. I’ve begun to ask myself: does what I look at make my heart brighter or darker? I’m still learning, and I’d like to hear your experience.
ask: How do you usually feel after scrolling social media?
What kind of phone user do you think Mom and Dad are? Escaping, working, comparing, or using it as a babysitter?
youth.do: Parent and child each open their phone’s screen-time record, look at it together and talk about how it feels. Parents share first, and neither criticizes the other.

fam.pray: Lord Jesus, please make our eyes bright like lamps, looking at beautiful things. When we want to hide in a screen, help us to come to you and to come to our family. Amen.

lessons.title: Who Is Shaping My Child’s Heart?
lessons.theme: I believe: God’s word shapes our family more than any algorithm

v: Therefore I urge you, brothers, by the mercies of God, to present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable to God, which is your spiritual service.
Don’t be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may prove what is the good, well-pleasing, and perfect will of God.

lessons.still: Imagine yourself standing in a fast current that keeps pushing you downstream. Find a rock in the water and stand on it, and say to the Lord, “Lord, you are the place where I stand.” Stand quietly for a while.
teach: Paul says, “Don’t be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind.” To be “conformed” means to be pressed into a shape, like making mooncakes: dough is pressed into a mold and comes out with the mold’s pattern. This world has its molds every day: what is beautiful, what is success, what is worth pursuing, what it takes to be loved. If we are not careful, we are pressed into the shape it wants, and we don’t even notice.

The molds of the digital age are closer than in any other age. The algorithm is like a salesman who never sleeps. It remembers which video your child lingered on for a few extra seconds and keeps sending similar ones. Day after day, a child’s views on body image, money, friendship, sex and success are shaped without his noticing. It never asks the parents’ permission first. And the parents themselves are often being shaped by the same molds.

But we need not live in fear. Paul’s way out is not to flee the world but to be “transformed by the renewing of your mind.” God’s word, God’s love and a family that truly loves one another are a deeper mold than any algorithm. What parents can do is not seal their children off from the world, but bring them back before God day after day, so that they may “prove what is the good, well-pleasing, and perfect will of God.” Today, move from knowing to conviction, and write down your “I believe.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: A shift in perspective, from worldly to godly, from temporary to eternal. The algorithm shapes people by “what you like”; God renews people by “who he is.” When parents are renewed first, the family has a different mold. Change the way you think and your life changes; change your life and your daily living changes.
q: Who is God? — God doesn’t only want us to avoid the world; he wants to renew our minds. What kind of God is he?
Who am I? — Which of my values were actually shaped by advertising and social media?
How should I respond? — Write your “I believe”: I believe God’s word…; I believe my child…; I believe our family…
lessons.jesus: When Jesus was tempted in the wilderness, the devil set all the kingdoms of the world and their glory before his eyes. He was not drawn in, and did not argue with him, but answered with God’s word: “It is written.” Jesus shows us a heart shaped by God’s word that can stand even under the strongest temptation.
lessons.pray: Heavenly Father, I confess that my mind is often shaped by the world’s molds: afraid my child will fall behind, envying other people’s success, led around by a screen. I believe your word has more power than any algorithm. Renew my mind and my children’s minds, so that our whole family may prove what is your good, well-pleasing and perfect will. Amen.
acts: Write three “I believe” statements: I believe God’s word…; I believe my child…; I believe our family…
Find one thing you recently wanted to buy or pursue because of advertising or social media, and weigh it again before God
Tonight, spend ten minutes reading a passage of Scripture instead of scrolling your phone before bed
lessons.noon: “Don’t be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind.” — Lord, renew my mind with your own hands today.

fam.key: God’s word shapes me, not a screen.

lamb.do: Play with clay or dough together: press a circle with the rim of a cup, then hold your baby’s little hands and squeeze it into a heart shape.
lamb.say: God made you with love, and you are God’s treasure.

sprout.story: Grandma was making pineapple cakes. She pressed the dough into a little mold, and when she took it out it was square. Xiaoan asked, “Why is every one the same?” Grandma said, “Because the mold is square. Our hearts can be pressed into different shapes too. If we often watch cartoons that are fierce, our hearts become fierce; if we often listen to God’s word, our hearts become more and more like Jesus.” Xiaoan said loudly, “I want Jesus’ mold!”
sprout.ask: Who would you like your heart to be like?
sprout.do: Make a heart from clay or thick paper and draw a cross on it. Say together: “Jesus, please be the mold for my heart.”

soldier.story: The Chen brothers in Singapore recently became hooked on a gaming channel. The older brother, Weien, noticed that he was talking more and more like the streamer: he liked mocking people who lost and kept saying, “You’re useless.” Dad didn’t scold him. He watched a clip with him and asked, “What do you think he’s teaching you about how to see other people?” Weien was stunned. Paul says not to be pressed into the world’s shape but to let God renew our minds. What we often watch and listen to slowly makes us into a certain kind of person.
ask: What ways of talking or thinking have you picked up from the channels or games you watch most?
How do you think Jesus sees people who are laughed at?
soldier.do: Each person writes an “I believe” card: “I believe God says I am…” and sticks it on their bedroom door, as a reminder of who defines us.

youth.talk: I used to think it was enough if you just didn’t watch bad things. Later I realized that what influences people is not only the obviously bad things but the “normal” things pushed at you every day: what counts as good-looking, what counts as popular, how much money counts as success. Honestly, these things influence me too. Paul says not to be conformed to this world but to have our minds renewed. I’d like to think with you: how many of our ideas were fed to us by our phones?
ask: What is the one thing you think the internet most wants your generation to believe?
What is one thing about yourself that you are sure “God said, not the internet”?
youth.do: Parent and child each write three “I believe” statements, swap and read them, and then each add a Bible verse to the other’s as support.

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you that your word is good. Please keep our hearts from being pressed into another shape by the voices in screens, and make us more and more like Jesus. In Jesus’ name, amen.

lessons.title: Put the Phone Down, Sit at the Lord’s Feet
lessons.theme: Only one thing is needed: presence first, busyness after

v: As they went on their way, he entered into a certain village, and a certain woman named Martha received him into her house.
She had a sister called Mary, who also sat at Jesus’ feet and heard his word.
But Martha was distracted with much serving, and she came up to him, and said, “Lord, don’t you care that my sister left me to serve alone? Ask her therefore to help me.”
Jesus answered her, “Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things,
but one thing is needed. Mary has chosen the good part, which will not be taken away from her.”

lessons.still: Breathe deeply three times. Imagine sitting at Jesus’ feet like Mary, with no to-do list and no notification sounds. Say just one sentence: “Lord, I am here.”
teach: Martha was not doing anything wrong; she was serving Jesus. But the Bible says she “was distracted with much serving.” Jesus gently called her name twice: “Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things, but one thing is needed.” Today the “many things” often hide in our phones: group chats, work notifications, shopping deals, news alerts. Every ping says, “Look at me, quick!”

Practice does not start with a big plan but with one small change. For example, set “screen-free times,” such as dinner and the hour before bed; set “screen-free zones,” such as the dining table and the bedrooms; turn off unnecessary push notifications; put the whole family’s charging spot in the living room instead of at the bedside. These are not laws but ways to keep “the good part” for God and for family. A boundary is like a riverbank: it is not there to block the water but to make it flow in the right direction.

Mr. Lin in Taichung is an engineer who still answered work messages after leaving the office. He and his wife agreed that from seven to half past eight every evening, both their phones would go into a basket by the door. The first few days were very awkward, and his hand kept reaching for it. On the third day his eight-year-old son pulled him downstairs to play badminton, telling him about school as they played. Mr. Lin said it was the first time in months that he had heard his son talk so much.
lessons.light: 321 Light: People matter more than tasks, and relationships matter more than things. A screen is not a sin in itself, but when it makes us neglect people for the sake of tasks, we have drifted from God’s order. Letting Jesus reign means letting him decide what the one needed thing is.
q: Who is God? — Jesus said “Martha, Martha” twice. How does he see you in your busyness?
Who am I? — Of the “many things” in my phone, which could actually wait?
How should I respond? — Which screen-free time or screen-free zone will I set up in our home today?
lessons.jesus: Jesus did not scold Martha for being busy; he invited her back to what matters most. He lived this way himself: in a pressing crowd he stopped to respond to the woman who touched his clothes; while hurrying along he stopped to call to Zacchaeus in the tree. He shows us that real presence takes choosing and letting go.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, thank you for calling my name so gently. I confess that I am often pulled along by many things and am absent even in front of my family. Today I choose the good part: to sit at your feet first, and then to sit beside my children. Help our whole family keep our screen-free times so that we truly see one another. Amen.
acts: Tonight agree with your family on a screen-free stretch of at least thirty minutes, with the parents’ phones going into the basket first
Turn off three unnecessary push notifications on your phone
Move tonight’s phone charging spot to the living room and don’t take it into the bedroom
lessons.noon: “One thing is needed. Mary has chosen the good part.” — Lord, right now I put down the many things and come first to your feet.

fam.key: Put down the screen and see your family.

lamb.do: Sit on the floor and let your baby crawl into your lap. Turn off the sound of the TV and phone, and just pat him gently and hum a hymn.
lamb.say: There’s no phone now, only you and me, and Jesus.

sprout.story: One day Jesus visited Martha’s home. Martha was busy cooking, setting out bowls and wiping the table, rushing about. But her sister Mary sat at Jesus’ feet and listened closely to him. Martha got cross: “Jesus, tell my sister to come and help me!” Jesus said gently, “Martha, you are busy with too many things. The most important thing is to be with me.”
sprout.ask: What do you like doing best as a whole family?
sprout.do: Make a “phone sleeping basket”: let your child decorate a box with stickers, and before dinner invite him to collect everyone’s phones into it, saying, “The phones are going to sleep, and we’re going to talk!”

soldier.story: The Huang family in Ipoh, Malaysia, has four children. In the living room everyone was often staring at their own screen, and though they sat together, it was as if they lived in different worlds. One day the youngest said, “Our home is so quiet, like a library.” Her parents were sad to hear it. So the family held a meeting and made a “Huang family rule”: at dinner and for an hour afterward, all the phones go into the basket, and they play a board game or go for a walk together. Jesus told Martha that only one thing is needed, being with him; and those who love him will treasure being with one another too.
ask: If our family had a screen-free time, what would you most like us to do together?
Who in our family do you think finds it hardest to put down the phone? How can we help?
soldier.do: Set this week’s “screen-free time” as a family, write it on the whiteboard or the fridge, and let the children be in charge of reminding everyone and collecting the phones.

youth.talk: I know that for you a phone isn’t only entertainment; it’s connected to your friends and your homework, and being told to put it down suddenly may make you worry about missing something. So I don’t want to just demand it of you. I want to start with myself: in the evening I will put my phone down for a while and be with the family. I’d also like to invite you to think about whether there is a time you would be willing to try.
ask: When in the day do you think it would be easiest to put the phone down?
If the phone isn’t with you, what are you most afraid of missing?
youth.do: Parent and child choose a “shared screen-free time” together, such as dinner or weekend breakfast, try it for one week, and talk about how it felt at the weekend.

fam.pray: Lord Jesus, thank you that you love being with us most of all. Help us put down our screens and truly see and hear one another. In Jesus’ name, amen.

lessons.title: Lord, Search My Screen
lessons.theme: Review & Adjust: letting God see my heart, and my phone

v: Search me, God, and know my heart. Try me, and know my thoughts.
See if there is any wicked way in me, and lead me in the everlasting way.

lessons.still: Open your phone’s usage record or photo album and look through this week as if turning the pages of a diary. Then put the phone down and say to the Lord, “You know it all. Please look at it with me.”
teach: In Psalm 139 David marvels that God knows when he sits down and when he rises up, and even every word on his tongue. In the light of being so completely known, he doesn’t hide. Instead he says, “Search me, God, and know my heart. Try me, and know my thoughts.” Being seen through by God is not frightening surveillance but the healing of being loved. Just as a doctor must see the wound clearly to bandage it, God searches us so that he may “lead me in the everlasting way.”

This week we saw that we should set no vile thing before our eyes; that the eye is the lamp of the body; that we must not be pressed into the world’s mold; and that only one thing is needed. Today is not about grading ourselves but about asking honestly: what happened at home this week when I put my phone down? And what did I miss when I picked it up? Bring both answers to God: the good, give the glory to him; what was missed, hand over to him to heal.

Adjustments should be specific and small. Instead of saying “I’ll use my phone less,” say, “For one hour after dinner every day, my phone stays in the living room.” Shufen, a single mother in Vancouver, found that her hardest time was scrolling before bed, often until midnight, which left her with no patience for her children the next day. She asked her fourteen-year-old daughter to help set up her phone’s sleep mode, and her daughter laughed and said, “Mom, I’ll keep an eye on you.” Sometimes adjusting begins with being willing to be reminded by your child.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Review, adjustment and repetition are the necessary road to changing the way we think. A proud parent only checks the children’s phones; a humble parent first lets God and the family check his own. Humility leads to humility, and when parents admit things first, children are willing to open their hearts too.
q: Who is God? — God searches me and knows me, yet still leads me in the everlasting way. What kind of love is this?
Who am I? — At what moment this week did I miss my family because of a screen? At what moment did I choose the good part?
How should I respond? — What is the one specific phone habit I will adjust next week? Who can remind me?
lessons.jesus: Peter denied his Lord three times, yet Jesus did not give up on him. After the resurrection, he prepared a charcoal fire and fish by the sea and asked him three times, “Do you love me?” Jesus searches the heart in order to restore, not to shame. He looks with the same gentle eyes as he walks with us back through this week’s failures and progress.
lessons.pray: God, search me and know my heart. For the moments this week when I put down my phone and was truly with my family, thank you; for the time stolen by screens, please forgive me. Make me humble, willing to be reminded by my family, and ready to adjust step by step, and lead our whole family in the everlasting way. Amen.
acts: Talk with your spouse for ten minutes: what was different at home this week when you put the phone down? When was it hardest to put down?
Ask your child: “This week, did I become more like Jesus, really seeing you and listening to you?” Only listen; don’t defend yourself
Write down one specific phone adjustment for next week, and ask a family member to be your reminder
lessons.noon: “Search me, God, and know my heart. Try me, and know my thoughts.” — Lord, my heart and my phone are open before you.

fam.key: I’m willing to let God see my heart.

lamb.do: Play “find it” with your baby: hide his favorite toy under a small blanket, let him find it, and hug him happily when he does.
lamb.say: God sees everything, and he is always watching you and loving you.

sprout.story: Xiaole secretly hid cookie crumbs under the sofa, afraid Mommy would find out. But that night the ants came out! Xiaole was nervous. He hung his head and said to Mommy, “I’m sorry, I hid them.” Mommy wasn’t angry. She hugged him and said, “Thank you for telling the truth. Let’s clean it up together!” God is like this too. He knows everything, he loves it when we tell the truth, and then he helps us become better.
sprout.ask: Is there something this week you would like to tell Mommy and Daddy the truth about?
sprout.do: Clean one small corner of the house together as a family, saying as you clean, “God, please clean our hearts too.”

soldier.story: David was a king, yet he prayed like this: asking God to look at his heart, to see whether anything in him was wrong, and to lead him on the right path. That takes great courage! Most people are afraid of others seeing their faults, but David knew that God sees us in order to help us. This week our family tried to use screens less and look at one another more. Now it is time to check, like David: what went well? What still needs to change? Mom and Dad will check together with you.
ask: Of our screen-free times this week, which did you like best? Why?
Do you think Mom and Dad improved with their phones this week? What still needs to change?
soldier.do: Hold a ten-minute family meeting: each person names one screen habit that went well this week and one they want to adjust next week. Mom and Dad go first, and at the end the whole family picks one adjustment to make together.

youth.talk: This week I tried to put my phone down, and honestly, some days I managed it and some days I scrolled until late again. I found I depend on it more than I thought. I don’t want to check only your phone and not let anyone check mine. So I’d like you to be my “honest mirror”: do you think I paid better attention to the family this week? When did you actually wish I would put my phone down?
ask: Was there a moment this week when you wished I would put my phone down and I didn’t?
What do you think is the one screen habit our family most needs to adjust next week?
youth.do: Parents first apologize for one time they neglected their child because of the phone, and then write down together with the child one screen adjustment that both sides will keep next week.

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, you know everything and you love us always. Thank you for walking with us through this week. Help us next week to see one another more and to be pulled away by screens less. In Jesus’ name, amen.

27.memT: I will set no vile thing before my eyes. I hate the deeds of faithless men. They will not cling to me.

mem.t: Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.

sat.d: Prepare a few scenario cards, for example: “A stranger messages you offering free game credits if you send a photo.” “Classmates in a group chat are laughing at someone and telling everyone to forward the joke.” “The game says ten more minutes and you’ll level up.” “Your phone shows a prize notification and asks you to tap a link.” Take turns drawing a card and act out your response: stop, don’t reply, take a screenshot, tell Mom or Dad. Parents draw cards and model it too. Finish with a snack and declare together: “In our family, telling the truth never gets you scolded.”

sun: When you think about the risks your child may meet online, what worries you most? What kind of parent does that worry make you?
When something happens to your child online, will he come and tell you first? Why, or why not?
Next week, which online safety agreement will you make together with your child? You could also invite another family to try it with you.

lessons.title: Keep Your Heart Above All
lessons.theme: The heart of online safety is guarding our child’s heart and the parent-child relationship

v: My son, attend to my words. Turn your ear to my sayings.
Let them not depart from your eyes. Keep them in the center of your heart.
For they are life to those who find them, and health to their whole body.
Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.

lessons.still: Think quietly: where is my child right now? And where is his heart? There is no need to worry. Just bring your children’s names one by one before the Lord and say, “Lord, you love him more than I do.”
teach: Solomon is like a father sitting beside his son, saying, “My son, attend to my words,” and then he gives the core of the whole passage: “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.” In ancient times the most important part of a city was its gate. The watchmen guarded it day and night, because once the enemy came in through the gate, the whole city was lost. The heart is a person’s city gate.

Today our gates have one more entrance: the “online gate.” Standing at this gate, a child may meet several kinds of risk: pornography, which often pops up unexpectedly; cyberbullying, being laughed at or shut out in group chats or comments; strangers posing as friends, who use kindness and gifts to win trust, photos or a meeting; and games and short videos designed so that you can’t stop. We know these things not to frighten ourselves but to know where the gate is.

Yet guarding a child’s heart cannot depend on filtering software alone. Software is like a city wall: useful, but there are always gaps. The real gatekeeper is a heart filled with love, and a parent-child relationship in which it is safe to tell the truth. When your child meets something frightening or shameful online, who is the first person he thinks of? If the answer is “Mom and Dad must never find out,” even the best software cannot guard him.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Out of the heart come the wellsprings of life: use your heart, relying on the Holy Spirit, not your head, relying on yourself. Parents who protect their children only by control and technology are using their heads and relying on themselves; parents who first guard their own hearts and then win their children’s hearts with love are letting Jesus be the gatekeeper of the home.
q: Who is God? — God is like a father saying “My son, attend to my words.” How does he keep my heart?
Who am I? — Do I care more about guarding my child’s phone, or guarding my child’s heart?
How should I respond? — When my child meets trouble online, will he think of me first? What can I do to open that door?
lessons.jesus: Jesus said, “I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep.” He knows his own sheep, and they know his voice; when the wolf comes, he does not run away. He protects the flock not by shutting the sheep in but through close relationship. The more familiar a child is with the sound of his parents’ love, the better he can tell the voice of a stranger.
lessons.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for keeping my heart. I confess that when I think of what my children might meet online, I am often afraid and often don’t know what to do. Be the gatekeeper of our home, and guard my children’s hearts and mine. Help me build a relationship in which my child is willing to tell the truth, so that when danger comes, he thinks of you first, and of us. Amen.
acts: Write down the apps, games and social platforms your child uses most, circle the ones you don’t understand, and ask your child to teach you this week
Say to your child today: “Whatever you meet online, you can tell me. I will listen first and not scold first.”
Check the Wi-Fi and the parental controls on your child’s devices and adjust them to his age
lessons.noon: “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.” — Lord, please guard my child’s heart today, and guard mine.

fam.key: I will guard my heart.

lamb.do: Gently cup your baby’s little hand in both of yours like a tiny house and say “safe, safe,” then open your hands and kiss his palm.
lamb.say: God keeps you safe, and Mommy and Daddy keep you safe too.

sprout.story: Baa-baa the little lamb lived in the shepherd’s sheepfold. One night a big wolf outside the door copied the shepherd’s voice: “Little lamb, come out! I’ll take you to eat yummy grass!” Baa-baa listened carefully: “No, that’s not my shepherd’s voice!” He did not go out, and he ran quickly to tell the shepherd. The shepherd hugged him and said, “Well done. Telling me was exactly right!”
sprout.ask: If someone you don’t know offers you candy, or tells you on the tablet to tap here and tap there, what will you do?
sprout.do: Play “Whose voice is it?”: Mom and Dad take turns talking in different voices while your child closes his eyes and guesses who it is. At the end practice saying together: “I won’t listen to people I don’t know. I’ll tell Mommy and Daddy!”

soldier.story: Solomon says to guard your heart, because everything in your life flows from it. The heart is like the gate of a city. There are “enemies” online who want to come through the gate: someone pretends to be a friend your age, sends you game credits, and then asks for your photo or address; someone laughs at a classmate in a group chat and tells everyone to forward it; some pictures suddenly pop up and make you very uncomfortable. A good gatekeeper doesn’t open the gate to someone suspicious, and reports it straight away. In our family, Mom and Dad are the people you can report to.
ask: If someone online tells you to keep a secret and not to tell Mom and Dad, what do you think that means?
Have you ever seen something online that made you uncomfortable or scared? Would you like to tell us about it?
soldier.do: Write down the “three steps at the gate” as a family: stop and don’t reply, take a screenshot or make a note, tell Mom and Dad straight away. Stick it up beside the computer or tablet.

youth.talk: I know you understand the internet better than I do, and sometimes what I worry about may look exaggerated to you. But I also know that some things online can really hurt people: being laughed at, being compared, seeing things you don’t want to see, even someone pretending to care when they have other motives. I don’t want to manage you by fear. I want to stand on the same side as you. If you ever run into trouble, I want you to know that you can come to me.
ask: What do you think are the most common dangers or pressures people your age meet online?
If something bad happened, what would make you afraid to tell Mom and Dad?
youth.do: Have a one-to-one talk with your child. Parents go first, telling about a mistake they made online or a time they nearly got scammed, and then make an agreement: “When something happens, come to me. I will listen all the way through before I say anything.”

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for keeping us safe. Please guard our hearts, and when we see something bad online or meet a bad person, give us the courage to speak up. In Jesus’ name, amen.

lessons.title: A Fearful Parent, or a Loving One?
lessons.theme: There is no fear in love: am I protecting my child with fear, or with love?

v: There is no fear in love; but perfect love casts out fear, because fear has punishment. He who fears is not made perfect in love.
For God didn’t give us a spirit of fear, but of power, love, and self-control.

lessons.still: Ask the Holy Spirit to light up your worries. Name specifically the thing you most fear your child will meet online, and then say to the Lord, “Lord, I give this fear to you.”
teach: At the mention of online safety, many parents’ hearts tighten at once: scams, sexual exploitation and bullying in the news seem as if they could happen to their own child at any moment. Fear often pushes parents to one of two extremes. One is the “controlling” type: reading messages in secret, banning everything, searching every day, so the child learns to hide. The other is the “hands-off” type: feeling they don’t understand technology, they simply leave it alone, or pretend the problem does not exist.

John says, “There is no fear in love; but perfect love casts out fear.” And Paul reminds us, “For God didn’t give us a spirit of fear, but of power, love, and self-control.” Power is daring to set boundaries and to talk about the things that are hard to say. Love is letting the child know that love lies behind the boundaries. Self-control is seeing our child’s world clearly, neither naive nor panicked.

Mr. He in Penang found his son still playing a game in the middle of the night, and in a rage he smashed the phone on the floor. From then on his son hid his phone better, and between father and son there was only a cold war. Later Mr. He admitted in his small group, “That day I wasn’t protecting him. I was too scared and too angry myself.” Fear makes us grip tighter, but love lets us walk closer. Seeing which kind of parent we are is the beginning of change.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Pride is leaving our place and grabbing power. Parents who want to guarantee their children one hundred per cent safe by control are really trying to take God’s place; and giving up in helplessness is escaping the steward’s place. Humility is returning to our place: doing the steward’s duties and handing the results to God.
q: Who is God? — God gave me a spirit of power, love and self-control. How does he cast out my fear?
Who am I? — Facing my child’s online life, am I more of a controlling parent, a hands-off parent, or one learning to watch over with love?
How should I respond? — What is my biggest fear? What has it led me to do to my child?
lessons.jesus: The disciples cried out in panic in the storm: “Save us, Lord! We are dying!” Jesus first asked them, “Why are you fearful, O you of little faith?” and then got up and rebuked the wind and the sea. He did not deny that the storm was real, but he let the disciples see that the Lord in the boat with them is greater than the storm. As parents face the storms of the online world, this same Lord is with them.
lessons.pray: Lord, I confess that when I face my child’s online world I am often led by fear: sometimes I grip too tightly, sometimes I am too weak to let go. Thank you that you gave me not a spirit of fear but of power, love and self-control. Cast out my fear with your perfect love, so that I may watch over my child with love and not control him with fear. Amen.
acts: Write down your three biggest worries about your child’s online life and pray over each one
Think of the last time you lost your temper with your child over the phone or the internet, and find a chance to apologize for your attitude today
Spend fifteen minutes looking up the parental settings or safety features of the app your child uses most
lessons.noon: “There is no fear in love; but perfect love casts out fear.” — Lord, please cast the fear out of my heart with your love.

fam.key: God’s love means I am not afraid.

lamb.do: Hold your baby close so his ear rests on your chest and he can hear your heartbeat, pat his back slowly and whisper, “Don’t be scared, don’t be scared.”
lamb.say: God is here, and Mommy and Daddy are here too. You don’t need to be afraid.

sprout.story: Xiaoyu was watching a cartoon on the tablet when a very scary picture suddenly popped up, and she was so frightened that she threw the tablet onto the sofa. She was afraid of being scolded, so she hid in her room. Mommy found her, crouched down and asked, “What happened?” Xiaoyu told her in a small voice. Mommy hugged her and said, “Thank you for telling me. It isn’t your fault. If you see something scary again, come to Mommy, all right?” Xiaoyu nodded, and she wasn’t scared any more.
sprout.ask: If you saw something scary on the tablet, what would you do?
sprout.do: Practice “cover, go, tell”: pretend you see a scary picture, cover the tablet, walk away, and go and tell Mom and Dad. When your child does it, give a big hug.

soldier.story: Zhihao, ten, from Kuala Lumpur, had been playing an online game. Someone messaged him in the game and said they could give him rare gear if he gave them his account password. Zhihao really wanted it, but was afraid that if he told his parents he would be banned from the game. After two days of hesitating, he told them anyway. Dad was not angry. Instead he said, “Thank you. You made a very brave choice. This is a scam, and we’ll deal with it together.” Father and son changed the password together and reported the account. Love means you don’t need to be afraid to tell the truth.
ask: If you ran into trouble online, what would make you afraid to tell Mom and Dad?
What could Mom and Dad do to make it easier for you to tell the truth?
soldier.do: Mom and Dad promise their child one sentence and write it on a card: “When you tell us something yourself, we will first thank you, and then deal with it together.” Everyone signs it, and it goes on the fridge.

youth.talk: To be honest, sometimes when I am strict about your phone, behind it is my own fear. I am afraid you will meet bad people, see bad things or be bullied, but the way I handle it sometimes only makes you want to avoid me. The Bible says there is no fear in love. I want to learn to walk with you through the online world with love, not control you with fear. What do you think I need to change?
ask: On the internet question, do you think Mom and Dad are more controlling or more hands-off?
How would you like us to “help” you with online safety, rather than “manage” you?
youth.do: Parents apologize to their child for one time they were too controlling or too hands-off, and then ask the child to suggest one approach that is both safe and trusting, and try it together for two weeks.

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for loving us. When we are afraid, please hold us; when we get something wrong, give us courage to tell the truth. In Jesus’ name, amen.

lessons.title: The LORD Is Your Keeper
lessons.theme: I believe: God is the final protector, and I am a faithful watchman

v: He will not allow your foot to be moved. He who keeps you will not slumber.
Behold, he who keeps Israel will neither slumber nor sleep.
The LORD is your keeper. The LORD is your shade on your right hand.
The sun will not harm you by day, nor the moon by night.
The LORD will keep you from all evil. He will keep your soul.
The LORD will keep your going out and your coming in, from this time forward, and forever more.

lessons.still: Lift your head and look at the sky outside the window, or into the distance. Like the psalmist, ask, “Where does my help come from?” and then answer quietly, “My help comes from the LORD, who made heaven and earth.”
teach: Psalm 121 was sung by pilgrims on their way up to Jerusalem. On the road there were scorching sun, cold nights and robbers. They lifted their eyes to the hills and declared, “He who keeps you will not slumber.” In just eight verses the word “keep” comes again and again. This is the best song of watching for parents: when children leave for school, lie in bed scrolling their phones, or sit in their rooms wearing headphones, God sees even those places we cannot see.

This brings an important change of view: parents are watchmen, not almighty. We must do our duty: understand the platforms our children use, set suitable protection, and give company and conversation. But we cannot watch our children twenty-four hours a day, and we don’t need to. When we give God his place back, we are released from anxiety and can accompany our children with a peaceful heart.

This doesn’t mean parents can let go and do nothing. A watchman must stay awake, look out and sound the trumpet. Like a watchman on the city wall, he is not the owner of the city but he keeps watch faithfully. Today, declare: I believe the LORD, who keeps my child, will not slumber. I believe God has called me to be a faithful watchman. I believe love and a real relationship are my child’s best protection.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Let people be people and God be God. Parents do what people should do: watch, teach, accompany. What only God can do, they hand back to him: watching over a child’s whole life and changing a child’s heart. When humility returns to its place, anxiety is replaced by trust, and we can let our children grow up step by step.
q: Who is God? — How is the God who “will neither slumber nor sleep” watching over my child at this moment?
Who am I? — Do I often try to be my child’s “almighty protector,” until I wear myself out and weigh him down?
How should I respond? — Write your “I believe” declaration: I believe the one who keeps my child is…; I believe my responsibility is…
lessons.jesus: On the night he was betrayed, Jesus prayed for his disciples: “I pray not that you would take them from the world, but that you would keep them from the evil one.” He did not hide his disciples away; he placed them in the Father’s hands and sent them into the world. This prayer of Jesus is the best pattern for parents praying for their children.
lessons.pray: Heavenly Father, I confess that I often want to be my child’s almighty protector, worrying day and night, forgetting that you are the God who neither slumbers nor sleeps. I believe it is you who keep my child. Help me do my part as a watchman: to accompany, to teach, to set suitable protection; and give back to you what only you can do. Keep my child from the evil one. Amen.
acts: Write your “I believe” declaration: I believe the LORD keeps my child; I believe my responsibility is…; I believe our family…
Use Jesus’ prayer in John 17 to pray by name for each child, asking God to keep him from the evil one
Today share with your child one time God protected you in your own life
lessons.noon: “The LORD is your keeper. The LORD is your shade on your right hand.” — Lord, I place my child in your hands, and you will not slumber.

fam.key: God keeps me and never dozes off.

lamb.do: When your baby falls asleep, rest your hand gently on him and softly sing a hymn, then say a blessing over him.
lamb.say: God doesn’t sleep. He watches over you all night.

sprout.story: One night Xiaoyu couldn’t sleep and asked Daddy, “Daddy, when you’re asleep, who looks after us?” Daddy said, “God does! God never dozes off and never sleeps. When Mommy and Daddy are asleep, God is still awake looking after us.” Xiaoyu smiled: “God is so amazing, he never gets tired!” He hugged his teddy bear and fell asleep, feeling safe.
sprout.ask: When do you feel afraid? What can you say to God?
sprout.do: Play the “watchman” game: the whole family pretends to be asleep and snoring while one person is the watchman, walking around with wide-open eyes and saying, “God is watching over you!” Take turns being the watchman.

soldier.story: In ancient times there were watchmen on the city walls. Day and night they stood high up, and when they saw enemies coming they blew a trumpet to get the whole city ready. But watchmen also got tired and dozed off. The psalm says the God who keeps us “will neither slumber nor sleep.” Mom and Dad are like watchmen on the wall: we set up protection and we remind you; but there are times we cannot see. The one who really protects you twenty-four hours a day is God. So we rely on God together, and we keep watch together.
ask: What do you think is different between the protection Mom and Dad set up online and God’s protection?
How can you help watch over yourself, and your younger siblings or friends?
soldier.do: Make a “watchman list” as a family: write down people you can ask for help when something happens online (Mom and Dad, grandparents, teachers, Sunday school teachers), put “God” at the very top, and stick it up by the desk.

youth.talk: You are growing up, and one day there will be places I cannot manage or see. Honestly, that makes me uneasy. But I read Psalm 121, and it reminds me that it is God who keeps you, not me. My responsibility is to accompany you, remind you, trust you, and pray for you. I also want you to know that you don’t face the online world alone: you have God, and you have us.
ask: Which of Mom and Dad’s protective measures seem reasonable to you? Which make you feel you aren’t trusted?
How do you keep yourself safe online?
youth.do: Parent and child go through the privacy settings on the child’s accounts together: who can see, who can message, whether the location is public. The child does the tapping, the parent sits alongside, and at the end the parent prays a blessing over the child.

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you that you never sleep and always keep us safe. Please watch over our going out and our coming in, at school, at home and online. In Jesus’ name, amen.

lessons.title: A Home That Walks in the Light
lessons.theme: Bring online life into the light and set age-appropriate family online rules

v: For you were once darkness, but are now light in the Lord. Walk as children of light,
for the fruit of the Spirit is in all goodness and righteousness and truth,
proving what is well pleasing to the Lord.
Have no fellowship with the unfruitful deeds of darkness, but rather even reprove them.
“All things are lawful for me,” but not all things are expedient. “All things are lawful for me,” but I will not be brought under the power of anything.

lessons.still: Imagine a lamp being lit and shining into every corner of your home, and into every person’s phone. Say to the Lord, “Lord, let your light shine into our home, so that we have nothing to hide.”
teach: Paul says, “You were once darkness, but are now light in the Lord. Walk as children of light.” The greatest dangers online often happen in the dark: late at night behind a closed door, in deleted messages, in a stranger’s “this is our secret.” The first principle of family online safety is to bring online life back into the light, and that includes the parents’ own phones.

The details can be adjusted by age. Preschool: use only beside an adult, with content chosen by parents first. Elementary school: keep devices in shared spaces such as the living room, use parental controls and age ratings, never give out real name, school or address, and never meet online friends. Secondary school: hand back independence step by step, go through privacy settings together, and agree that devices stay outside the bedroom late at night. At any age: if anyone asks you to keep a secret, asks for your photo, or asks to meet you, tell your parents at once.

Paul also says, “All things are lawful for me, but I will not be brought under the power of anything.” Games and short videos are not sin in themselves, but when a child lies for them, loses sleep, becomes irritable, or gives up other things he loves, it needs to be taken seriously. If a child is facing online blackmail, sexual exploitation or serious bullying, or has fallen into use he cannot control, keep the evidence and seek help quickly from the school, professional agencies, the police and the church’s pastors.
lessons.light: 321 Light: People matter more than tasks, and relationships matter more than rules. Rules without relationship only produce hiding; relationship without rules leaves a child unprotected. When parents walk in the light first, and are willing to let the family see their own phones, humility leads to humility, and the home becomes a home of children of light.
q: Who is God? — God is light. How does he bring me from darkness into light?
Who am I? — In my own online life, is there anything I hide and dare not let my family see?
How should I respond? — Which three online safety rules will our family make today?
lessons.jesus: Jesus said, “I am the light of the world. He who follows me will not walk in the darkness, but will have the light of life.” He is not afraid to bring people’s sin into the light, because his light is not for shaming but for healing. The Lord who accepts us in the light also makes our home a place where children can bring their darkness into the light.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, you are the light of the world. Shine on every screen in our home and on my own online life, and let me walk in the light first. Give me wisdom to set suitable rules for my children’s ages, and to support those rules with love and a real relationship. If my child has already been hurt or bound, heal and free him, and lead us to the help we need. Amen.
acts: Today set the charging spot for every device in the home in the living room, including the parents’ own
Make three “family online rules” with your child, write them down and stick them up beside the computer or tablet
Set the parental controls and content ratings on the devices according to your child’s age, and explain to him why
lessons.noon: “You were once darkness, but are now light in the Lord. Walk as children of light.” — Lord, let every screen in our home be in your light.

fam.key: In the light, I don’t need to hide.

lamb.do: Turn off the lights, switch on a flashlight, shine it on your baby’s favorite toy for him to find, then shine it on your face and his, and laugh together.
lamb.say: Jesus is the light. With the light, there’s nothing to fear.

sprout.story: One night the power went out and the house was pitch dark. Xiaomi was very scared and bumped into the table leg. Daddy took out a flashlight, click, and the light came on! Xiaomi could see the way, and she saw Daddy’s smiling face, and she wasn’t scared any more. Daddy said, “Jesus is like this light. In the light we can see clearly, and we don’t have to hide.”
sprout.ask: Is there anything you would like to tell Mom and Dad?
sprout.do: Play “good secret, bad secret”: Mom and Dad give some examples (preparing a birthday surprise for the family is a good secret; someone telling you not to tell Mom and Dad, which makes you uncomfortable, is a bad secret), and your child answers with thumbs up or thumbs down.

soldier.story: In Tainan, Yating saw in her class group chat that a classmate had turned an unflattering photo of another girl into a sticker. Everyone was laughing, and someone told her to forward it too. She felt it was wrong, but was afraid of being called a bad sport. At home, she told her mom. Her mom helped her think of three things to do: don’t forward it and don’t like it; send the girl a private message to show you care; hand the screenshot to the teacher. Paul says to walk as children of light. Children of light don’t join in the deeds of darkness, and they help those who are being bullied.
ask: If someone is bullying another person in a group chat, what could you do?
What kind of online rules do you think would help our family most?
soldier.do: Make three to five “family online rules” together, such as: devices stay in the living room; if a stranger asks for a photo or to meet, tell Mom and Dad; don’t forward content that laughs at others. Everyone signs.

youth.talk: I want to make our family’s online rules together with you, not decide them on my own. I know you need privacy, which is perfectly normal, and I will respect it. But about some things, like someone asking for your photo, asking you to keep a secret, asking to meet you, or you seeing a friend being bullied, I really want you to know that you can tell me right away. I won’t scold you first, and I won’t confiscate your phone straight away.
ask: Which online rules do you think are reasonable? Which need adjusting for your age?
If a friend of yours ran into trouble online, what would you advise them to do?
youth.do: Parent and child draw up an “online safety agreement” together: write down the child’s rights (privacy, being trusted) and responsibilities, and the parents’ promise (listen first, then deal with it), and both sign.

fam.pray: Lord Jesus, you are the light of the world. Help us to be children of light online too, not doing deeds of darkness, and bravely helping those who are bullied. Amen.

lessons.title: When My Child Tells the Truth, How Do I Respond?
lessons.theme: Review & Adjust: making home a place a child will come back to after he falls

v: “He arose and came to his father. But while he was still far off, his father saw him and was moved with compassion, and ran, fell on his neck, and kissed him.
The son said to him, ‘Father, I have sinned against heaven and in your sight. I am no longer worthy to be called your son.’
“But the father said to his servants, ‘Bring out the best robe and put it on him. Put a ring on his hand and sandals on his feet.
Bring the fattened calf, kill it, and let’s eat and celebrate;
for this, my son, was dead and is alive again. He was lost and is found.’ Then they began to celebrate.

lessons.still: Recall one thing your child told you this week, big or small. What was your very first reaction? What was the expression on your face? Ask the Holy Spirit to look at it with you.
teach: When the prodigal son went home, he had prepared a confession in his heart. But “while he was still far off, his father saw him and was moved with compassion, and ran, fell on his neck, and kissed him.” The father’s embrace came faster than the son’s confession. This picture is the deepest foundation of online safety: when a child has made a mistake or is in danger, is the road home open?

Imagine that one day your child says with his head down, “I accidentally saw something bad, and then I went back and looked at it on purpose.” Or: “Classmates were insulting me in the group chat, and I insulted them back.” A parent’s first reaction decides whether the child will tell next time. If it is shouting, shaming and confiscating everything at once, the child learns “next time, hide it better.” If we first thank him for telling the truth and then face it together, the child learns “home is safe.” This does not mean there are no consequences, only that consequences are handled within love and relationship.

This week we have talked about guarding the heart, love casting out fear, God as protector, and walking in the light. Today, husband and wife, look back together: is our family’s “road home” open? If in the past our reactions were so strong that our child shut the door, today is a good time to adjust. A parent apologizing first is often the key that opens a child’s heart again.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Pride provokes pride, and both lose; humility leads to humility, and both win. When a child confesses, if parents respond with pride, the relationship is broken; if they respond with the compassion of the heavenly Father, the child learns he can be honest before God too. Deal with your own heart first, then with your child’s behavior.
q: Who is God? — The heavenly Father was “moved with compassion” and “ran” to embrace his returning son. How does he treat me when I turn back?
Who am I? — When my child told me the truth this week, was my first reaction an embrace or a judgment?
How should I respond? — What is one reaction I will adjust next week? How will I let my child know that home is safe?
lessons.jesus: A woman was brought to Jesus, and everyone held a stone in their hand. Jesus said, “He who is without sin among you, let him throw the first stone at her.” When they had gone away one by one, he said to the woman, “Neither do I condemn you. Go your way. From now on, sin no more.” Grace and truth appear together in him.
lessons.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for running to embrace me while I was still far off. This week, when my child opened up to me, I was sometimes quick to blame and forgot to thank him first for his honesty. Forgive me and give me your compassion. Make our home a place a child will come back to when he falls, and let grace and truth appear together in our home. Amen.
acts: Talk with your spouse for ten minutes: when our child told us the truth this week, how did we respond? How could we be more like the heavenly Father next time?
Ask your child: “This week, have I been more like Jesus? When you talk to me, do you feel safe?” Only listen; don’t defend yourself
Write down one response you will adjust next week, for example: first say “Thank you for telling me,” and then ask what happened
lessons.noon: “While he was still far off, his father saw him and was moved with compassion.” — Lord, give me the heavenly Father’s compassion, to wait for my child and embrace him.

fam.key: Tell the truth, and home always welcomes you.

lamb.do: Play peekaboo with your baby, and when he comes out from his hiding place, open your arms and give him a big hug.
lamb.say: You’re back! Mommy and Daddy always welcome you.

sprout.story: A younger son took the money his father gave him and ran far away. He spent it all and was hungry and dirty. He thought, “I’ll go home and say sorry to Dad.” He was still far down the road when his father saw him, ran to him and hugged him tight, and gave him new clothes and held a party! Jesus said the heavenly Father is like this father: when we do wrong and come back, he opens his arms and welcomes us.
sprout.ask: When you’ve done something wrong, how do you want Mom and Dad to treat you?
sprout.do: Act out the prodigal son’s homecoming: your child walks slowly from the other side of the room, and Mom and Dad run to hug him and say, “Welcome home!” Then swap roles.

soldier.story: Ajie, eleven, from Johor Bahru, secretly used his mom’s phone to buy game credits and spent quite a lot of money. He was so frightened he could not sleep for several days, and finally he plucked up courage and told his dad. Dad was silent for a moment and then said, “Thank you for telling me yourself. That took a lot of courage.” Then he and Ajie worked out the amount, agreed that Ajie would pay it back slowly with chores and pocket money, and set purchases to need a password. Ajie said, “I thought Dad would shout at me, but he hugged me instead.” This is the father in the story of the prodigal son.
ask: Why does it take courage to tell the truth?
Was there a time this week in our family when someone told the truth and was received well?
soldier.do: Hold a family meeting: each person says one thing they wanted to say this week but haven’t (it can be very small), the others first say “Thank you for telling me,” and then together decide one thing to adjust next week.

youth.talk: I want to be honest about something: in the past when you told me things, I often started lecturing before you had finished, and even got angry. I think that made it feel dangerous to tell me the truth. I read the story of the prodigal son, where the father ran to hug him before the son had finished his confession. I really want to learn to be that kind of parent. How do you think I did this week?
ask: Was there a time this week when you felt I listened to you better?
Is there something you were afraid to tell me before? Would you like to tell me now? It’s fine if you don’t want to.
youth.do: Parents apologize to their child for one time they overreacted, and then write down together an agreement: when the child tells the truth, the parents first say “Thank you for telling me.”

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for loving us like the prodigal son’s father. When we do wrong, give us courage to tell the truth, and help us forgive one another and embrace one another. Amen.

28.memT: Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.

mem.t: Finally, brothers, whatever things are true, whatever things are honorable, whatever things are just, whatever things are pure, whatever things are lovely, whatever things are of good report: if there is any virtue and if there is anything worthy of praise, think about these things.

sat.t: Family Day: A Family Film Review
sat.d: Choose a film or cartoon suited to the youngest child in the family (parents check the summary and rating first). Make popcorn, and afterward let everyone take a turn as “film critic.” Take out six little cards from Philippians 4:8: true, honorable, just, pure, lovely, of good report. Find one example of each in the film, and also one place where the film falls short. Finally, each person gives the film one to five stars and says why, and then you talk together: “If Jesus were sitting among us watching, how would he see this story?”

sun: This week, what kind of media content did you notice you took in most? What did it quietly put into your heart?
Are you more used to “forbidding” things for your child, or to “discerning” alongside him? Share a real example.
Next week, which program, video or advertisement will you watch with your child and discuss using Philippians 4:8? You could also invite another family to a film review night.

lessons.title: Think About These Things
lessons.theme: The soul has a diet too: choosing what we think about by Philippians 4:8

v: Finally, brothers, whatever things are true, whatever things are honorable, whatever things are just, whatever things are pure, whatever things are lovely, whatever things are of good report: if there is any virtue and if there is anything worthy of praise, think about these things.
Do the things which you learned, received, heard, and saw in me, and the God of peace will be with you.

lessons.still: Think about what your eyes and ears have taken in so far today: news, messages, videos, advertisements. As if checking the day’s meals, quietly hand them over to the Lord for him to see.
teach: Paul wrote to the church in Philippi from prison, and near the end of his letter he said, “Whatever things are true, whatever things are honorable, whatever things are just, whatever things are pure, whatever things are lovely, whatever things are of good report: if there is any virtue and if there is anything worthy of praise, think about these things.” To “think about” does not mean a passing thought but turning it over again and again and letting it settle in the heart. Whatever we think about, we slowly become.

The soul has a diet too. If the body lives on fried snacks for a long time, it gets ill; if the soul lives on mockery, violence, lust, comparison and fear, it gets ill as well. Today’s parents can hardly control everything their children see: advertisements are on the bus, short clips are on classmates’ phones, and news is in everyone’s notifications. What we can do is help our children fit a “sieve” in their hearts, so that they slowly learn to discern for themselves.

The starting point of media literacy is to understand that behind every video, advertisement and post is someone who wants to get across a message: what they want you to believe, to buy, to feel. This does not mean media is all bad; many videos, films and books bring truth and beauty. Philippians 4:8 is not a list of prohibitions but a sieve, helping us keep what is good and let go of what is harmful. This sieve needs to be fitted in the parents’ own hearts first.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Scripture is my standard. Discernment does not rest on personal taste or follow the trend, but lets God’s word be the measuring rod for everything. Change the way you think and your life changes: when what parents think about changes, conversation changes, and the atmosphere of the home changes with it.
q: Who is God? — God wants us to think about what is true, honorable and lovely. What does this say about what kind of God he is?
Who am I? — This week, what I have thought about most: is it among the things in Philippians 4:8, or the very opposite?
How should I respond? — What will I take out of my “soul diet” today, and what will I add?
lessons.jesus: Jesus was surrounded by every kind of voice: the Pharisees’ questions, the crowds’ expectations, the disciples’ arguments, and even Peter urging him to avoid the cross. Jesus recognized at once whose voice that was and said, “Get behind me, Satan!” His heart was full of the Father’s words, so in the din of voices he could hear the truth and choose the truth.
lessons.pray: Lord, I confess that my heart often takes in many useless things: mockery, comparison, fear and temptation, yet I seldom think about what is true, lovely and of good report. Cleanse my soul’s diet. Teach me to discern first, so that I can discern alongside my children. Let your word be the sieve for our whole family, keeping what is good and letting go of what is harmful. Amen.
acts: Copy Philippians 4:8 onto a small card and put it by your phone or the television
Recall one advertisement or video you saw today and ask yourself: what does it want me to believe, to buy, to feel?
Unfollow one account that often takes away your peace, and follow one that brings truth and beauty
lessons.noon: “Whatever things are true, whatever things are honorable, whatever things are just, whatever things are pure, whatever things are lovely, whatever things are of good report.” — Lord, today help me to think about these things.

fam.key: I will think about good things.

lamb.do: Look at a picture book with your baby, pointing to flowers, birds and a rainbow, saying their names in a gentle voice, and then say, “So beautiful.”
lamb.say: The world God made is so beautiful. Let’s look at lovely things together.

sprout.story: Xiaoyun’s grandma had a sieve for sifting flour. She poured the flour in and shook it, and the fine white flour fell through while the hard little lumps stayed on top. Grandma said, “Our hearts need a sieve too, to let the good things in and keep the bad things out.” Xiaoyun asked, “Where is the sieve in our hearts?” Grandma smiled and said, “It’s God’s word!”
sprout.ask: What lovely thing did you see or hear today?
sprout.do: With a sieve or strainer, sift flour or sand together with your child, saying as you sift, “Good things come in, bad things go out!”

soldier.story: Paul gives us six “holes in the sieve”: true, honorable, just, pure, lovely, of good report. When you watch a video, play a game or listen to a song, you can ask: Is it real, or is it lying? Does it respect people? Is it fair to others? Is it clean? Does it make hearts feel warm? Would I be glad to recommend it to others? Not everything needs full marks, but if something can’t get through any of the six holes, we should think: do we still want it in our hearts?
ask: Which holes can your favorite cartoon or game get through?
Is there anything that you think can’t get through any hole?
soldier.do: Make six “sieve cards” as a family, each with one word. This week, before and after watching anything, draw a card and discuss.

youth.talk: I’ve noticed that the amount of information I take in every day is frightening: news, short clips, forwarded messages, ads. Often I can’t even remember what I looked at, yet my mood has been affected. Paul says to think about what is true, honorable, just, pure, lovely and of good report. I want to ask myself first: how much of what I put into my heart is of that kind? I’d also like to hear your view. How do you filter things yourself?
ask: Which item in Philippians 4:8 do you think online content lacks most today?
Do you have your own way of telling what is worth watching and what isn’t?
youth.do: Parent and child each recommend one thing that they feel “passes Philippians 4:8,” such as a song, a video or a channel, enjoy it together this week and swap thoughts.

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for giving us so many beautiful things. Help our eyes and ears choose what is good, and let our hearts think about what you love. In Jesus’ name, amen.

lessons.title: Chew It for Them, or Teach Them to Chew?
lessons.theme: Senses exercised to discern: do I only forbid, or do I train discernment alongside my child?

v: For everyone who lives on milk is not experienced in the word of righteousness, for he is a baby.
But solid food is for those who are full grown, who by reason of use have their senses exercised to discern good and evil.
