lessons.still: Ask the Holy Spirit to help you remember: the last time your child wanted to watch a certain program or play a certain game, how did you respond? See yourself quietly, without rushing to explain.
teach: The writer of Hebrews says that whoever lives on milk is a baby, “But solid food is for those who are full grown, who by reason of use have their senses exercised to discern good and evil.” Discernment is not inborn, and it is not learned by hearing it once; it is “exercised” through use. Like a muscle, it must be trained again and again to have strength.

Ask the Holy Spirit to show us what kind of parent we are. The “forbidding” type says no to everything and never explains why, and the child leaves home with no discernment at all. The “hands-off” type thinks the child will judge for himself and never asks. The “double-standard” type forbids what the child may watch but watches it himself late at night. All three kinds of parents have love, but lack one thing: accompanying the child, time after time, in practicing discernment.

Mrs. Zheng in Perth, Australia, used to say no to anything her children wanted to watch. Then her eldest son’s faith was shaken in his first semester at university by all kinds of claims on the internet, and she understood: protection in childhood matters, but its purpose is that the child will be able to discern for himself when he is grown. It is like teaching a child to eat: from feeding him, to eating with him, to letting him choose his own dishes. Discernment too has to be handed over step by step.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Parents are stewards, not a child’s lifelong goalkeeper. A self-ruled parent uses prohibition to keep a sense of control; a self-emptied parent is willing to spend time explaining, accompanying and discussing, so that the child’s senses are gradually trained. Life first, then relationships, then ministry: parents practice discernment first, so that they can lead their children in practicing it.
q: Who is God? — God wants us to grow from milk to solid food. How patiently does he train me?
Who am I? — Forbidding, hands-off or double-standard: which am I most like?
How should I respond? — At my child’s present age, which part of discernment can I hand over to him to practice?
lessons.jesus: When Jesus taught his disciples, he seldom gave only rules. He often used parables and questions to make them think for themselves: “What do you think?” “Which of these three do you think seemed to be a neighbor to him who fell among the robbers?” He patiently trained the disciples’ hearts, because one day he would place his mission in their hands.
lessons.pray: Lord, I confess that I often only say “no” to my children without spending time with them on “why”; sometimes I let go and do not ask, or even watch what I shouldn’t watch myself. Forgive me. Let my own senses be exercised first, and give me patience to accompany my children, time after time, in learning to discern good and evil. Amen.
acts: Think of the last time you said “you can’t watch that,” and today find time to add “because…” and hear his thoughts
Honestly check whether you privately watch what you forbid your children to watch, and be open about it with God
Choose a program your child often watches and watch ten minutes of it with him today, only observing, not criticizing
lessons.noon: “Solid food is for those who are full grown, who by reason of use have their senses exercised to discern good and evil.” — Lord, train my heart, and train my child.

fam.key: I will practice telling good from bad.

lamb.do: Play “can eat, can’t eat” with your baby: hold up a banana and say “can eat,” hold up a building block and say “can’t eat,” and let him nod or shake his head. Clap when he gets it right.
lamb.say: Well done! God helps you tell what is good and what is not.

sprout.story: When Xiaobao was just learning to walk, Daddy held his hand. Later Daddy only supported his back. Later still Daddy walked beside him and watched, and Xiaobao walked steadily by himself! Mommy said, “Telling good things from bad things is like learning to walk. At first Mommy and Daddy choose for you, and slowly you will choose for yourself, because we practice with you every day.”
sprout.ask: Can you tell for yourself which cartoon is a good one? How?
sprout.do: Play “good choice, bad choice”: Mom and Dad describe a situation, such as “I see a cartoon person hit someone, so I go and hit my little brother,” and your child gives a thumbs up or a cross.

soldier.story: The twin brothers Jiaen and Jiale in Singapore are different: one loves watching cartoons, the other loves playing games. Dad used to say only, “Turn it off!” and they would sneak a look when he wasn’t there. Later Dad changed his approach. Each week he chose a program with them, and afterward they asked together, “Did the hero do the right thing? Was there a better way?” A few months later, Jiale switched off a clip himself one day and said, “This keeps laughing at people. It’s not good.” Dad was so pleasantly surprised: his senses were being exercised.
ask: When Mom and Dad only say “no,” and when they talk it over with you, which helps you understand more?
Has there been a time recently when you yourself decided not to watch or play something?
soldier.do: This week each person chooses a favorite video or game to introduce to the family, saying one good thing about it and one thing to be careful about.

youth.talk: I want to admit that in the past I often said only, “You’re not allowed to watch that,” and seldom told you why or asked what you thought. I understand now that one day you will have to judge for yourself what is good. I will still have my boundaries, but what I would rather do is practice discernment alongside you, not keep deciding for you. Which things do you think I can let you decide for yourself now?
ask: In the things you watch, where do you think Mom and Dad are reasonable, and where do they control too much?
In what ways do you think you are already strong at discerning online content, and where do you still need practice?
youth.do: Parent and child list together the kinds of content “you can already decide yourself” and those “we still need to discuss together,” and agree to look at the list again in six months.

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for always teaching us so patiently. Help us practice telling good from bad every day, and become more and more like Jesus. In Jesus’ name, amen.

lessons.title: Examining Daily: God’s Word Is My Measure
lessons.theme: I believe: Scripture is the standard for weighing all information

v: Now these were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind, examining the Scriptures daily to see whether these things were so.
Test all things, and hold firmly that which is good.
Abstain from every form of evil.

lessons.still: Pick up your Bible and run your hand over its cover. Say quietly to the Lord, “Lord, among so many voices, I will take your word as my standard.”
teach: When Paul preached in Berea, the people there “received the word with all readiness of mind, examining the Scriptures daily to see whether these things were so.” They did not accept everything simply because Paul was the preacher. They went back to the Scriptures to check, and the Bible praises them as “more noble” than the others. Being willing to listen and willing to verify is exactly the spiritual character the digital age needs most.

Today’s children face all kinds of information every day: influencers’ recommendations, forwarded “studies show,” synthetic photos and videos that pass for real, opinion leaders who sound convincing. Paul says, “Test all things, and hold firmly that which is good. Abstain from every form of evil.” We can teach children four questions: Who said this? What do they want me to believe, buy or feel? Is there another reliable source that confirms it? Is it consistent with God’s word?

This is a change of view: from “everyone says so” to “what does God say”; from “I like it, I feel it” to “Scripture is my standard.” If parents verify before forwarding a message, and return to God’s word when watching the news, children learn that truth is not decided by the number of likes. Today, write down your “I believe” declaration.
lessons.light: 321 Light: One of the three foundations: Scripture is my standard. In the digital flood it is easy to let an algorithm, the crowd or our feelings become the standard. Letting Jesus reign means giving his word the last say, even before I press “share.”
q: Who is God? — God has given us his word as our standard. What does this say about how he cares for us living in a flood of information?
Who am I? — What have I believed or forwarded without checking? What was my standard then?
How should I respond? — Write your “I believe”: I believe God’s word is…; when I face information online, I will…
lessons.jesus: When Jesus faced the arguments and hard questions of the religious leaders, he always brought people back to Scripture itself. After his resurrection, on the road to Emmaus, “Beginning from Moses and from all the prophets, he explained to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself.” Jesus himself is the example of taking Scripture as the standard and explaining everything by Scripture.
lessons.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for giving us your word. I confess that I am often swayed by what everyone says, by my own feelings or by voices online. I believe your word is the measure of all things. Give me the heart of the Bereans, to receive it with readiness and examine it daily, and let my children recognize your voice in the din of many voices. Amen.
acts: Write your “I believe” declaration: I believe God’s word is…; when I face information online, I will…
Before forwarding any message today, stop and check the source
Use the “four questions” with your child on an advertisement or news item: Who said it? What do they want from me? Is there evidence? Is it consistent with Scripture?
lessons.noon: “Received the word with all readiness of mind, examining the Scriptures daily to see whether these things were so.” — Lord, today let me take your word as my standard.

fam.key: God’s word is my ruler.

lamb.do: Open the Bible in front of your baby and let him touch the pages with his little hand, while you point to the words and slowly read one short verse.
lamb.say: This is God’s word, and God’s word is true.

sprout.story: Xiaozhi took a ruler and measured his pencil, his book, and even the dog’s tail. His little brother said, “My blocks are taller than yours!” Xiaozhi said, “Let’s measure and find out!” After they measured, neither of them argued. Mommy said, “God’s word is like a ruler. Sometimes people say different things, and we measure with God’s word to find out what is right.”
sprout.ask: If someone says something different from the Bible, whom will you believe?
sprout.do: Take a ruler and measure things around the house together, and each time you measure something, say, “God’s word is my ruler!”

soldier.story: Grandma Wang in Taipei lives with her grandson Kevin. One day Kevin saw a video saying that if you recited a lucky chant three times a day, you would do well in exams. Lots of people liked it, and he nearly believed it. Grandma didn’t laugh at him. She helped him check with the four questions: Who said it? What do they want us to do? Is there evidence? Is it consistent with Scripture? In the end Kevin laughed himself: “So this person wants us to buy his course!” Grandma said, “The Bereans examined the Scriptures daily, and you can do it too.”
ask: What things online have you seen that sounded real but were fake?
Why isn’t something true just because lots of people liked it?
soldier.do: Play “truth detectives” as a family: parents prepare three messages, some true and some false, and the children check them with the four questions. The one who guesses the most right chooses the weekend snack.

youth.talk: Honestly, I have been fooled by false information myself and even forwarded it to the relatives’ group chat, and only found out later that it was fake, which was a bit embarrassing. Your generation faces something harder, where even photos and videos may be synthetic. I really admire the Bereans, who went back to Scripture no matter who was speaking. I’d like to learn with you to take God’s word as the standard and not the number of likes.
ask: How do you decide whether a piece of news or a claim online is true?
On faith or values, is there an online claim that confuses you? We could check the Bible together.
youth.do: Parent and child each pick one claim about values they saw online recently, look up Scripture together to see what God says, and write down both of your conclusions.

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you that your word is true. Help us read your word every day and use it to tell right from wrong, so that we are not fooled by what is fake. In Jesus’ name, amen.

lessons.title: Seeing Through the Serpent’s Advertisement
lessons.theme: Watch together, ask together: taking media messages apart with truth

v: Now the serpent was more subtle than any animal of the field which the LORD God had made. He said to the woman, “Has God really said, ‘You shall not eat of any tree of the garden’?”
The woman said to the serpent, “We may eat fruit from the trees of the garden,
but not the fruit of the tree which is in the middle of the garden. God has said, ‘You shall not eat of it. You shall not touch it, lest you die.’”
The serpent said to the woman, “You won’t really die,
for God knows that in the day you eat it, your eyes will be opened, and you will be like God, knowing good and evil.”

When the woman saw that the tree was good for food, and that it was a delight to the eyes, and that the tree was to be desired to make one wise, she took some of its fruit, and ate. Then she gave some to her husband with her, and he ate it, too.

lessons.still: Imagine sitting side by side with your child, watching a video together. Your heart is relaxed and curious, not tense and defensive. Say to the Lord, “Lord, as we watch together, please sit among us too.”
teach: The first “advertisement” in human history appeared in the Garden of Eden. The serpent first questioned God’s word: “Has God really said…?” Then he told half the truth: “You won’t really die.” Finally, the woman saw that the fruit was “good for food,” “a delight to the eyes,” and “to be desired to make one wise.” Many advertisements and pieces of content today use much the same methods: questioning the truth, telling only half of it, and moving the heart with what looks good, tastes good and is fun.

The best practice ground for media literacy is watching together as a family. It can be done by age. Preschool: parents choose the content, sit beside the child while watching, and ask, “Is he happy or sad?” Elementary school: after watching ask, “Who did the right thing? What would Jesus do?” Teenagers: take apart together the values behind advertisements, influencers and plots: “What does it want me to believe? What is it not telling me?”

Watching together is not for picking faults from the side but for thinking together. Mrs. Li in Kuching watches one episode of a program her two children have chosen every Friday evening, and afterward each person names one “true and lovely” thing and one “be careful” thing. She says the biggest gain was not that her children learned to discern but that they began to be willing to share with her what they normally watch.
lessons.light: 321 Light: People matter more than tasks. Media literacy is not a game of “catching mistakes” but an opportunity to accompany. If parents only want to win, they will lecture; if they value the relationship, they will ask with curiosity and listen with patience. Practice means bringing information, revelation and conviction into the living room tonight.
q: Who is God? — God saw through the serpent’s scheme and promised to send a savior. What kind of God is he, who protects his people?
Who am I? — What kind of message that is “good for food and a delight to the eyes” moves me most easily?
How should I respond? — What will I watch with my child today, and what will we ask?
lessons.jesus: When Jesus was tempted in the wilderness, the devil quoted Scripture too, but out of context. Jesus answered, “Again, it is written,” and used the whole truth to see through a one-sided claim. At his hungriest and weakest he still discerned clearly, and he overcame the ancient serpent for us.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, thank you for overcoming the serpent’s temptation for us. Give me eyes that discern and a heart that accompanies, so that I can watch and think with my children and not only criticize from the side. In our living room, teach us to see through lies and hold on to truth. Amen.
acts: Tonight watch a video or program your child likes together with him, and afterward ask one open-ended question
Find an advertisement with your child and talk about what methods it uses to attract people
Write down three “must ask after watching” questions suited to your child’s age and put them beside the television
lessons.noon: “When the woman saw that the tree was good for food, and that it was a delight to the eyes.” — Lord, today help me to see through enticing lies and hold on to your truth.

fam.key: Watch together, ask together, think together.

lamb.do: Look at a picture book with your baby, and as you turn each page point to a face and ask, “Is he smiling or crying?” to help him learn to read expressions.
lamb.say: We look together and learn together.

sprout.story: In the Garden of Eden there was a sly serpent. He said to Eve, “The fruit of that tree is so yummy, and if you eat it you’ll be so clever!” Eve looked at the fruit. It was so pretty and looked so good to eat, and she forgot that God had said not to eat it. She ate it, and gave some to Adam too. Afterward they were very sad, because they had listened to the serpent and not to God. Let’s remember: something that looks great is not always good.
sprout.ask: Why isn’t something that looks great always good?
sprout.do: Play “the serpent says, God says”: Mom and Dad say a sentence and your child decides whether it is what “the serpent says” (a lie) or “God says” (true). If it’s the serpent, hiss; if it’s God, make a heart shape.

soldier.story: How did the serpent trick Eve? Step one, he asked, “Did God really say that?” to make her doubt God’s word. Step two, he said, “You won’t really die,” half true and half false. Step three, he made Eve keep looking at the fruit, and the more she looked the more she wanted it. Many advertisements and videos use similar tricks today: “Everyone has one except you!” “Use this and you’ll be popular!” If you learn to see through these tricks, you are a smart viewer who won’t be led by the nose.
ask: What advertisement have you seen lately that made you really want that thing? What tricks did it use?
What do you think it takes to “see through” a program so that it doesn’t lead you around?
soldier.do: Play “advertisement breakdown champion” as a family: each person finds an advertisement and says which of the serpent’s tricks it used (making you doubt, half-truth, keeping you looking). The one who explains most clearly is today’s champion.

youth.talk: I’ve noticed that very often the cleverest thing media does is not lie but show you only half: influencers show you only the most beautiful life, plots make wrong things look cool, advertisements make you feel incomplete without the product. The serpent in Eden did the same. I don’t want only to forbid you to watch; I want to watch with you and hear what you think. Is there something you watch that you think is worth us watching together?
ask: What values does your favorite drama or channel try to pass on? Do you agree with them?
Is there a kind of content that you think packages wrong things in a very attractive way?
youth.do: This week let your child choose a video or series he likes, and watch it with him. Afterward each shares one thing they appreciated and one thing they would like to discuss. Parents listen to the child’s views first.

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for making us clever. Help us see through lies, choose together what is true and lovely, and listen only to your word. In Jesus’ name, amen.

lessons.title: Turn My Eyes Away
lessons.theme: Review & Adjust: what did our hearts feed on this week?

v: Turn my eyes away from looking at worthless things. Revive me in your ways.
Let the words of my mouth and the meditation of my heart be acceptable in your sight, LORD, my rock, and my redeemer.

lessons.still: Recall what your family watched, heard and played this week. Like cleaning out the fridge, take things out one by one, and ask the Holy Spirit to tell you which are nourishing and which have gone off.
teach: The psalmist prays, “Turn my eyes away from looking at worthless things. Revive me in your ways.” He knows that by his own will alone it is hard to turn his eyes away, so he asks God to help. Discernment is not only a skill but a prayer: asking God himself to change what we long for. When the heart has fallen in love with God’s way, what is worthless gradually loses its attraction.

This week we have learned that the soul has a diet; that discernment is trained through use; that Scripture is our ruler; and that we should see through the serpent’s advertisement. Today husband and wife, please sit down and review honestly: what worthless things did our eyes rest on this week? Did we watch with our children and ask together? Which discussion surprised us most?

David also prays, “Let the words of my mouth and the meditation of my heart be acceptable in your sight.” What we take in eventually comes out in what we say. Adjustments can be very specific: let the whole family choose the program after dinner; have a weekly “film review time”; parents first delete one app that leads them to dwell on worthless things. An adjustment is not done once for all, but by coming back before God again and again.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Review, adjustment, repetition. A proud parent only checks what the children watch; a humble parent first asks himself: what has my heart fed on? When parents are willing to admit that they too are drawn to what is false, children learn that discernment is not for judging others but for becoming more like Jesus.
q: Who is God? — God is willing to turn our eyes away himself. What kind of grace is this?
Who am I? — Where did I look at worthless things this week? Where did I accompany my child in discerning what is true?
How should I respond? — What is one media habit I will adjust next week?
lessons.jesus: Jesus said, “Out of the abundance of the heart, the mouth speaks.” His heart was full of the Father’s words, so what came out of his mouth was grace and truth. When we turn our eyes to him, he slowly renews what fills our hearts, and renews the words spoken in our homes too.
lessons.pray: Lord, turn my eyes away from looking at worthless things, and revive me in your ways. For the times this week I accompanied my child in discerning, thank you; for the times I let worthless things take over my eyes, forgive me. Let the words of my mouth and the meditation of my heart be acceptable in your sight, and let what our family watches, hears and says please you. Amen.
acts: Talk with your spouse: of our family’s “soul diet” this week, what was nourishing and what should be thrown away?
Ask your child: “This week, have I become more like Jesus, watching with you and listening to your thoughts, and not only forbidding?” Only listen; don’t defend yourself
Write down one media adjustment for next week, for example a weekly family film review time
lessons.noon: “Turn my eyes away from looking at worthless things. Revive me in your ways.” — Lord, today turn my eyes away and make me look up to you.

fam.key: I will turn my eyes to good things.

lamb.do: When your baby is drawn by noisy sights and sounds, gently cup his face and turn it toward you, smile at him and sing a line of a hymn.
lamb.say: Look here, look at Mommy and Daddy. Let’s look at Jesus together.

sprout.story: Xiaoqing was watching a cartoon in which people often shouted rude things. As she watched, she said to her little sister, “You’re so stupid!” Mommy heard, but she didn’t scold her. She sat down and asked, “Where did you learn that sentence?” Xiaoqing thought and pointed at the television. Mommy said, “Whatever we watch, we end up saying. Shall we change to a cartoon that says kind words?” Xiaoqing nodded, and even said sorry to her sister.
sprout.ask: What kind word did you learn lately? Where did you learn it?
sprout.do: Play “turn your head”: when Mom and Dad say, “Something bad is coming,” your child turns his head away; when they say, “Something lovely is coming,” he turns back to Mom and Dad, and everyone laughs.

soldier.story: There is a prayer in the Psalms: “Turn my eyes away from looking at worthless things.” The one who wrote it knew that some things keep catching your eyes and it is hard to turn away by yourself, so he asked God to help. This week our family practiced watching, asking and discerning. Now let’s look back: what good things did we watch? Is there anything that, after watching, made you quick to scold, restless, or unwilling to do homework? Mom and Dad will be honest about what they watched too.
ask: Of what we watched or discussed together this week, which time did you like best?
What would you like to swap out next week? What would you like to add?
soldier.do: Hold a family meeting: each person names one piece of “good soul nutrition” and one piece of “soul junk food” from this week. Mom and Dad go first, and then the whole family chooses an adjustment for next week.

youth.talk: This week I deliberately paid attention to what I was watching, and I found that some content made me anxious and ready to compare, and I really should turn my eyes away from it. I also tried to watch with you and hear your thoughts, and I don’t know how that felt for you. I’d like honest feedback: this week was I more like someone accompanying you, rather than someone monitoring you?
ask: When I watched things with you and talked about media this week, were you at ease? Where could I do better?
What media habit do you think our whole family could adjust together next week?
youth.do: Parents first name one thing they have decided to “turn their eyes away from,” then invite the child to share one too if he likes, and together set next week’s family film review time.

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, help us turn our eyes away from what is false, to look more at good things and to speak more kind words. Thank you for being with us this week. In Jesus’ name, amen.

29.memT: Finally, brothers, whatever things are true, whatever things are honorable, whatever things are just, whatever things are pure, whatever things are lovely, whatever things are of good report: if there is any virtue and if there is anything worthy of praise, think about these things.

mem.t: Therefore watch carefully how you walk, not as unwise, but as wise, redeeming the time, because the days are evil.

sat.t: Family Day: A Digital Covenant Signing Party
sat.d: Copy the family digital covenant you have drafted together this week onto a large poster, and take turns reading one article each aloud. Everyone signs; the little ones add a handprint; the parents sign first, to show “we keep it first.” Take a family photo with the poster and put it up in the living room. Then put all the phones into a basket and do something to celebrate together: a picnic, a board game, or baking something sweet. Finally, circle the review day ten days from now on the calendar, hold hands and pray over this covenant.

sun: Looking back over weeks 22–30 (morning and evening rhythms, the table, the bedtime blessing, the Sabbath, family worship, digital watchfulness), which has borne the most fruit in your home?
As you set the digital covenant, which article is hardest for you to model yourself? Why?
As this life stage comes to a close, which family in your group will you share your family health check with, so that you can pray for each other and remind each other?

lessons.title: Redeeming the Time
lessons.theme: The purpose of a digital covenant: to buy time back and spend it on what God treasures

v: Therefore watch carefully how you walk, not as unwise, but as wise,
redeeming the time, because the days are evil.
Therefore, don’t be foolish, but understand what the will of the Lord is.

lessons.still: Look at a watch or clock and watch the second hand go once around. That minute has passed and will not come back. Say to the Lord, “Lord, my time is yours. Teach me how to use it.”
teach: Paul says, “Therefore watch carefully how you walk, not as unwise, but as wise, redeeming the time, because the days are evil.” “Redeeming the time” means buying time back, like snapping up something precious in the market. Time does not become meaningful by itself; if we do not deliberately redeem it, something else buys it.

In the digital age there are especially many merchants who want to buy our time. One more episode, one more scroll, and an evening is gone. Children’s childhoods are the same, slipping quietly away in front of screens year after year. A family digital covenant is the whole family deciding together: we will buy our time back and spend it on God, one another, rest, learning and service.

A good digital covenant is not a decree issued by parents alone but an agreement the whole family discusses and keeps together. It usually answers a few questions: When may we use screens? Where? For what? What will the parents keep? What happens if someone breaks it? How often do we review it? This week we will draw it up step by step, and the first step is to “understand what the will of the Lord is.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: One purpose: build what belongs to God. A digital covenant is not only about managing screens but about building a God-centered order of life at home. Letting Jesus reign includes letting him be Lord of our time; letting Jesus receive all the glory includes our daily time with screens.
q: Who is God? — God is Lord of time. How does he see each day of our family’s life?
Who am I? — If my time were a purse, who “bought” most of it this week?
How should I respond? — On which three things do I want our family to “buy back” our time and spend it?
lessons.jesus: Jesus’ public ministry lasted only a little over three years, yet he was never in a rush. He knew “My time has not yet come,” and he knew when to stop and welcome the children and when to withdraw to the mountain to pray. He lived every moment in the Father’s will, and that is the perfect way of redeeming the time.
lessons.pray: Lord, my time is your gift, yet I often let screens buy it. Teach me to watch carefully how I walk and to redeem the time like a wise person. Give our whole family wisdom to understand your will, to make a digital covenant that pleases you, and to spend our time on what you treasure. Amen.
acts: List three things you would like the family to spend more time doing together, for example Bible reading and prayer, exercise, conversation
Observe tonight how each person in the family uses screens. Don’t comment, just note it, as a reference for making the covenant
Invite your spouse and children to take part in the digital covenant discussion this week, and fix the time of the family meeting first
lessons.noon: “Redeeming the time, because the days are evil.” — Lord, teach me today to buy my time back and spend it on what you treasure.

fam.key: Our time is a gift from God.

lamb.do: Take an hourglass or timer and watch it with your baby as the sand slowly runs down. When it finishes, pick him up and spin him around.
lamb.say: Time is a gift from God, and I love being with you most.

sprout.story: Xiaoqian had a piggy bank. Every time she got a coin, she carefully put it in. Mommy said, “Time is like coins. God gives us lots of them every day. We can spend them on watching television, or on playing with family, helping others and talking with God.” Xiaoqian thought and said, “Then today I’ll spend one coin to play blocks with my little sister!”
sprout.ask: Where would you like to spend your time coins today?
sprout.do: Cut ten “time coins” from paper and let your child decide what each coin will be spent on: playing, reading, helping, praying, screens. Look together at how best to share them out.

soldier.story: Imagine that every morning someone puts a sum of time into your account: twenty-four hours, no more and no less, and whatever you haven’t used disappears at night. How would you use it? Paul says to redeem the time, which means to buy it back. Many games and videos are very good at snatching your time, and before you know it an afternoon is gone. This week our family will make a “digital covenant” together and decide where our time goes. Your opinion matters!
ask: What do you think “snatches” your time most often?
If our family had a digital covenant, what is the one article you think most needs to be in it?
soldier.do: Each person draws a circular “time pie” showing how they usually spend a day, then draws a “time pie I hope for,” and compares and shares at dinner.

youth.talk: This week I’d like to make our family’s digital covenant together with you. Not something I write and ask you to sign, but something we discuss together. Paul says to redeem the time, because time once gone does not come back. Thinking back to when you were small, a lot of that time was actually spent by me scrolling my phone, and I regret it. Your time is precious too. I want to respect your needs and also to guard the time we have together as a family. Would you think it over with me?
ask: What do you think matters most in a fair family digital covenant?
Which screen times matter a lot to you, so that you would like us to understand and keep them?
youth.do: Set a time when parents and child each list the things they “must use screens for” and those they “could cut down,” as a draft for the Thursday family meeting.

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for giving us time every day. Help us use our time well, to be with family more and draw near to you more, and not let screens steal our time. In Jesus’ name, amen.

lessons.title: Be Imitators of Me
lessons.theme: Children watch what we do more than they listen to what we say

v: Be imitators of me, even as I also am of Christ.
You therefore who teach another, don’t you teach yourself? You who preach that a man shouldn’t steal, do you steal?

lessons.still: Ask the Holy Spirit to be like a mirror and show how you look when you use your phone in front of your children: at meals, while driving, when your child speaks to you. Look quietly, without defending yourself.
teach: Paul dared to say to believers, “Be imitators of me, even as I also am of Christ.” This is a weighty statement: his life could stand being copied. In another letter he asks soberly, “You therefore who teach another, don’t you teach yourself?” These two verses are like a mirror held up before every parent, showing how far apart what we say and what we do may be.

Children learn more by imitating than by listening. We want children not to look at phones at meals, yet we answer messages as we eat; we want them to go to bed early, yet we scroll until late; we want them not to be hooked on games, yet we can’t put down short videos or stock apps. Children may not say it, but they see it clearly, and quietly learn that rules are for children and adults don’t have to keep them.

Ask the Holy Spirit to shine his light: on the matter of screens, what kind of parent am I? The “lawmaker”: makes rules for the children and makes an exception for himself. The “exempt”: uses work as the reason that none of the rules count for me. The “fellow traveler”: willing to be the first to keep them and the first to admit fault. We don’t have to be perfect, but we can be honest. When a parent says, “I’m not good at this one either, so let’s work on it together,” the child sees what imitating Christ looks like.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Life first, then relationships, then ministry. A parent’s life is the most powerful teaching material. A proud parent asks the children to change and does not change himself; a humble parent changes himself first and admits his weakness. Humility leads to humility, and children learn from their parents how to imitate Christ.
q: Who is God? — Christ himself became our example. How does he help me become an example to my children?
Who am I? — Lawmaker, exempt or fellow traveler: which am I most like on the matter of screens?
How should I respond? — Which screen rule do I ask of my child that I cannot keep myself?
lessons.jesus: At the Last Supper, Jesus rose, wrapped a towel around himself and washed his disciples’ feet, and then said, “For I have given you an example, that you should also do as I have done to you.” He did not teach humility with words alone; he bent down first. The way parents lead a family is the same: do first, then speak.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, you bent down first to wash your disciples’ feet and gave us an example. I confess that with screens I often ask much of my children and let myself off. Forgive my double standard. Help me to be a fellow traveler, the first to keep the rules and the first to admit fault, so that my children can see in me what it looks like to imitate you. Amen.
acts: List the screen rules you have for your child and honestly tick each one: do I keep it myself?
Choose the rule you find hardest to keep, and begin keeping it yourself today
Admit your double standard to your child once, saying, “I need to learn this one too.”
lessons.noon: “Be imitators of me, even as I also am of Christ.” — Lord, let how I live today be worth imitating.

fam.key: Grown-ups go first, and children follow.

lamb.do: Play “do what I do” with your baby: you clap, he claps; you touch your nose, he touches his nose; at the end you open your arms and hug him.
lamb.say: You learn from me, and I learn from Jesus.

sprout.story: The ducklings lined up behind Mother Duck. Mother Duck waddled, and the ducklings waddled too; Mother Duck jumped into the water, and the ducklings jumped in one by one. Xiaokai laughed and laughed: “The ducklings copy their mommy!” Daddy said, “Yes, and you often copy Daddy. So Daddy needs to copy Jesus, and then when you copy me, you are learning Jesus too.”
sprout.ask: What do you copy Mom and Dad doing most?
sprout.do: Play “ducklings in a line”: Daddy or Mommy is Mother Duck and walks around the house doing all sorts of actions, while your child follows behind and copies.

soldier.story: Mingzhe, who lives in Los Angeles, was often reminded by his dad, “No phones at the table!” One dinnertime, Dad was replying to work messages as he ate. Mingzhe couldn’t help saying, “Dad, you said we can’t use phones at the table.” The whole family went quiet. Dad put down his phone, thought for a moment and said, “You’re right. Thank you for reminding me. I need to keep this rule too.” That evening, Mingzhe felt as if Dad had grown taller. A good example is not someone who never makes mistakes but someone who is willing to change when he is wrong.
ask: Have you seen a grown-up ask a child to do something that they didn’t do themselves? How did you feel?
If Mom and Dad don’t keep our family agreement, how can you remind us?
soldier.do: As a family agree on a gentle “reminder signal,” such as tapping the table twice. Anyone who sees a family member break the screen agreement may use it, and it applies to parents too.

youth.talk: I want to say sorry to you. I often ask you to use your phone less, but you have probably seen that I scroll non-stop myself, and use “I’m working” as the excuse. Paul says, “You therefore who teach another, don’t you teach yourself?” That sentence makes me very uncomfortable, but it is also very true. Next we will make a digital covenant together, and I hope it has articles written for me, and I ask you to help me keep them.
ask: Which of my phone habits makes you feel it is a “double standard”?
If the digital covenant had one article just for Mom and Dad, what would you write?
youth.do: Ask your child to draft two “parents’ screen articles” for the parents, who will consider them seriously, accept at least one, and write it into Thursday’s family digital covenant.

fam.pray: Lord Jesus, thank you for being our example. Help Mom and Dad to learn from you first, and help our whole family to learn from you together, and do what we say. In Jesus’ name, amen.

lessons.title: Count Our Days, Gain Wisdom
lessons.theme: I believe: a child’s childhood is a limited season entrusted by God

v: The days of our years are seventy, or even by reason of strength eighty years; yet their pride is but labor and sorrow, for it passes quickly, and we fly away.
So teach us to count our days, that we may gain a heart of wisdom.

lessons.still: Picture your child as a newborn, and then picture him as he is today. The years in between seem to have passed in the blink of an eye. Say quietly to the Lord, “Lord, teach me to count my days.”
teach: Moses spent forty years in the wilderness, watching a generation grow old there. He wrote, “The days of our years are seventy, or even by reason of strength eighty years,” and “it passes quickly, and we fly away.” So he prayed, “So teach us to count our days, that we may gain a heart of wisdom.” To count our days is to admit that time is limited and therefore to choose to live wisely.

Try counting: how many more summer vacations will your child live under the same roof as you? How many weekends? How many bedtime evenings? When we look at it in numbers, we find that the season of being together is shorter than we thought. Many parents find out only after their children have left home that those evenings spent in front of screens could have been evenings of walking together, praying together and laughing together.

This calls for a change of view: from “temporary” to “eternal.” Most of what is on a screen passes quickly, but a child’s life is eternal. Today, write down your “I believe”: I believe my time is entrusted by God. I believe my child’s childhood is a limited season. I believe that spending time on God and family is an investment I will never regret. This conviction will be the root of the digital covenant.
lessons.light: 321 Light: A shift in perspective, from temporary to eternal, from earth to heaven. The algorithm wants us to live in the stimulation of the moment; God wants us to live with an eternal view. Change the way you think and your life changes: when parents see how precious time is, putting down the phone is no longer a sacrifice but a choice.
q: Who is God? — God is from everlasting to everlasting. How does he see our brief lives?
Who am I? — Count it: how many more summers will my child live with us? What does that make me think of?
How should I respond? — Write your “I believe”: I believe my time is…; I believe my child’s childhood is…
lessons.jesus: Jesus said, “I must work the works of him who sent me while it is day. The night is coming, when no one can work.” He knew clearly that his time on earth was limited, so he lived every day in the Father’s will. He also invites us, while we still have today, to love well the people we are meant to love.
lessons.pray: Eternal God, teach me to count my days, that I may gain a heart of wisdom. I believe my time is entrusted by you, and I believe my child’s childhood is a limited season. Forgive me for letting things that pass quickly take over precious time. From today, help me to spend my time on eternal things. Amen.
acts: Work it out: before your child turns eighteen, how many summer vacations and how many weekends are left? Write the numbers down
Write down your three “I believe” declarations: I believe my time is…; I believe my child’s childhood is…; I believe our family…
Tonight swap fifteen minutes of phone scrolling for time alone with one of your children
lessons.noon: “So teach us to count our days, that we may gain a heart of wisdom.” — Lord, let me live today with an eternal view.

fam.key: Every day is a precious gift.

lamb.do: Bring out the photos from your baby’s birth, hold him and look together, touching the little hand in the photo and then his little hand now.
lamb.say: You’ve grown so much! Every day with you is a gift from God.

sprout.story: Xiaoen planted a sunflower seed in the garden. She went to look at it every day, watering it and measuring its height. One day the sunflower bloomed, so tall and so beautiful! But after a while the flower faded, and Xiaoen was a little sad. Mommy said, “That’s why we must treasure the time when it is in bloom. The days when you and your brother grow up together are as precious as a flower in bloom, and we must treasure them.”
sprout.ask: What would you most like to do with Mom and Dad?
sprout.do: Look through photos of your child when small, talk about funny things that happened then, and thank God together for letting us grow up together.

soldier.story: Moses led the Israelites in the wilderness for forty years and watched many people grow old. He wrote a psalm asking God to teach us to “count our days,” which means to remember that time is limited, so we should live every day wisely. Think about it: if you knew that in a year you would move far away, how would you spend that year with your best friend? You would treasure it much more! It is the same with family time. It seems long, but one day you will grow up and leave home.
ask: If you only had two hours left in a day, what would you choose to do?
When do you think are the times most worth treasuring in our family?
soldier.do: Make a “treasure-the-time jar” as a family: each person writes three things they would like to do with the family and puts them in the jar, and each week this month you draw one and do it.

youth.talk: One day I did some counting: in a few years you will be going to university or out to work, and the days when we can see each other every day are really fewer than I thought. Suddenly I was afraid, afraid these days would be spent on scrolling my phone and dealing with work, or even on arguing with you about your phone. Moses said, teach us to count our days. I want to treasure the time I have with you from now on.
ask: Before you leave home, what is the one thing you would most like to do with the family?
Which part of your own time would you like to make more meaningful?
youth.do: Parent and child write a list of “things we want to do together before you leave home,” pick one from it and set it for this month.

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for giving us every day. Teach us to treasure the time we have together, to spend time loving you and loving our family. In Jesus’ name, amen.

lessons.title: Making Our Family’s Digital Covenant
lessons.theme: Make a covenant together as a family, try it for ten days, with the parents leading by example

v: But Daniel purposed in his heart that he would not defile himself with the king’s delicacies, nor with the wine which he drank. Therefore he requested of the prince of the eunuchs that he might not defile himself.
“Test your servants, I beg you, ten days; and let them give us vegetables to eat and water to drink.
Then let our faces be examined before you, and the face of the youths who eat of the king’s delicacies; and as you see, deal with your servants.”
So he listened to them in this matter, and tested them for ten days.

lessons.still: Imagine the whole family sitting round the table, everyone having a chance to speak, even the youngest child listened to seriously. Say to the Lord, “Lord, sit among us and lead our discussion.”
teach: Daniel was taken captive to Babylon, and the food from the king’s table was set before him. “Daniel purposed in his heart that he would not defile himself with the king’s delicacies, nor with the wine which he drank,” yet he did not clash head-on. He made a concrete proposal: “Test your servants, I beg you, ten days,” and agreed how it would be checked. A good covenant has a clear resolve, a workable method, a trial period and a way of reviewing.

Call a family meeting today and draw up the covenant together using this outline. One, purpose: why we are making this covenant. Two, times: when we don’t use screens, such as dinner, the hour before bed, Sunday morning. Three, places: devices stay in the living room, not in bedrooms or at the table. Four, content: who chooses, how, what we don’t watch. Five, parents’ articles: rules the parents keep too. Six, when it is broken: a reminder signal, natural consequences, apology and repair, no shaming. Seven, review: after a ten-day trial, adjust together.

These age guidelines can be adjusted for each family. Under three: apart from video calls with relatives, replace screens with real-person interaction as much as possible. Three to six: small amounts, chosen by parents and watched together. Elementary school: homework and chores first, then use in shared spaces at fixed times. Teenagers: negotiate together, hand back independence step by step, and leave devices outside the room at bedtime. A covenant is for protecting relationships, not for managing people.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Humility leads to humility, and both win. If parents impose rules by authority, children obey on the surface and resist in their hearts; if children take part and parents keep the rules first, the covenant becomes the whole family’s agreement. In the eight steps, practice is followed by review and adjustment, and a ten-day trial is that very spirit.
q: Who is God? — God gave Daniel favor with the prince of the eunuchs. How does he help our family hold to our resolve?
Who am I? — In the family meeting, do I only want to persuade, or am I willing to listen sincerely to my child?
How should I respond? — In our digital covenant, what are the parents’ articles that I will keep myself?
lessons.jesus: Jesus walked with his disciples for three years, and he did not only issue commands; he ate, walked and lived with them. At the Last Supper he himself broke the bread and passed the cup, made a new covenant with his disciples, and sealed it with his own life. Jesus’ way of leading is to give first and commit first, and this is the pattern for parents leading the family in a covenant.
lessons.pray: Lord, thank you that Daniel could hold to his resolve in a foreign land. Today we will make our family’s digital covenant together. Give us wisdom and humility so that everyone is heard. Help me to keep it first and commit first; when we fail, give us grace to start again. Let this covenant protect our relationships and honor your name. Amen.
acts: Call a family meeting today and use the seven items in the outline to draft the digital covenant together
Write the covenant on a poster, have the whole family sign it, with the parents signing first
Mark the review date ten days after the start of the trial on the calendar
lessons.noon: “Daniel purposed in his heart that he would not defile himself.” — Lord, help our whole family to purpose in our hearts and to keep the covenant we make.

fam.key: We make a covenant together and keep it together.

lamb.do: Each time you turn off the television or put away a phone, wave to the screen with your baby and say “bye-bye,” and then pick him up to go and do the next thing.
lamb.say: The screen says bye-bye, and now we play together.

sprout.story: Daniel and his three good friends lived in the king’s palace, and the king gave them rich food and meat, but that food did not please God. Daniel said very politely, “Please let us try for ten days, with only vegetables to eat and water to drink.” After ten days, they were healthier and stronger than everyone else! Because they had made up their minds together, God helped them. Our family will make a covenant together too, and work together to keep it.
sprout.ask: Which covenant can our family keep together?
sprout.do: Let your child draw on the family’s digital covenant poster and add a handprint as his “signature.”

soldier.story: Daniel and his three friends were being trained in the king of Babylon’s palace, and they decided not to eat the king’s food. But they did not make a fuss; they proposed a plan: try it for ten days, then look at the result. After ten days, they were healthier than anyone else! A family digital covenant can be made the same way: everyone discusses together, writes clearly the purpose, times, places and what to do if it is broken, then tries it for ten days and reviews it together. And Mom and Dad must keep it too!
ask: Which article of our family’s digital covenant do you find hardest? Which is easiest?
If someone forgets to keep it, what is the best way to remind them without making anyone sad?
soldier.do: Ask your child to be the secretary of the family meeting, writing down the covenant everyone agrees on, and to design a “ten-day challenge chart” that the whole family ticks every evening.

youth.talk: Today we are going to make a digital covenant together. I want to be clear first: it is not to take away your freedom but for our whole family to protect one another’s time and relationships. You can give your opinion, and I will tell you my worries, and together we will find a version everyone can accept. Like Daniel, we try it for ten days first, and adjust if it doesn’t fit. I will keep the articles written for parents myself.
ask: Which article in this covenant do you think needs adjusting because of your age?
When someone breaks the covenant, what consequence would you think fair and not hurtful to relationships?
youth.do: Before the family meeting, parents first spend ten minutes one-to-one with the child to hear his ideas and worries; at the meeting, ask the child to make the first proposal.

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for helping Daniel hold to his resolve. Please help our whole family keep our digital covenant together, reminding and forgiving one another. In Jesus’ name, amen.

lessons.title: Looking Back: A Health Check for Our Family Rhythms
lessons.theme: Review & Adjust: looking back over weeks 22–30 and giving the family a health check

v: Let us search and try our ways, and turn again to the LORD.
These words, which I command you today, shall be on your heart;
and you shall teach them diligently to your children, and shall talk of them when you sit in your house, and when you walk by the way, and when you lie down, and when you rise up.

lessons.still: Recall the past nine weeks as if turning the pages of a family album: the morning prayers, the laughter at the table, the bedtime blessings, the evenings with phones put down. Ask the Holy Spirit to look with you, page by page.
teach: After the holy city was destroyed, the writer of Lamentations wrote amid the ruins, “Let us search and try our ways, and turn again to the LORD.” Searching is not for condemnation but for turning back. Nine weeks ago we began to learn the “family rhythms”: God’s words are to be “on your heart,” and we are to talk of them “when you sit in your house, and when you walk by the way, and when you lie down, and when you rise up.” Faith in the family lives in these everyday rhythms.

Let us look back together: week 22, the rhythm of morning and evening; week 23, the table as the family altar; week 24, the bedtime blessing; week 25, the family Sabbath; week 26, worshiping together as a family; week 27, screens and watching over the heart; week 28, online safety; week 29, media discernment; week 30, the family digital covenant. We don’t have to do all nine weeks’ lessons. What matters is: which have already taken root in our home?

Today I invite husband and wife, or a single parent with a spiritual companion, to do a “family health check”: give yourselves one to five for each week’s theme, not to compare but to see. Then choose the one rhythm that has borne most fruit and should be kept, and the one that most needs strengthening, as your practice for what follows. From next week we enter the “relationship” stage and learn to build loving connections with our children.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The last of the eight steps for changing a mindset are repetition and multiplication. Life’s rhythms are not learned all at once but become habits through review, adjustment and repetition. When our family’s rhythms are standing firm, we can become a blessing to other families, and that is multiplication.
q: Who is God? — Looking back over these nine weeks, in what have you seen God at work in your home?
Who am I? — In the family health check, which item makes me most thankful? Which makes me most want to turn back?
How should I respond? — Before moving to the next stage, which rhythm will I keep, and which will I strengthen?
lessons.jesus: When the seventy Jesus sent out came back full of joy, they reported what had happened in their ministry. After he heard them, Jesus reminded them of a deeper joy: “rejoice that your names are written in heaven.” He values looking back, and he brings the looking back into our relationship with the Father. When we look back over our practice at home, in the end it is so that we may draw nearer to him.
lessons.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for walking with us through these nine weeks. Thank you for giving our home morning prayer, thanks at the table and a blessing at bedtime, and for helping us begin to watch over our screens and our hearts. Some rhythms we have kept, and some we are still struggling with. Forgive our weakness and strengthen our resolve. Lead us into the next stage, to love our children more deeply. Amen.
acts: Do a family health check with your spouse or a spiritual companion: give each theme of weeks 22–30 a score of one to five and write down the reasons
Choose one rhythm to keep and one to strengthen, and write them on the family calendar
Ask your child: “In these weeks, have I become more like Jesus? Which new habit in our family do you like best?” Only listen; don’t defend yourself
lessons.noon: “Let us search and try our ways, and turn again to the LORD.” — Lord, we look back, and we come back to you.

fam.key: Look back and count God’s blessings.

lamb.do: Look through the photos of recent weeks with your baby, point to the family members in them and call their names one by one, then clap together to thank God.
lamb.say: Thank you, God, for the many good times we have had together.

sprout.story: Xiaole’s family fridge was covered with things: stickers for morning prayer, thank-you cards from the table, drawings of the bedtime blessing, and a photo of the phone sleeping basket. Mommy said, “Let’s look at all the good things our family has done these past weeks.” Xiaole pointed to them one by one: “I remember this one! I remember this one too!” In the end he said, “I like it best when Daddy puts his hand on my head and blesses me at bedtime.” The whole family thanked God together.
sprout.ask: In these weeks, which new habit in our family do you like best?
sprout.do: As a family, gather the stickers, cards and drawings from these weeks and stick them on a big sheet of paper to make “our family’s wall of grace.”

soldier.story: After the Israelites crossed the Jordan, God told them to take twelve stones from the river and pile them into a memorial, so that later their children would ask, “What do these stones mean?” and their parents could tell them the great things God had done. In these nine weeks our family has had many “memorial stones” too: morning and evening prayers, table talk, bedtime blessings, the Sabbath, family worship, and the digital covenant we made together. Now let’s look back and count them, and see where we still need to strengthen.
ask: Of our family’s new habits in these nine weeks, which do you like best? Why?
Which habit do you think we most need to try harder at?
soldier.do: Make a “family health check chart” together: list the nine themes, let each person give one to five stars, then choose one habit to keep and one to strengthen, and pile up a few stones or blocks as a “memorial stone.”

youth.talk: In these two-plus months our family has tried a lot of new things: praying in the morning, no phones at meals, bedtime blessings, worshiping together, and the digital covenant we have just made. Some of it you may have found awkward, and some of it may have been quite good. I want to listen seriously to your assessment, because this is not just my home, it is our home. Which things have really helped you? Which could be done another way?
ask: Of the new family rhythms in these weeks, which feels most natural and most helpful to you?
Which feels most awkward or hardest? How would you suggest adjusting it?
youth.do: Ask your child also to score the themes of weeks 22–30, and parents and child compare scores and start talking from the item with the biggest gap, then decide together which habits to keep and which to strengthen.

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for helping us in these days to pray together, worship together and guard our hearts together. Please keep leading our family to love you more and more, and to love one another more and more. In Jesus’ name, amen.

30.memT: Therefore watch carefully how you walk, not as unwise, but as wise, redeeming the time, because the days are evil.

mem.t: We love him, because he first loved us.

sat.t: Family Day: I Am Your Harbor
sat.d: Set aside a stretch of “special time” for each child with Dad or Mom, one on one, for at least thirty minutes. Wherever possible, let the child decide what to do: a walk in the park, drawing, ball games or browsing a bookshop. Parents keep their phones away the whole time, simply following, appreciating and responding. At dinner, let everyone say, “My favorite moment today was…”. Finally, tell each child, “I love being with you, not because of anything you have done, but because you are you.”

sun: Think back to your own childhood. What is your safest memory, and who gave it to you?
This week, did you notice that you gave your children “things” more often, or gave them “yourself”?
Which child would you like to plan some one-on-one time with next week? You could also ask another member of the group to share how they do it, so you can learn from each other.

lessons.title: We Love Because He First Loved Us
lessons.theme: A child’s sense of security begins with parents who are first filled with God’s love

v: We know and have believed the love which God has for us. God is love, and he who remains in love remains in God, and God remains in him.
In this, love has been made perfect among us, that we may have boldness in the day of judgment, because as he is, even so we are in this world.
There is no fear in love; but perfect love casts out fear, because fear has punishment. He who fears is not made perfect in love.
We love him, because he first loved us.

lessons.still: Sit quietly and let yourself be loved. Don’t hurry to pray for your children or plan your day. Simply say to the Lord, “Lord, you loved me first.” Let those words slowly fill your heart.
teach: When John wrote his letters in old age, he kept coming back to one thing: love. He said, “God is love, and he who remains in love remains in God, and God remains in him.” And again, “We love him, because he first loved us.” Love has a source, and it has an order: we are loved first, and then we are able to love. This is true for children, and it is true for parents too.

From this week we move into the “relationships” stage, and our first theme is “secure attachment”. It sounds technical, but the meaning is simple: deep in his heart, the child is sure that “when I need you, you will be there.” A little boat only dares to sail out and explore when it has a safe harbor to return to. A child with such a harbor dares to learn, to make friends and to face failure.

Many parents think children need better toys, more tutoring and a bigger house. These all have their place, but a child’s deepest need is for a parent who sees him, responds to him and stays beside him. And for a parent to be that harbor, he or she must first be anchored in God’s love. Only a full cup can pour out water; only a heart filled with love can love a child steadily.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The order of relationships is first with God, then with ourselves, then with others. If parents are not first filled with God’s love, they will look to their children for worth and comfort. When parents first live in God’s love, they can love their children in the self-emptied way, without asking for anything in return. This is “life first, then relationships” put into practice.
q: Who is God? — God is love, and he loved me first. When have I most truly experienced his love?
Who am I? — Does the love I give my children flow from God, or am I squeezing it out of my own limited strength?
How should I respond? — In what way can I help my child be sure today that “when you need me, I will be there”?
lessons.jesus: When Jesus was baptized, a voice from heaven said, “This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased.” At that point he had not yet performed a single miracle or preached a single sermon. The Father’s love came before his ministry. Jesus set out from that love into the wilderness and onto the cross. Parents, too, can receive this love first, and then go and love their children.
lessons.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for loving me first. I admit that I am often tired and empty, yet I keep pushing on to love my children, and the more I try, the more irritable I become. Today I come to you first and ask you to fill me with your love. Make me a safe harbor for my children, so that through me they may come to know the God who loved us first. Amen.
acts: Spend five quiet minutes today meditating on 1 John 4:19. Receive God’s love first, then begin your day
When your child comes to you today, stop what you are doing at least three times, turn around and answer them with your eyes on theirs
At bedtime, say to each child, “When you need me, I will be there.”
lessons.noon: “We love him, because he first loved us.” — Lord, fill me first, so that your love may flow through me to my children.

fam.key: God loved us first, and we love one another.

lamb.do: When your baby cries, pick him up right away, hold him against your chest and rock him gently until he is calm.
lamb.say: I am here. You are not alone. God loves you, and I love you.

sprout.story: Bobo the little boat went out to sea to play every day. Sometimes the waves were big, and he sailed quickly back to the harbor. The harbor was so quiet and so safe. When Bobo had rested enough, he bravely set out to sea again. Xiaomi asked Mommy, “Where is my harbor?” Mommy hugged her and said, “Mommy and Daddy are your harbor! Whenever you are scared or sad, you can come back to us any time. And our harbor is God.”
sprout.ask: When you are scared or sad, who do you most want to go to?
sprout.do: Play “Boat Back to Harbor”: the child is the little boat “sailing” around the living room, and Mom and Dad open their arms to be the harbor. When someone calls out, “The wind is up!”, the child runs back to be hugged.

soldier.story: Jiahao in Johor had just changed schools and had no friends yet. He came home quiet every day. Mom did not rush to ask about his test marks. Instead she put down her phone, sat beside him and said, “Changing schools must be really hard.” Suddenly Jiahao burst into tears and poured out how hurt he had felt these past few days. Mom didn’t lecture him. She just held him. The next day Jiahao said, “Mom, today I started talking to a classmate.” When there is a place to come back to, a person finds the courage to go forward. John says we are able to love because God loved us first.
ask: In our family, when do you feel safest?
When something sad happens, how do you want Mom and Dad to be with you?
soldier.do: Each person writes a card to one family member: “When you need me, I can…” (for example, keep you company, listen to you, pray for you). Then swap cards.

youth.talk: You are growing up and becoming more independent, and in many things you don’t need us any more. But I want you to know that, whatever your age and whatever you are going through, this home is always a place you can come back to. I am not perfect either. Sometimes I am too busy or too hurried, and you may have felt that I wasn’t there. The Bible says we love because God first loved us. I am learning to be loved by God first, and then to love you well.
ask: What do you feel you need most from Mom and Dad right now?
Has there been a time when you needed us but felt we weren’t there?
youth.do: Choose a relaxed moment and tell your child, “Whatever happens, you can come to me.” Then ask, “What can I do to help you trust those words more?” Just listen, without defending yourself.

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for loving us first. Fill our home with your love, so that everyone knows that when they need us, family will be there. In Jesus’ name, amen.

lessons.title: Giving Things, or Giving Yourself?
lessons.theme: Willing to give even ourselves: what children need most is their parents’ presence

v: But we were gentle among you, like a nursing mother cherishes her own children.
Even so, affectionately longing for you, we were well pleased to impart to you not the Good News of God only, but also our own souls, because you had become very dear to us.

lessons.still: Ask the Holy Spirit to take you back through some scenes of this week with your children. Look at yourself: my body was there, but was my heart there too? Look quietly, without rushing to blame yourself.
teach: Paul described his love for the believers as that of “a nursing mother” who “cherishes her own children”. He said, “we were well pleased to impart to you not the Good News of God only, but also our own souls.” What Paul gave was not only teaching, but himself. This is what children need most too: not only the things their parents give, but the parents themselves, with their time, their attention and a tender heart.

Let the Holy Spirit show us what kind of parent we are. The “provider”: works hard so that the children lack nothing, but is seldom at home. The “manager”: arranges tutoring, activities and routines every day, until conversation is reduced to instructions. The “present but absent”: physically beside the child, but with the heart on the phone or at work. The “hot and cold”: close when in a good mood, and the children dare not come near when in a bad one. Behind all of these is often a heart that loves its children but is already very tired.

Mrs. Chen in Sydney is a mom in a two-income family. One day her six-year-old son asked her, “Mom, can I use my pocket money to buy an hour of you?” She was stunned. What the child wanted was not more toys, but his mother. Seeing this is painful, but pain is where change begins. God shines his light on us because he wants to help us give ourselves back to our children.
lessons.light: 321 Light: People matter more than tasks, and relationships matter more than things. The self-ruled parent uses things to make up for absence, and schedules in place of companionship. The self-emptied parent is willing to lay down the most precious thing, himself or herself. Life first, then relationships, then ministry: our children are not projects to complete, but people to love with our very lives.
q: Who is God? — God did not only give gifts; he gave us his own Son. What does this say about his heart?
Who am I? — Provider, manager, present but absent, or hot and cold: which am I most like?
How should I respond? — This week, what one thing can I give my child less of, and what kind of “me” can I give more of?
lessons.jesus: God so loved the world that “he gave his only born Son”. He did not simply drop gifts down from heaven. Jesus became flesh and lived among us, eating with people, walking with them and weeping with them. God’s greatest gift is his own presence, and this is also the greatest gift a parent can give a child.
lessons.pray: Lord, I admit that I often use things, schedules and busyness in place of being with my children. I am beside them, but my heart is somewhere else. Forgive me, and heal my weariness. Help me, like Paul, to give my children not only teaching but myself, so that in my presence they may sense your presence. Amen.
acts: Honestly write down: this week, what did I give my child most, things, instructions or companionship?
Tonight, spend at least five minutes with each child, body and heart beside them, doing nothing else
Next time you want to buy something to make up to your child, invite them to do something together instead
lessons.noon: “we were well pleased to impart to you not the Good News of God only, but also our own souls” — Lord, help me give myself to my children today, not just things.

fam.key: Having you with me is better than any present.

lamb.do: Today, skip the new toy and use yourself as the toy: let your baby climb on you, play “airplane”, or roll around together on the play mat.
lamb.say: Mommy and Daddy are your best toys. I love playing with you.

sprout.story: On his birthday, Xiaojie received lots of presents: cars, building blocks, dinosaurs. But his happiest moment was in the evening, when Dad built a tent with him in the living room, and the two of them hid inside, telling stories by torchlight. At bedtime, Mom asked, “Which present did you like best today?” Xiaojie said, “I liked Daddy being with me in the tent best!”
sprout.ask: What do you like best to do with Mom and Dad?
sprout.do: Use blankets and chairs to build a little tent. Dad or Mom crawls in with the child, and together they tell a Bible story by torchlight.

soldier.story: Paul wrote to his friends in Thessalonica and told them he loved them like a mother caring for her little baby. He didn’t only tell them God’s good news; he was willing to give them his very life. The best gifts are not bought with money, but are someone giving you their time, attention and heart. Think about it: what is the most unforgettable gift you have ever received? Very often, what we remember most is not a thing, but a day when someone was with us.
ask: What is the most unforgettable gift you have received? Was it a thing, or time with someone?
Do you feel Mom and Dad have given you enough time lately?
soldier.do: Each child writes a “time together coupon” for Dad or Mom, naming one thing they would like to do together. The parents must cash it in this week.

youth.talk: Sometimes I have thought that giving you good things and sending you to good tutoring classes was how I loved you. But I have also noticed that we rarely have a real conversation. Often I am next to you while my mind is on work or my phone. Paul said he gave people not only the gospel but himself as well. I want to ask you: more than the things I give you, what would you like me to give you?
ask: Which am I more like: very good at providing, very good at organizing, here in body but not in mind, or very different depending on my mood?
If you could choose, what is one thing you would like us to do together more?
youth.do: This week, parents arrange one-on-one time with a child, with the child choosing the place and the activity. Bring no “issue to discuss”, and simply be together.

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for sending us Jesus, who is always with us. Help everyone in our family to give each other not only things, but also our time and our hearts. In Jesus’ name, amen.

lessons.title: I Will Not Forget You
lessons.theme: I believe: true security comes from God’s never-changing love

v: “Can a woman forget her nursing child, that she should not have compassion on the son of her womb? Yes, these may forget, yet I will not forget you!
Behold, I have engraved you on the palms of my hands. Your walls are continually before me.
When my father and my mother forsake me, then the LORD will take me up.

lessons.still: Open your hand and look at your palm quietly. Imagine God’s palm with your name engraved on it, and your children’s names too. Say to the Lord, “You have never forgotten me.”
teach: Zion once cried, “The LORD has forsaken me, and the Lord has forgotten me.” God answered, “Can a woman forget her nursing child, that she should not have compassion on the son of her womb? Yes, these may forget, yet I will not forget you!” God uses the closest bond on earth, between a mother and her baby, to picture his love, and then says that his love is more dependable than a mother’s: “I have engraved you on the palms of my hands.”

Some parents feel sad when they read about secure attachment, because they did not receive it themselves as children. Perhaps their parents were busy or harsh, or there was hurt or absence in the home. David said, “When my father and my mother forsake me, then the LORD will take me up.” We cannot give what we do not have, but God can give it to us again. If childhood pain runs deep, please don’t carry it alone. Seek the company of a pastor or a professional counselor.

This brings a change of perspective: my security does not come from my childhood, my performance or my children’s achievements, but from the God who has engraved me on his palms. When parents are settled in God’s love, they can become a refuge for their children, rather than people who need their children to calm them. Today, please write down your own “I believe”: I believe God never forgets me; I believe he can give me back the ability to love; I believe I can become my children’s harbor.
lessons.light: 321 Light: A change of perspective, from a human point of view to God’s point of view. My past cannot define me; only God’s love can. The focus is on Jesus, not on my own scars or the shortcomings of the previous generation. Parents healed by God’s love can turn a cycle of hurt into a legacy of blessing.
q: Who is God? — God says, “I will not forget you,” and engraves me on his palms. What kind of love is this?
Who am I? — Where does my own sense of security come from? How has my childhood shaped the way I love my children now?
How should I respond? — Write your “I believe”: I believe God…; I believe I can…
lessons.jesus: After his resurrection, Jesus appeared to Thomas and held out his nail-scarred hands: “Reach here your finger, and see my hands.” The scars on those hands prove that his love is real and never changes. We are engraved on those hands. This love is the safe harbor shared by parents and children alike.
lessons.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for never forgetting me, and for engraving me on your palms. I admit that there are gaps in my heart left from childhood, and sometimes they leave me unsure how to love my children. I believe you can take me up, heal me and give me back the ability to love. Let me find rest in you and become my children’s harbor. Let the hurt stop with my generation, and let blessing begin with it. Amen.
acts: Write out your “I believe” declaration: I believe God never forgets me; I believe he can…; I believe I can become my children’s…
Write down a childhood memory in which you felt safe, and thank God for that person. If a painful memory comes up, give that to God too
If childhood pain often affects how you react to your children, arrange this week to talk with a pastor or counselor
lessons.noon: “Yes, these may forget, yet I will not forget you!” — Lord, thank you for never forgetting me, and never forgetting my children.

fam.key: God will never forget me.
