lamb.do: With your finger, gently draw a heart on your baby’s little palm, then kiss the palm.
lamb.say: God has written you on his hands. He will never forget you.

sprout.story: Xiao’an got separated from Mommy in the supermarket. She was so scared that she stood still and cried. Then an announcement came: “Little Xiao’an, your mommy is waiting for you at the service desk.” Xiao’an ran over, and Mommy hugged her tightly and said, “I’ve been looking for you. How could I ever forget you!” That night Mommy said, “God loves you even more than Mommy does. Even if Mommy one day forgets something, God will never forget you.”
sprout.ask: Do you know that God will never forget you? How does that feel?
sprout.do: Gently draw a heart on your child’s palm with a pen and say, “God has engraved you on his hand!” Then ask the child to draw one on Mom’s and Dad’s palms too.

soldier.story: When the Israelites were taken away to a foreign land, they thought God had forgotten them. But God said: how could a mother forget her nursing baby? Even if a mother could forget, I will not forget you. I have engraved you on my palms! Imagine a name engraved on your hand, so that you see it every day when you open your hand. That is how God remembers you all the time. Mom and Dad sometimes get busy, get tired and make mistakes, but God’s love never changes. That is our safest place.
ask: Have you ever felt forgotten by someone? How did it feel?
Knowing that God has engraved you on his hand, what would you like to say to him?
soldier.do: Each family member traces their own hand on paper, writes the names of the family and “God does not forget you” on the hand drawing, and sticks them on the wall.

youth.talk: There is something I rarely tell you. When I was little, the adults at home were all very busy, and I often felt I didn’t matter. As an adult, I have found that this feeling sometimes still affects how I treat you, making me too hasty and too controlling. But God says that even if parents forget, he will not forget us. I am learning to let God’s love heal me, and I hope I can love you well.
ask: Where do you feel your sense of security mainly comes from?
Have there been times when you felt forgotten, or not valued?
youth.do: Parents share a memory from their own childhood, good or hard, then read Isaiah 49:15–16 together and pray for each other.

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for never forgetting us, and for engraving us on your hands. When we feel lonely, remind us that you are always here. In Jesus’ name, amen.

lessons.title: Jesus Takes the Children in His Arms
lessons.theme: Daily moments of connection: eye contact, touch, focus and response

v: They were bringing to him little children, that he should touch them, but the disciples rebuked those who were bringing them.
But when Jesus saw it, he was moved with indignation and said to them, “Allow the little children to come to me! Don’t forbid them, for God’s Kingdom belongs to such as these.
Most certainly I tell you, whoever will not receive God’s Kingdom like a little child, he will in no way enter into it.”
He took them in his arms and blessed them, laying his hands on them.

lessons.still: Imagine Jesus opening his arms and taking the children up one by one. Imagine yourself being held by him as well. Be still for a while and let that warmth stay in your heart.
teach: People were bringing little children to Jesus, but the disciples thought he was too busy and rebuked them. When Jesus saw it, “he was moved with indignation” and said, “Allow the little children to come to me! Don’t forbid them.” Then he “took them in his arms and blessed them, laying his hands on them.” Holding, touching, blessing: Jesus used his body, his time and his words to let the children know they were welcome.

Secure attachment is not built on one big trip, but grows from small connections, day after day. You can try the “four connections”. Eye contact: when your child speaks, stop and look at him. Touch: a hug, a pat on the shoulder, a stroke of the head, in whatever way your child likes. Focus: ten minutes a day when the child leads the play or the conversation and the parent simply follows. Response: when a child is upset, first receive the feeling, then deal with the problem.

Three daily “connection points” are especially important. At parting, say goodbye with a regular blessing before leaving for school. At reunion, when picking up from school or coming home from work, hug first and greet first, and ask about homework later. At bedtime, spend a few minutes helping your child look back on the day. In Hsinchu, a grandfather and grandmother were raising two grandsons. Every day Grandpa stood at the school gate with open arms to greet them. One grandson said, “When I see Grandpa’s arms, I know I’m safe.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Use the heart and rely on the Holy Spirit, not the mind and your own strength. Connection is not a set of techniques but a willing heart, and the Holy Spirit will remind us when to stop. People matter more than tasks: when a child comes to us, that is a moment of connection given by God, and it matters more than whatever we have in our hands.
q: Who is God? — Jesus was indignant when the children were turned away. How does he see every child?
Who am I? — Eye contact, touch, focus, response: which of these four connections do I neglect most often?
How should I respond? — At parting, at reunion and at bedtime today, how will I connect with my child?
lessons.jesus: In the disciples’ eyes, the children were a nuisance. In Jesus’ eyes, they were a picture of the Kingdom. He did not merely allow the children to come near; he took them into his own arms. Our Lord is one who stops, who embraces and who blesses. His open arms are the example every parent can learn from.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, thank you for welcoming little children, and for welcoming me. I admit that, like the disciples, I often see my children as interruptions. Give me a heart willing to stop. Through eye contact, hugs, focus and response, let my children know they are welcome and loved. Bless my children through my hands. Amen.
acts: Today, give each child ten minutes of “special time”: the child leads, the parent follows, with no phone
Create a regular blessing for leaving home, for example, “God be with you. I love you.” Start saying it tomorrow morning
When you reunite with your child after school or work today, hug first and greet first, and ask about homework a little later
lessons.noon: “Allow the little children to come to me! Don’t forbid them” — Lord, help me open my arms to welcome my children today.

fam.key: Our family’s arms are always open.

lamb.do: When your baby wakes, and when you come home, the first thing to do is crouch down, open your arms, wait for him to fall into your embrace and hold him tight.
lamb.say: I am so happy to see you! Jesus opens his arms to welcome you too.

sprout.story: One day, many moms and dads brought their children to see Jesus. Jesus’ friends said, “Go away, go away! Jesus is busy!” The children were so sad. But Jesus said, “Let the little children come to me!” He picked up the children one by one, stroked their heads and blessed them. The children all smiled, because Jesus loved them most of all!
sprout.ask: How do you like Mom and Dad to hold you?
sprout.do: The whole family plays “Hug and Bless”: Mom and Dad open their arms, the child runs over to be picked up, and Mom and Dad say, “You are welcome here, and Jesus blesses you!”

soldier.story: Every day when Siying in Singapore came home from school, Mom’s first words were always, “Did you finish your homework? What did you get on the test?” Siying wanted to tell her about school less and less. Later Mom read the story of Jesus taking the children in his arms and decided to change. She waited at the door for Siying, gave her a hug first and said, “You’ve worked hard today. I missed you so much.” Then they ate a snack together. A few days later Siying began telling Mom about her class on her own, and even told her about something that had made her very sad. Mom discovered that when we connect first, children open their hearts.
ask: When you come home from school, what do you most want Mom and Dad to say first?
Which way of being loved do you like: a hug, a chat, playing together or something else?
soldier.do: As a family, make up three “connection signals”: a blessing for leaving home, a style of hug for coming home and a goodnight ritual for bedtime. Practice them every day this week.

youth.talk: I have noticed that when you come home, my first words are often about homework and grades, as if you were a project that needs managing. I want to change. Jesus first took the children in his arms and first blessed them. You are older now and may not like so many hugs, and I will respect that. I want to ask you: how do you like us to show we care? I want to learn to connect with you in a way that feels comfortable to you.
ask: When you come home, how would you most like us to welcome you?
How do you like me to show I care: a word, a pat on the shoulder, a text message, or sharing a late-night snack?
youth.do: Parent and child agree on a “daily connection point”, for example ten minutes over a late-night snack or a walk, and do it at least five days this week.

fam.pray: Lord Jesus, thank you for opening your arms to welcome little children. Help everyone in our family to open our arms every day to welcome and embrace one another. In Jesus’ name, amen.

lessons.title: He Rejoices Over You
lessons.theme: Review & Adjust: did my children feel “delighted in” this week?

v: The LORD, your God, is among you, a mighty one who will save. He will rejoice over you with joy. He will calm you in his love. He will rejoice over you with singing.
Surely I have stilled and quieted my soul, like a weaned child with his mother, like a weaned child is my soul within me.

lessons.still: Listen quietly: God rejoices over you with joy and calms you in his love. Not because of how well you did this week, but because you are his child. Let these words quiet your heart.
teach: The prophet Zephaniah described God this way: “The LORD, your God, is among you, a mighty one who will save. He will rejoice over you with joy. He will calm you in his love. He will rejoice over you with singing.” Picture a father looking at his sleeping child with a quiet smile, or, seeing the child learn to walk, unable to hold back a cheer. This is how God feels about his children. A child’s deepest security comes from being sure “I am delighted in”, and not only “I am disciplined”.

David said, “I have stilled and quieted my soul, like a weaned child with his mother.” A weaned child leans on his mother’s breast not to be fed, but simply because he likes to be there. This is the loveliest picture of secure attachment: the child does not have to perform or please, and feels at peace just being near his parents. This week, when our children are near us, do they feel that settled?

This week we have learned that God loved us first; that children need their parents themselves; that God never forgets us; and that Jesus took the children in his arms. Today is not for giving ourselves a score, but for an honest look back: this week, did my children see me frowning most of the time, or delighting in them? After the review, choose one small adjustment: perhaps saying “I really like you” every day, or adding a hug when they come home from school.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The focus is on Jesus, not on ourselves or our children’s performance. When parents look only at grades and behavior, children learn to trade performance for love. When parents delight in their children for who they are, as God does, children learn: I am loved because I belong to this family, and I belong to God.
q: Who is God? — God rejoices over me and calms me in his love. How does this change how I see myself?
Who am I? — This week, what did my children see most on my face, delight or impatience?
How should I respond? — Next week, what concrete action will let my children feel “I delight in you”?
lessons.jesus: When Jesus met Zacchaeus, he did not settle accounts first. He looked up and said, “today I must stay at your house.” He called his weak disciples friends. He delighted to be with people, and even tax collectors and sinners were drawn to him. Jesus lets us know that before God, we are not a burden, but people he delights in.
lessons.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for rejoicing over me and calming me in your love. For the moments this week when I was truly present with my children, thank you; for the times I was hasty, cold or only looked at performance, please forgive me. Let my face often reflect your joy, so that my children, in my arms, may be as calm and quiet as a weaned child with his mother. Amen.
acts: Talk with your spouse for ten minutes: in what moments this week did our children feel most secure? When did we make them feel they were not delighted in?
Ask your child, “This week, was I more like Jesus? Do you feel I like being with you?” Just listen, without defending yourself
Write down one concrete adjustment for next week, such as telling each child every day, “I really like you.”
lessons.noon: “He will rejoice over you with joy. He will calm you in his love.” — Lord, thank you for delighting in me. Help me delight in my children in the same way.

fam.key: God is happy because of me.

lamb.do: When your baby is asleep, sit beside the bed and quietly watch him. Gently stroke his head and thank God for him in your heart. When he wakes, give him a great big smile.
lamb.say: I like you so much, and God likes you so much.

sprout.story: Xiaochen drew a picture, but it was a little crooked. She was afraid it wasn’t nice, so she didn’t dare show Daddy. When Daddy saw it, his eyes lit up. “Wow! Did you draw this? I love it!” Xiaochen asked, “But it’s crooked.” Daddy picked her up and said, “I love it because you drew it!” The Bible says that when God sees us, he is so happy he sings and cheers!
sprout.ask: Did you know that God is very happy when he sees you?
sprout.do: Take turns standing in the middle while everyone else claps and cheers, “God is happy because of you!” Make sure everyone gets a turn.

soldier.story: The prophet Zephaniah said that God rejoices over us with joy, so happy that he even sings for joy! This is not because we scored one hundred on a test, but because we are his children. This week our family practiced hugging, being together and playing together. Now let’s look back: did you feel this week that Mom and Dad really liked being with you? Was there a moment when you felt ignored? Mom and Dad want to hear what is really in your heart, and when we have listened, we will say thank you first.
ask: This week, when did you feel most loved and happiest?
Was there a moment when you wished Mom and Dad had stayed with you a little longer?
soldier.do: Family meeting: each person shares one thing this week that made them feel liked by a family member. Parents go first. Finally, the whole family chooses one habit of connection to continue next week.

youth.talk: All this week I have been wondering: when you look at my face, do you mostly see delight, or worry and demands? Honestly, I am often so focused on your grades and performance that I forget to let you know that I like you just because you are you. The Bible says God rejoices over us with joy. I want to learn to love you that way. Do you think I was even a little different this week?
ask: Do you feel Mom and Dad care more about how you perform, or about who you are? What makes you think so?
Next week, what can I do to help you feel more that I like being with you?
youth.do: Parents write a short card to their child with three reasons “I like you because you are you”, without mentioning grades or performance, and leave it on the child’s pillow.

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for being happy because of us. Help everyone in our family also to delight in one another, to hug and love one another. In Jesus’ name, amen.

31.memT: We love him, because he first loved us.

mem.t: He who answers before he hears, that is folly and shame to him.

sat.d: Take the whole family for a walk in a park or around the neighbourhood. On the first stretch, nobody talks and everyone just listens: birdsong, wind, footsteps. See who can hear the most different sounds. On the second stretch, pair up. One person shares something happy or worrying from recent days, and the other only listens, without interrupting. Then the listener says it back in their own words: “So you’re saying… is that right?” Then swap. Back home, each person finishes the sentence, “Being really listened to feels like…”. Finally, hold hands and pray for one another.

sun: This week, when did you catch yourself “answering before you had heard”? How did your child react?
Judge, fixer, lecturer or distracted: which kind of listener are you most often? Where might you have picked up that habit?
How could you bring “hear first, speak later” to another family or a colleague around you? What one listening action will you practice next week?

lessons.title: Hear It All, Then Answer
lessons.theme: To answer before hearing is both folly and shame

v: He who answers before he hears, that is folly and shame to him.
So, then, my beloved brothers, let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger;
for the anger of man doesn’t produce the righteousness of God.

lessons.still: Before you speak your first words today, be quiet for one minute. Don’t rush to pray or run through your to-do list. Just listen: the sounds outside the window, your own breathing, and the gentle Holy Spirit in your heart. Softly say to the Lord, “Lord, today I will listen to you first.”
teach: Many parents listen to their children like people listening to a news story whose ending they already know. The child has only just said, “Today my teacher…”, and in our heads we already have the answer and our mouths are ready with the next lecture. Proverbs says, “He who answers before he hears, that is folly and shame to him.” It is folly, because what we answer is often not the child’s real question. It is shame, because what the child hears in our interruption is, “What you say doesn’t matter.”

James says, “let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger.” It is like the accelerator and brake of a car: parents often press the accelerator with the mouth and the brake with the ears, but James wants it the other way round. He puts hearing and anger in the same sentence because much anger begins when we judge before we have heard. “The anger of man doesn’t produce the righteousness of God”: however loudly we shout, we cannot shout righteousness into a child’s heart.

Listening has two layers: hearing the words, and hearing the heart behind the words. When a child says, “I don’t want to go to school,” behind it there may be a classmate leaving him out, fear of a test, or simply tiredness. Rush to correct the sentence and we miss the heart. Listening is a form of respect: I am willing to let you finish, because you are more important than the point I want to make. People matter more than tasks. First receive the person, then deal with the matter.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Rushing to answer is often the self-ruled life: my opinion, my time and my reasoning matter most. Listening gives up the center place, so that the child can be a child and God can be God. Deal first with our own hasty hearts, then respond to the child’s words. Relationship matters more than reasoning.
q: Who is God? — God sees right through the heart, yet still patiently hears people out. Where have you experienced his patience?
Who am I? — After which sentence of my child’s do I most often find myself interrupting?
How should I respond? — What will I do today to let my child “finish what he is saying”?
lessons.jesus: When Jesus was twelve, he stayed behind in the temple, “sitting in the middle of the teachers, both listening to them and asking them questions.” The Son of God did not rush to preach; he listened first and then asked. Later, when he talked with the Samaritan woman at the well, he also listened step by step until her deepest thirst came to the surface. Jesus is the loveliest example of a listener.
lessons.pray: Lord, I admit that I often answer before I have heard, and my reasoning interrupts my child’s heart. Give me ears quick to hear, a mouth slow to speak and a heart slow to anger. Today, let my children sense in me that what they say matters, because they matter. In the name of the Lord Jesus, amen.
acts: At least once today, wait until your child has finished, then count three seconds in your head before you speak
When your child talks, put down your phone, turn to face them and look into their eyes
At bedtime, ask, “Is there anything you’d like to tell me about today?” Then only listen
lessons.noon: “let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger” — Lord, guard my mouth and open my ears right now.

fam.key: Listen to the end, then speak.

lamb.do: When your baby babbles, stop what you are doing, look at him, copy his sounds back and take turns “talking”, like a conversation.
lamb.say: You are talking, and Mommy is listening. I want to hear everything you say.

sprout.story: Every time Bouncy the little rabbit listened to someone, he would shout, “I know! I know!” One day Grandpa Tortoise said, “Over by the forest there is a…” Bouncy at once said, “A big tree hollow, I know!” and hopped off. But what Grandpa Tortoise had been about to say was, “…a very deep pit, be careful!” Bouncy nearly fell in. From that day on, Bouncy learned: listen to the end, then speak.
sprout.ask: Why should we listen to the end of what people say?
sprout.do: Play “Finish Before You Move”: Mom or Dad gives one long instruction, such as “Touch your nose, clap twice, then jump once.” Wait until it is all said before starting.

soldier.story: Samuel was a little boy who lived in the temple. One night he heard someone call, “Samuel!” He thought it was Eli, the old priest, and ran to him three times. At last Eli understood that God was calling Samuel, and taught him to say, “Speak, for your servant hears.” Samuel did so, and God told him something important. The first spiritual lesson Samuel learned was not speaking but listening. Those who know how to listen can hear God, and can understand other people’s hearts.
ask: Who in our family do you think is best at listening to others? Why?
How do you feel when someone interrupts you before you have finished?
soldier.do: At dinner tonight, play “Relay Listening”: each person shares one thing about their day, and the next person must first repeat the main point of what the last person said, then share their own.

youth.talk: Mom and Dad want to admit something first: when you talk, we often start giving opinions, or even lecturing, before we’ve finished listening. The Bible says, “He who answers before he hears, that is folly and shame to him,” and when we read it we felt it was about us. We want to learn to hear you out first, without rushing to fix the problem or prove we’re right.
ask: When do you think Mom and Dad interrupt you most?
If you only want us to listen and not give advice, how would you like to remind us?
youth.do: Agree with your child on a signal for “listening-only mode”. For example, when the child says, “I just need you to listen,” the parents only nod and respond to feelings, without giving advice.

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for listening to us every time. Help everyone in our family to listen first and speak later, so that we all feel loved. In Jesus’ name, amen.

lessons.title: What Kind of Listener Am I?
lessons.theme: Job’s friends sat with him for seven days, but once they spoke, they became judges

v: Now when Job’s three friends heard of all this evil that had come on him, they each came from his own place: Eliphaz the Temanite, Bildad the Shuhite, and Zophar the Naamathite; and they made an appointment together to come to sympathize with him and to comfort him.
When they lifted up their eyes from a distance, and didn’t recognize him, they raised their voices, and wept; and they each tore his robe, and sprinkled dust on their heads toward the sky.
So they sat down with him on the ground seven days and seven nights, and no one spoke a word to him, for they saw that his grief was very great.

lessons.still: Ask the Holy Spirit to replay your most recent conversation with your child, like a video. Watch your expression, your eyes and your first sentence. Don’t rush to defend yourself. Just ask, “Lord, at that moment, was I listening, or was I waiting to speak?”
teach: In a single day, Job lost his property, his children and his health, and three friends hurried from far away to see him. They did one very precious thing right: “they sat down with him on the ground seven days and seven nights, and no one spoke a word to him, for they saw that his grief was very great.” Those seven days of silence are among the loveliest pictures of companionship in the Bible. They did not analyze, preach or hurry to find a cause. They simply sat beside the sufferer and let him know: you are not alone.

But when Job opened his mouth and poured out his pain, his friends could not hold back. They began to explain, to correct and to condemn, chapter after chapter, sure that Job must have sinned. Job later sighed, “You are all miserable comforters!” They changed from companions into judges, not because they did not love Job, but because they were too eager for an answer, to make themselves feel a bit more comfortable.

Many parents are like this. When our children are silent, we are good at being with them. When they complain, cry, or say things we don’t like to hear, we change roles. There are four common types. The judge decides right and wrong first. The fixer immediately offers solutions. The lecturer uses the moment to preach. The distracted listener says “mm-hmm” while looking at a screen. Today, ask the Holy Spirit to show you: which am I most often?
lessons.light: 321 Light: Seeing ourselves is where change begins. The proud listener hurries to prove himself right; the humble listener is willing to put down his answers first so that the other person’s heart can be heard. When parents are humble first, children dare to open up. Humility draws out humility; pride only stirs up pride, and both people get hurt.
q: Who is God? — He is not a comforter who adds to the grief but the God of all comfort. How have you experienced his comfort?
Who am I? — Judge, fixer, lecturer or distracted: which kind of listener am I most often?
How should I respond? — The next time my child complains, what will I say first instead of passing judgment?
lessons.jesus: After Lazarus died, Mary fell weeping at Jesus’ feet. Jesus did not correct her first, nor did he immediately teach about the resurrection. Scripture says he “groaned in the spirit and was troubled”, and then “Jesus wept.” He wept first with those who wept, and only then did the miracle. This is the deepest kind of listening.
lessons.pray: Lord, shine your light on me. I admit that when my children pour out their hearts to me, I am often like Job’s friends, hurrying to judge, to fix and to lecture. Forgive me. Teach me to sit quietly with them as those seven days did, so that my children feel safe beside me and come to know your comfort through me. In the name of the Lord Jesus, amen.
acts: Think back over your last three conversations with your child and write down what kind of listener you were
Today, when your child complains, begin with: “It sounds like you feel… (sad / angry / hurt).”
Ask your spouse to tell you honestly: “When I listen to people, what is the most unbearable habit I have?”
lessons.noon: “So they sat down with him on the ground seven days and seven nights, and no one spoke a word to him” — Lord, teach me to be with people first, and speak afterward.

fam.key: Stay with them first; don’t rush to speak.

lamb.do: When your baby cries and fusses, don’t rush to stop the crying. Hold him against your chest, rock him gently and wait for him to calm down slowly.
lamb.say: You’re sad. Daddy is here with you.

sprout.story: Duoduo the little bear’s balloon flew away, and he sat under a tree and cried. The little deer ran over and said, “Why are you crying? Just buy another one!” Duoduo cried even louder. The little squirrel came and said, “Who told you not to hold on properly!” Duoduo felt even sadder. Then the little hedgehog walked over slowly. He said nothing, just sat beside Duoduo and looked at the sky with him. After a while Duoduo wiped his tears and said, “Thank you for staying with me.”
sprout.ask: When you are sad, how do you most want others to be with you?
sprout.do: Act it out: one person pretends to be sad, and another practices sitting quietly beside them, then gently asking, “Would you like to tell me about it?”

soldier.story: Haoran, ten years old, from Penang, came home from soccer one day and said loudly, “I’m never playing soccer again!” Dad at once said, “Giving up that easily? You need perseverance!” Haoran slammed his bedroom door. The next day Mom tried a different way. She sat on his bed and asked, “What happened at soccer yesterday?” Haoran slowly told her: he had kicked a ball wide, his teammates laughed at him and the coach scolded him. He did not hate soccer; he just felt so embarrassed. Mom didn’t give advice straight away. She only said, “Being laughed at by everyone must hurt.” Haoran nodded, tears fell and his heart felt lighter.
ask: What do you think Haoran really wanted to say at the beginning?
When you are in a bad mood, what do you want Mom and Dad to say first?
soldier.do: Each of you tells Mom and Dad about a time when “that’s not what I actually meant”. Guess together what the real feeling behind the words was.

youth.talk: You may have noticed that when you tell us something, we often turn quickly into judges or advisers: “That’s your own problem,” “You should do it this way.” Job’s friends in the Bible did the same. At first they were wonderful company, but later they became judges. We want to ask you, and we want to hear the truth: when you talk to us, which kind of person do we seem more like? Whatever you say, we won’t be angry.
ask: Judge, fixer, lecturer or distracted: which do you think Mom and Dad are most like? Can you give an example?
Are there things you haven’t told us because you were afraid of being lectured?
youth.do: Parents only listen to the child’s answer, without explaining or arguing back, and say just one thing at the end: “Thank you for telling me. I will learn.”

fam.pray: Dear Heavenly Father, thank you for being with us when we are sad. Help everyone in our family to know how to stay with one another and comfort one another, without rushing to scold or to lecture. In Jesus’ name, amen.

lessons.title: He Turned His Ear to Me
lessons.theme: I believe: God listened to me first, so I can listen to my children

v: I love the LORD, because he listens to my voice, and my cries for mercy.
Because he has turned his ear to me, therefore I will call on him as long as I live.
The LORD’s eyes are toward the righteous. His ears listen to their cry.

lessons.still: Imagine the Heavenly Father bending down and bringing his ear close to you. You don’t have to speak beautifully or quickly. Slowly tell him the heaviest thing on your heart right now, then quietly sense his attention: he is listening.
teach: The psalmist said, “I love the LORD, because he listens to my voice, and my cries for mercy.” His reason for loving God is simple: God listened to him. “Turned his ear” is a vivid picture, like an adult crouching down and bringing an ear close to a little child to catch a tiny voice. The almighty God turns his ear to a weak person like this. He doesn’t mind that our voice is small, or that our concerns are trivial.

Many parents find it hard to listen to their children because they have rarely been listened to well themselves. The previous generation was busy making a living and had no strength left to hear our private thoughts, and when we grew up, we didn’t know what being heard felt like. So listening begins not with technique, but with being heard by God. A person who has been heard by the Heavenly Father has a full heart, and is in no hurry to grab the conversation or prove himself.

Turn from a human point of view to God’s point of view: from “my child must listen to me” to “I am willing, like the Heavenly Father, to listen to my child first.” God is not impatient with our prayers, even when they are repetitive, childish or muddled. He listens to the end and answers, sometimes by granting, sometimes by making us wait, but he never hangs up. Today we don’t only know that listening matters; we declare from the heart: I believe God listened to me first, so I can listen to my children.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Conviction is truth moving from the head into the heart. We love because God first loved us, and we listen because God first listened to us. Listen with the heart, relying on the Holy Spirit, not with the mind, thinking how to argue back. The heart brings joy; the mind brings worry. When the focus is on Jesus, listening has a source.
q: Who is God? — He is the God who turns his ear to me and hears my pleas. Picture the look on his face as he listens closely to you. What kind of God is that?
Who am I? — I am a child whom the Heavenly Father hears. How will this identity change how I listen to my children?
How should I respond? — Write your “I believe”: I believe God listens to my…; so I will listen to my children like this…
lessons.jesus: By the road outside Jericho, blind Bartimaeus cried out loudly. Many rebuked him and told him to be quiet. But Jesus stood still, said, “Call him,” and asked him, “What do you want me to do for you?” Jesus knew his need, yet let him say it with his own mouth. He stopped and listened closely for a man whom the crowd found noisy.
lessons.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for turning your ear to me. I believe you have heard each of my pleas, and understand even the sighs I cannot put into words. Because you listened to me first, I am willing to learn to listen to my children, not because I am patient, but because your patience is in me. Let my children come to know, through my listening, that you are a God who hears prayer. Amen.
acts: Write three “I believe” statements. The first is, “I believe God has always been listening to me.”
Tell God today something you haven’t said aloud for a long time, believing that he is listening
Say to your child, “I really want to hear what you say, and the Heavenly Father wants to hear too.”
lessons.noon: “Because he has turned his ear to me, therefore I will call on him as long as I live.” — Heavenly Father, thank you for listening to me, and help me listen well to people today.

fam.key: God is always listening to me.

lamb.do: At bedtime, hold your baby and bring your ear close to his little mouth. When he makes a sound, nod and smile with delight.
lamb.say: The Heavenly Father listens to you, and Mommy and Daddy listen to you too.

sprout.story: One night Xiao’an lay in bed and asked softly, “Mommy, if I pray very quietly, can God hear?” Mommy said, “Yes, he can! The Bible says God turns his ear to listen to us, just like this.” Mommy bent down and put her ear close to Xiao’an’s mouth. Xiao’an giggled and whispered in Mommy’s ear, “God, I love you.” Mommy said, “God heard that, and he is so happy!”
sprout.ask: What would you like to whisper to God today?
sprout.do: Play “Whispers”: take turns whispering a sentence into a family member’s ear. At the end, the whole family whispers one sentence to God together.

soldier.story: The Psalms are full of words spoken to God from the heart: happy songs, and also poems written in tears. The psalmists spoke to God when they were being chased, when they were ill, and even after they had done wrong. Why did they dare to tell God everything? Because they knew God was always listening. One psalm begins like this: “I love the LORD, because he listens to my voice.” God doesn’t listen only to well-behaved children. He also listens to angry, scared and sad hearts. Whatever you say, God is willing to hear it all.
ask: Is there anything you don’t dare tell God or Mom and Dad?
If God is always listening, what do you most want to say to him now?
soldier.do: Each person writes a short “letter to the Heavenly Father”. When it is written, you may read it aloud or put it away, trusting that God has already heard.

youth.talk: Sometimes you may feel that adults only want you to obey and rarely really listen to you. Honestly, Mom and Dad often are like that. But the God of the Bible is very different: he turns his ear to people and is willing to hear their pleas to the end, even their complaints and doubts. Today we want to declare something: we believe God is listening to us, so we want to learn to listen to you well, as he does.
ask: Do you think God really listens when you pray? Have there been times when you doubted it?
How do Mom and Dad listen in a way that makes you feel truly “heard”?
youth.do: Parent and child each write an “I believe…” statement, swap and read them, and agree on one time this week for a chat where you only listen and don’t lecture.

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for always listening to us. You hear us whether we are loud or quiet, or crying as we speak. We love you, and we will learn to listen to one another too. In Jesus’ name, amen.

lessons.title: Ask One Question, Listen to the End
lessons.theme: Like Jesus on the road to Emmaus: walk with them first, then ask, and speak last

v: Behold, two of them were going that very day to a village named Emmaus, which was sixty stadia from Jerusalem.
They talked with each other about all of these things which had happened.
While they talked and questioned together, Jesus himself came near, and went with them.
But their eyes were kept from recognizing him.
He said to them, “What are you talking about as you walk, and are sad?”

lessons.still: Think of the roads you will walk with your children today: the way to school, the ride home, the dinner table. Ask the Lord to show you that each stretch is your own Emmaus road, where he wants to walk with you.
teach: On the day of the resurrection, two disciples were walking home to Emmaus with heads bowed. Jesus himself came near and went with them, but he did not reveal who he was at once, nor did he begin to preach. He asked a question first: “What are you talking about as you walk, and are sad?” Then he let them pour out all their disappointment, confusion and broken hope. Only after they had finished did Jesus begin with Moses and all the prophets and explain the Scriptures to them.

This is listening in three steps: walk with them, ask, and hear them out. For modern parents, the best listening time is often not sitting face to face saying, “Let’s talk,” but side by side: driving, walking, washing dishes, or in the dark at bedtime. Side by side makes it easier to tell the truth than face to face, just like the two disciples, who spoke what was on their hearts as they walked. Children don’t have to look into your eyes, so they aren’t afraid of being judged by your expression.

The techniques are really simple. Ask open questions: “What was the funniest thing today?” opens up conversation better than “Was today good?” Restate your child’s meaning in your own words: “So you’re saying… is that right?” Name your child’s feelings: “It sounds like you’re disappointed.” Only at the end, ask: “Do you need me to give advice, or do you just need me to listen?” When you have listened first, your child will be able to take in what you say.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Practice means putting truth on the road of every day. Jesus is my example: he walked with them first, asked first and listened first. People matter more than tasks. More important than finishing our teaching is letting our children know: Mom and Dad are willing to walk this stretch of road with me. We hear and then do, and so listening becomes life.
q: Who is God? — The risen Lord was willing to step onto the road of two discouraged disciples, and he is willing to step into our family’s everyday life.
Who am I? — When I talk with my children, am I more like an interrogator, or a companion on the road?
How should I respond? — On which stretch of road today will I ask my child an open question, then listen to the end?
lessons.jesus: Jesus knew everything, yet he often asked questions. He asked his disciples, “Who do you say that I am?” He asked those who followed him, “What are you looking for?” He asked not because he did not know, but to let people say what was in their hearts. A good question is a door, and Jesus used it to open people’s hearts. He is the teacher who asked best and listened best.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, thank you for walking with me on my discouraged road, and for patiently hearing me out. Today, guide every conversation between me and my children on the road: let me ask gently, listen attentively and speak fittingly. When I want to interrupt or lecture, let the Holy Spirit remind me to hear it through to the end. Amen.
acts: On the school run or a walk today, ask your child an open question, such as, “What made you laugh today?”
Use “So you’re saying… is that right?” to restate your child’s words at least once
When your child has finished, ask, “Would you like me to give advice, or just listen?”
lessons.noon: “What are you talking about as you walk, and are sad?” — Lord, on the road today, teach me to ask first, and then to listen.

fam.key: Ask well, and listen closely.

lamb.do: As you walk with the stroller or carry your baby, point at what you see and ask, “What’s that?” Pause, wait for him to look and make a sound, then respond.
lamb.say: What do you see? Mommy is listening.

sprout.story: On Saturday morning, Grandma took Xiaojie by the hand to the wet market. All the way, Xiaojie kept calling, “Grandma, look! That cat! That balloon!” Each time Grandma stopped and asked, “Where do you think that cat is going?” Xiaojie thought and said, “He’s going home to find his mommy!” Grandma smiled and said, “So that’s what you thought!” Back home, Xiaojie said, “Going to the market with Grandma is the most fun, because Grandma always listens to me.”
sprout.ask: Who do you most like to walk and chat with? Why?
sprout.do: Take a short walk nearby as a family. Each person takes a turn to say, “I see…”, and the others must follow up by asking, “And then?”

soldier.story: On the day Jesus rose again, two disciples were walking along the road, very sad. Jesus came up beside them, walked with them and asked what they were talking about. They didn’t recognize him, so they told him all the sadness in their hearts. Jesus listened all the way, and only when they had finished did he tell them what the Scriptures say. In the evening, when they ate together, they finally recognized Jesus, and their hearts burned within them. Jesus accompanied them first, asked first and listened first, and spoke last.
ask: Why do you think Jesus didn’t say “I am Jesus” right at the start?
The next time a friend is sad, what question could you ask them?
soldier.do: At dinner tonight, each person prepares a “good question” for a family member (it can’t be answered with just good or bad). When the answer is given, the asker says, “So you’re saying… is that right?”

youth.talk: We have noticed that the best conversations are often not when we sit down to “have a talk”, but in the car, on a walk or over a late-night snack. Jesus and the two disciples also talked on the road: he asked first and listened first, and let them say all their disappointment. Mom and Dad want to try this, not to interrogate you but to walk a stretch of road with you and hear what you’ve been thinking about lately.
ask: When and where are you most willing to talk with Mom and Dad?
Has something disappointed or confused you lately that you’d be willing to talk about?
youth.do: This week, invite your child to do something “side by side”: a walk, a bike ride, or going out for a late-night snack. Ask only one question on the way and then listen to the end. Don’t give advice unless your child asks.

fam.pray: Lord Jesus, thank you for walking every road with us. Help us today to greet one another and listen to one another on the road, so that all our hearts burn within us. In Jesus’ name, amen.

lessons.title: This Week, Did I Hear My Child’s Heart?
lessons.theme: Review & Adjust: the words in a heart are like deep water, drawn out with patience

v: Counsel in the heart of man is like deep water, but a man of understanding will draw it out.
A fool has no delight in understanding, but only in revealing his own opinion.

lessons.still: Look back over this week’s conversations with your child, like drawing water from a well, one bucket at a time. Ask the Holy Spirit to walk through it with you: when did you bring the water up? When did you drop the bucket before the water came?
teach: “Counsel in the heart of man is like deep water, but a man of understanding will draw it out.” A child’s heart is like a deep well. On the surface it is “I don’t want to do my homework,” “Nothing,” “Whatever,” but underneath are hidden fear, hurt, longing and dreams. Someone in a hurry to draw water only scoops up the fallen leaves at the mouth of the well; only someone who lets down a long rope and patiently waits can draw the cool water below. A child’s heart does not open at the first question. We must wait, stay with them, and lower the bucket again and again.

Another proverb says, “A fool has no delight in understanding, but only in revealing his own opinion.” This week, did we prefer showing our children our own opinions, worries and reasoning to understanding them? Review is not about giving ourselves a mark, but honestly seeing when we heard and when we missed. What we missed can still be mended.

Listening can be practiced. Perhaps this week you managed to wait for your child to finish only once, and that too was a bucket of living water. Adjustments can be very concrete: set a regular time each day for listening, give up one interrupting phrase, and apologize to your child for one time you scolded before hearing the whole story. When a parent says, “I scolded you before I had heard you out, and I’m sorry,” the child learns to hear others out as well. A family culture of listening is built up in just this way, bit by bit.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Review, adjustment, repetition: life is renewed through practice, time after time. The proud parent only demands that children obey; the humble parent first learns to listen to the child. Life first, then relationships: when the parent’s ears change, the parent-child relationship changes with them. Change doesn’t come overnight, but through daily repetition.
q: Who is God? — He sees into the deep water of the heart, and is willing to give me understanding to draw out my child’s heart.
Who am I? — This week, when did I “draw up water” in a conversation? When did I only delight in revealing my own opinion?
How should I respond? — What regular listening time will I set up next week? How exactly will I start?
lessons.jesus: When Jesus met the Samaritan woman at the well, he began with “Give me a drink,” and step by step listened and asked until the deepest thirst of her heart came to the surface. He did not condemn her the moment he opened his mouth. He first drew out her heart, and then gave her living water. Jesus is the most patient drawer of water.
lessons.pray: Lord, thank you for walking back through this week with me. The times I heard my child’s heart were your grace. There were more times when I hurried to speak and hurried to teach, and I ask you to forgive me. Give me understanding, to draw out the words in my child’s heart with the patience of drawing water, and make our home a place where everyone dares to speak the truth. Amen.
acts: Talk with your spouse: in which conversation this week was our child most open? What interrupting habit does each of us most need to change?
Ask your child, “This week, have I got better at listening to you? What still needs to improve?” Just listen, without defending yourself
Write down next week’s adjustment, for example: “Ten minutes at bedtime every day, only listening, no lecturing.”
lessons.noon: “Counsel in the heart of man is like deep water, but a man of understanding will draw it out.” — Lord, give me patience to draw out the words in my child’s heart.

fam.key: Our family is willing to listen to one another’s hearts.

lamb.do: Play a scooping game with your baby using a little cup: slowly pour water cup by cup into a basin, and clap together when it is full.
lamb.say: Take your time. Mommy will wait for you, and Mommy is listening.

sprout.story: Xiaole’s mom is a nurse and often works night shifts. One morning Xiaole said nothing for a long time. Mom was about to say, “Hurry up and eat breakfast!” but she remembered this week’s lesson. She sat down, stroked Xiaole’s head and asked, “Xiaole, is there something on your heart?” Xiaole said softly, “I really want Mommy to sleep beside me at night.” Mom hugged him and said, “Thank you for telling me. Tonight I will stay with you.”
sprout.ask: Is there something on your heart that you really want to tell Mom and Dad?
sprout.do: Make a “heart-words bucket”: use a paper cup as the bucket, and each person writes or draws one heart-word to put inside. In the evening, open it up and listen together.

soldier.story: Junwei in Singapore is the middle one of three children and often feels that no one listens to him: his brother talks loudly, and whenever his little sister cries, everyone runs to her. This week the family began “taking turns” at dinner: when one person talks, no one else can interrupt. On the first day Junwei said only one sentence. By the fourth day he finally said, “I feel like I’m invisible at home.” Mom and Dad were surprised and heartbroken, and told him they were sorry. That night Junwei felt he had been seen.
ask: This week, did you feel you were listened to well? When?
How could our family get better at listening to each other next week?
soldier.do: Family meeting: each person says in one sentence who listened to them most carefully this week. Then decide together on one new listening agreement for next week.

youth.talk: All this week we have been learning to “hear first, then speak”. Honestly, Mom and Dad have improved, and several times we also fell into the old habit again: drawing conclusions before we had finished listening, or using the moment to lecture. We don’t want to pretend we did well. We want to hear how you really feel, because your view matters to us, and it can help us become more like Jesus.
ask: Was there a time this week when you felt Mom and Dad were really listening? What was that like?
If you gave Mom and Dad’s listening an “improvement score”, how much would you give? Where does it still fall short?
youth.do: Parents apologize to their child for one time they responded without hearing them out, then ask the child to help set next week’s “listening agreement”.

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for helping us learn to listen this week. Sometimes we listened well, and sometimes we rushed to speak. Forgive us, and help our family get better and better at hearing one another’s hearts. In Jesus’ name, amen.

32.memT: He who answers before he hears, that is folly and shame to him.

mem.t: Pleasant words are a honeycomb, sweet to the soul, and health to the bones.

sat.t: Family Day: A Honey Blessing Meal
sat.d: Prepare a small jar of honey and some toast or pancakes, and gather round the table. Take turns, and when it is someone’s turn, everyone says one specific “honey word” to him. Not “You’re great”, but “I saw you offer to carry Grandma’s shopping yesterday, and that was so thoughtful.” For every word the blessed person hears, he spreads a little honey on his toast, and at the end he eats it up sweetly. To close, parents put a hand on each child’s head and say, “You are a child God loves, and God delights in you.”

sun: What is one thing that was said to you as a child (good or hurtful) that you still remember? How did it shape you?
This week, what did you notice you said to your children most often? Was it honey, or a knife?
Who would you like to bless with one specific word of affirmation (a family member, a colleague or a child in your group)? How will you say it next week?

lessons.title: Pleasant Words Are a Honeycomb
lessons.theme: Words have power: they can sweeten the soul and bring health to the bones

v: Pleasant words are a honeycomb, sweet to the soul, and health to the bones.
Death and life are in the power of the tongue; those who love it will eat its fruit.

lessons.still: Be still and remember: what were the first and last words you said to your children yesterday? No need to grade them, just recall. Then say to the Lord, “Lord, speak to me first today, so that my words come from you.”
teach: In ancient times there was no sugar, and honey was the most precious sweetness. Weary Jonathan, on the battlefield, tasted a little honey, and “his eyes brightened.” Proverbs says, “Pleasant words are a honeycomb, sweet to the soul, and health to the bones.” A good word does not only make a child happy for the moment; it can sink into the bones and become his confidence for life. Many adults at fifty can still remember an encouraging word from a teacher or parent in childhood, and can still remember the one that stung.

Another proverb is even more direct: “Death and life are in the power of the tongue.” A parent’s tongue has a special authority, because children come to know themselves through their parents’ words. If we say, “You’re so clumsy,” the child thinks he is a clumsy person. If we say, “I can see how much care you put into that,” the child learns to see his own care. Words are like seeds: sown today, they take shape in the child’s heart tomorrow.

There are three kinds of affirming words. Affirming behavior: “Thank you for putting your bowl away.” Affirming effort and character: “You practiced for a whole week, and that perseverance is precious.” Affirming identity: “You are loved by God, and I love you, not because you do well.” All three are needed, but the deepest root is the third. A child who knows he is loved has strength to face failure; a child who knows who he is doesn’t need grades to prove himself.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Change your beliefs and you change your life. If a parent believes that “shouting makes them improve”, words become a whip. If a parent believes that “God’s word gives life”, words become honey. Our tongues belong to Jesus. When we let him reign over them, our words build what belongs to God in our home, and are not an outlet for our own emotions.
q: Who is God? — God created heaven and earth by his word, and his word carries life. By which of God’s words have you been healed?
Who am I? — This week, was the tongue I used on my children mostly sowing honey, or knives?
How should I respond? — What specific word of affirmation will I say to each child today?
lessons.jesus: When Jesus spoke in the synagogue at Nazareth, everyone “wondered at the gracious words which proceeded out of his mouth”. His words held both truth and grace. He rebuked the hypocrisy of the Pharisees, yet spoke comfort to the crushed. Jesus’ mouth was a honeycomb, and all who came to him tasted the sweetness of life.
lessons.pray: Lord, thank you that your word has brought me back to life. I admit that my mouth often says hasty, critical, comparing words that hurt my children’s hearts. Cleanse my lips, so that every word I say today may be as sweet as a honeycomb, comforting my children’s hearts and bringing health to their bones. In the name of the Lord Jesus, amen.
acts: Today, say one specific word of affirmation to each child, naming the behavior and the character you saw
Notice the negative sentence you say most often, write it down and ask the Lord to help you replace it
Leave a small note with a blessing in your child’s school bag or under their pillow
lessons.noon: “Pleasant words are a honeycomb, sweet to the soul, and health to the bones.” — Lord, let the words I speak right now be sweet, and healing to others.

fam.key: Kind words are as sweet as honey.

lamb.do: When bathing your baby or changing his clothes, gently rub his hands and feet and speak blessings softly, such as, “These are helpful little hands.”
lamb.say: You are a gift God gave us, and Mommy loves you so much.

sprout.story: Buzzy the little bee flew to the garden every day to gather nectar, then flew back to the hive and stored the honey drop by drop. One day a little ant fell down and was hurt, and cried and cried. Buzzy flew over and said, “You are so brave. I’ll walk you home.” The little ant heard this and felt so sweet inside, as if he had tasted honey. Buzzy said, “So kind words are a kind of honey too!”
sprout.ask: Who can you say a honey-sweet word to today?
sprout.do: Prepare a small spoon of honey. Each person says one kind word to a family member, and then lets that person lick a little taste, and together you say, “So sweet!”

soldier.story: Meiqi, eleven, from Kuching, had always struggled with math. For this test she practiced an extra half hour every night, and improved by only eight marks. She brought the paper home nervously, thinking Mom would say, “Only seventy?” Instead Mom said, “I saw you practice hard every day for two weeks, and that perseverance is worth more than the mark.” Meiqi was stunned, and her eyes turned red. That night she said, on her own, “Mom, next time I’ll work even harder.” One kind word gave her the strength to keep going.
ask: Do you remember a time when someone said something to you that gave you strength?
Which is more helpful, “You’re so clever” or “You worked so hard”? Why?
soldier.do: This week, be a “kind word detective”: every day find one good thing a family member did, and say it specifically at dinner: “I saw you…”

youth.talk: Mom and Dad want to tell you something from our hearts. When we were small we rarely heard adults say, “I’m proud of you,” as if praise would make people proud and only scolding would make them improve. So we often swapped encouragement for criticism without realizing it. The Bible says pleasant words are a honeycomb, and bring health to the bones. We want to learn to say more words that are sincere and specific, not as politeness, but because you really are worth seeing.
ask: When Mom and Dad praise you, can you tell whether it is sincere or just polite?
Is there something we said that still hurts you now? Would you be willing to tell us?
youth.do: Parents write a small card to their child, specifically naming three good qualities you see in them, and give it to them by hand, with no need for a response.

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for giving us mouths to speak. Help us today to say kind words as sweet as honey, so that everyone at home is happy. In Jesus’ name, amen.

lessons.title: The Same Mouth
lessons.theme: Praise and cursing come out of the same mouth, and this ought not to be

v: but nobody can tame the tongue. It is a restless evil, full of deadly poison.
With it we bless our God and Father, and with it we curse men who are made in the image of God.
Out of the same mouth comes blessing and cursing. My brothers, these things ought not to be so.

lessons.still: Ask the Holy Spirit to help you hear yourself. Recall the sounds of your home these past few days: the hurrying in the morning, the checking of homework at night. Ask quietly, “Lord, if my children recorded what I say, what would they hear most?”
teach: James speaks strongly: the tongue is “a restless evil, full of deadly poison.” What grieves him most is this: “With it we bless our God and Father, and with it we curse men who are made in the image of God.” On Sunday morning we sing praises in church; on the way home, the same mouth shouts at our child, “Why are you doing it again!” Our children are also made in God’s image, yet a parent’s words often turn that image into that of a fool.

What wounds most is often not one big outburst but the “labels” repeated again and again: “You’re just lazy,” “You’ll never learn,” “You’re just like your dad,” “Your brother would never do that.” A label is like a sticker on glass, and the first thing a child sees when he looks at himself is the sticker. In time, the child feels not just that he did something wrong, but that he himself is wrong. Comparison is a label too, telling the child: you only have worth when you beat someone else.

Today is not for sinking into self-blame, but for asking the Holy Spirit to show us: what kind of parent am I? The faultfinder who often says, “Why do you always…”? The comparer who loves to hold up other people? The exploder who says whatever comes out in a rage? The silent parent who rarely opens his mouth to praise? Admitting it is the beginning of healing. God doesn’t throw our mouths away. He wants to cleanse them, so that they become mouths of blessing again.
lessons.light: 321 Light: A self-ruled mouth speaks to vent, to win and to prove that I am right. A self-emptied mouth speaks to build people up. When we let Jesus reign over our tongues, the same mouth no longer praises God with one side and curses the children God made with the other, and Jesus receives the glory in our home too.
q: Who is God? — God made my child in his own image. How does he see my child?
Who am I? — Faultfinder, comparer, exploder, silent: which is my mouth most like? What label do I most often stick on my child?
How should I respond? — Which words will I confess to God, and which label will I take back from my child?
lessons.jesus: A woman who had suffered bleeding for twelve years had been labeled “unclean” by everyone, and she secretly touched Jesus’ cloak. Jesus stopped to look for her and said to her in front of everyone, “Your faith has made you well.” He didn’t call her by her illness. He tore off her twelve-year-old label by giving her a new name: “Daughter”.
lessons.pray: Lord, I admit that with the same mouth I have praised you and hurt the children you made. I have told them, “You’re just…”, and made a mistake into their identity. Forgive me. Cleanse my mouth as you cleansed Isaiah’s lips, so that from today I speak with the eyes with which you see my children. In the name of the Lord Jesus, amen.
acts: Write down the three negative sentences you say most often to your children, and confess them one by one before God
Watch today for “You always…” or “You never…”. The moment you hear yourself say it, stop and correct it
Find a quiet moment and say to your child, “I used to say you were…, and that wasn’t true. I’m sorry.”
lessons.noon: “Out of the same mouth comes blessing and cursing. My brothers, these things ought not to be so.” — Lord, cleanse my mouth so that today it is used only to bless.

fam.key: My mouth will speak blessings.

lamb.do: Hold your baby up to a mirror, point to his reflection, and say one by one, “These are God-made eyes, a God-made nose and a God-made little mouth.”
lamb.say: God made you, and you are so lovely.

sprout.story: Xiaokai had a water bottle full of clear water. As he drank he wondered: if I put mud in it and poured it out, what water would it be? Mommy said, “Muddy water, of course!” Then she said, “Our mouths are like water bottles. If the same mouth sometimes says kind words and sometimes says scolding words, it is like clear water mixed with muddy water. We need to ask Jesus to help us pour out only clear, good water.”
sprout.ask: Did your mouth pour out clear water or muddy water today?
sprout.do: Use two clear glasses, one with plain water and one with a drop of soy sauce. With each kind word, look at the clear water; with each unkind word, look at the soy-sauce water, and see which one you would want to drink.

soldier.story: Jiahao in Taichung is the eldest in his family and often heard adults say, “You’re the big brother. How can you be so thoughtless?” One day he spilled the milk, and Grandpa said offhandedly, “Butterfingers.” Jiahao didn’t cry; he quietly wiped up the milk. After that, at school, whenever he did something badly he said to himself, “I’m just a butterfingers.” Then one day Dad noticed. He crouched down and said, “I’m sorry. The grown-ups were wrong. You were just careless, not stupid. You are a good boy who takes responsibility for cleaning up.” That day it felt to Jiahao as if a sticker had been peeled off his heart.
ask: Is there something you often say about yourself? Is it true?
Have you ever stuck a “label” on a younger brother or sister or a classmate?
soldier.do: Take some sticky notes. Each person writes one thing someone said to them that made them sad, and you tear them up together and throw them away. Then each writes what God would say about you, and sticks it on the bedroom door.

youth.talk: One verse in the Bible has convicted Mom and Dad deeply: “Out of the same mouth comes blessing and cursing.” We sing hymns at church, but at home we often speak to you in ugly ways: “Why are you so lazy,” “Look at other people.” Perhaps we said these things in anger, but we know they stay in the heart for a long time. Today we don’t want to make excuses for ourselves. We just want to admit it first.
ask: Which sentence we often say, or which comparison, hurts you most?
Do you think those words have affected how you see yourself?
youth.do: Parents choose one hurtful thing they once said to their child and apologize specifically: “I said you were…, and that was wrong. In my eyes you are…”

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, we are sorry that sometimes we use our mouths to say hurtful things. Wash our mouths clean, so that what we say is always kind and full of blessing. In Jesus’ name, amen.

lessons.title: You Are My Beloved Son
lessons.theme: I believe: a child’s identity is that of one loved by God, not earned by performance

v: Jesus, when he was baptized, went up directly from the water: and behold, the heavens were opened to him. He saw the Spirit of God descending as a dove, and coming on him.
Behold, a voice out of the heavens said, “This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased.”

lessons.still: Be still and let the Heavenly Father speak to you. Put your own name in and listen slowly: “___, you are my beloved son. You are my beloved daughter.” Don’t rush to say, “I’m not worthy.” Just receive. Let those words rest in your heart for a while.
teach: When Jesus came up out of the water at his baptism, the heavens opened, the Spirit descended, and the Father said, “This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased.” Notice when this was said: Jesus had not yet performed a miracle, preached a sermon or healed a sick person. The Father’s delight was not a reward for his performance, but a declaration of his identity. Jesus was affirmed first, and only then went out to serve. Identity comes first, and then mission.

Right afterward, Jesus went into the wilderness to be tempted. The first words of the tempter were: “If you are the Son of God…” Satan attacked the very identity that had just been affirmed. It is the same with our children: classmates’ mockery, comparison on social media and exam rankings tell them every day, “If you have any worth, prove it.” The protection children need most is to have heard at home, before they step into the world: “You are loved.”

Many parents do love their children, but tie that love to performance: a good result earns a smile, and a poor result chills the air. Children quickly learn that love must be earned. Today we make a change of perspective, from the human view, “I delight in you if you do well”, to God’s view, “I delight in you because you are mine.” This is not permissiveness. It gives children solid ground to stand on, so that they dare to learn, dare to fail and dare to get up again.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Conviction is moving from “knowing” to “I believe”. If parents are still trying to earn God’s love by performance, it is hard to affirm their children unconditionally. Come back to where you belong: I am the Heavenly Father’s beloved child, not through achievement; my child is also loved by God, not through grades. The focus is on Jesus, not on performance.
q: Who is God? — God declared Jesus his beloved Son before he had done anything. What kind of father’s heart does this show you?
Who am I? — Am I also trying to earn God’s love by performance? Do I make my children feel that love must be earned by performance?
How should I respond? — Write your “I believe”: I believe I am the Heavenly Father’s…; I believe my child is…, not because…
lessons.jesus: The Father’s words became the foundation of Jesus’ whole life. In the wilderness he did not need to turn stones into bread to prove himself. On the cross, when people mocked, “If you are the Son of God, come down from the cross!”, he did not need to come down. He knew for certain who he was. His identity as the loved one made it possible for Jesus to give himself up.
lessons.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for calling me your child, not because I do well, but because you love me. I believe I am one you delight in, and I believe my child is one you love. Forgive me for tying love to grades. From today, let my eyes, my tone and my embrace tell my children: you are loved. In the name of the Lord Jesus, amen.
acts: Write three “I believe” statements: I believe I am the Heavenly Father’s beloved son/daughter; I believe my child is loved by God; I believe my love does not depend on their performance
Find an ordinary moment today when your child is “not performing” and say to them, “You are loved by God, and I love you so much.”
At bedtime, bless each child with a hand on their head: “You are God’s beloved son/daughter, and God delights in you.”
lessons.noon: “This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased.” — Heavenly Father, thank you for seeing me this way. Help me see my children this way too.

fam.key: I am a child God loves.

lamb.do: Hold your baby, look into his eyes, say his name and slowly say three times, “You are loved by God.” Then kiss his forehead.
lamb.say: You don’t have to do anything. God loves you so much, and so do we.

sprout.story: Baa-baa the little lamb ran the slowest and couldn’t jump high. One day he hid in a corner, sadly thinking, “The shepherd surely doesn’t like me.” That evening, as the shepherd counted his sheep one by one, he came to Baa-baa, picked him up and said, “Baa-baa, you are my little lamb, and I love you so much.” Baa-baa asked, “But I’m the slowest runner!” The shepherd smiled and said, “I don’t love you because you run fast, but because you are mine.”
sprout.ask: Why do you think God loves you?
sprout.do: Take turns standing in the middle while the rest gather round and say his name together: “You are a child God loves!”

soldier.story: When Jesus was about thirty, he went to the Jordan River to be baptized. As he came up out of the water, heaven opened, the Spirit of God came down on him like a dove, and a voice from heaven said, “This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased.” Strangely, at that time Jesus had not yet performed any miracles or started preaching. The Father was pleased with him not because of how much he had done, but because he was the Father’s Son. God loves you in the same way: not because of your marks, or how many matches you won, but because you are his child.
ask: If you did badly on a test, do you think God would still love you? What about Mom and Dad?
What do you think is the difference between being loved and being praised?
soldier.do: Each person writes an “identity card” that says, “I am God’s beloved ___.” Keep it in your school bag or wallet, and read it when you meet a setback.

youth.talk: We want to ask you an honest question: do you ever feel that Mom and Dad love you more when you do well and are obedient? If so, that is our fault. We also grew up in an environment where you were affirmed only if you performed well, and we often tied love to grades without realizing it. But the Heavenly Father said to Jesus, “This is my beloved Son,” before he had done anything. We want you to know: you don’t have to earn our love.
ask: In our family, do you feel love is “given” or “earned”? What makes you think so?
At school or online, what do you most often feel you have to “prove”?
youth.do: Parents choose an ordinary day, not tied to any achievement, and take your child out for a meal just to tell them, “I love you simply because you are you.”

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for loving me, not because I am good or capable, but because I am your child. Help me remember every day that I am loved by you. In Jesus’ name, amen.

lessons.title: Words That Build Up
lessons.theme: Speak what is good for building others up as the need may be, giving grace to those who hear

v: Let no corrupt speech proceed out of your mouth, but only what is good for building others up as the need may be, that it may give grace to those who hear.
Therefore exhort one another, and build each other up, even as you also do.

lessons.still: Ask the Lord to help you see one good thing in your child today, however small: a smile, a moment of patience, a “thank you”. Be quiet for a moment and first thank God in your heart for that thing, and then prepare to say it aloud today.
teach: Paul says, “Let no corrupt speech proceed out of your mouth, but only what is good for building others up as the need may be, that it may give grace to those who hear.” The words “as the need may be” matter: good words are not memorized lines, but seeing and saying what is there in each ordinary moment. A child putting on his shoes, clearing his bowl unasked, or handing his brother a tissue when he cries: these are all “moments” for good words. Good words don’t have to wait for the day of the prize certificate. There is material every day.

Specific affirmation is more powerful than general praise. “You’re great” is like a blank cheque: the child doesn’t know what is great. “You let your sister play first just now, and I saw how loving you were” is like a mirror, letting the child see the good God has put in him. You can say it in three steps: I saw (the specific behavior); this shows (the character); I am grateful (your feeling). Crouching down and looking into his eyes will reach the heart better than a passing remark in the corridor.

A word of caution: affirmation is not flattery, and it is not only praise for cleverness and looks. If we praise “You’re so clever”, a child may avoid hard problems to protect the label. If we affirm “You worked so hard” and “You were willing to try again”, he learns to value the process. Paul also says, “exhort one another, and build each other up.” Good words build our children brick by brick, and build the whole family too. Day after day, a strong house is built in the child’s heart.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Practice means hearing and then doing. Among the nine fruits of the Spirit are love, kindness and goodness, and they most often ripen in the mouth. A 920 life begins with saying one word that builds up to the “2” beside us. When good words are spoken more and more, the atmosphere of the home changes.
q: Who is God? — God sees everything good in people and delights to say so.
Who am I? — Am I better at “spotting mistakes” or “finding the good”? Is my praise a blank cheque, or a mirror?
How should I respond? — To whom will I say a good word today, using “I saw — this shows — I am grateful”?
lessons.jesus: Mary of Bethany poured very expensive perfume on Jesus, and the disciples criticized her for wasting it. But Jesus said, “Leave her alone. Why do you trouble her? She has done a good work for me.” He said specifically what she had done, and also what it meant. Jesus knew how to say words that build up when others saw only what was wrong.
lessons.pray: Lord, open my eyes to see what you have put in my children today, and open my mouth to speak good words that build up as the need may be. Not to make my children more obedient, but because you see me this way too and affirm me. Make our home a home that builds one another up. In the name of the Lord Jesus, amen.
acts: Today, use “I saw… this shows… I am grateful…” with each child once
Say one specific word of affirmation to your spouse too, where the children can hear
Record the good words you said today on your phone or in a notebook, and count them in the evening
lessons.noon: “Let no corrupt speech proceed out of your mouth, but only what is good for building others up as the need may be” — Lord, make my next words words that build people up.

fam.key: Speak good words and build one another up.

lamb.do: When your baby does something small, such as picking up the spoon himself or tossing the ball to you, clap and say with a smile what he did.
lamb.say: You picked up the spoon yourself! You’re working so hard!

sprout.story: Yating’s dad raised her on his own, and every morning was a rush. Today Yating put on her socks all by herself, even though one was blue and one was red. Dad was about to say, “Wrong socks!” but he stopped, crouched down and said, “Yating, you put your socks on all by yourself. You worked so hard!” Yating smiled happily and said, “Daddy, I’ll do it myself again tomorrow!” Dad smiled too: “Tomorrow we’ll find a matching pair together.”
sprout.ask: What did you work hard at today?
sprout.do: Play “Kind Word Chain”: one person says, “I saw Daddy…”, then the person named says, “I saw ___…”, and so on all the way round.

soldier.story: When Paul wrote to the churches, he often began with good words. To the church in Philippi he wrote that he thanked God every time he remembered them, and to the church in Thessalonica he wrote that he remembered their work of faith, labor of love and perseverance of hope. Paul also pointed out mistakes, but he first let people know: I see the good in you. He also wrote, “Therefore exhort one another, and build each other up.” To build up is like building a house: one kind word is one brick.
ask: What is the difference between saying good things first and then what needs to change, and starting straight away with mistakes?
Which family member can you “build up” with one sentence today?
soldier.do: Make a “kind word wall”: put a big sheet of paper on the fridge, and this week each person writes one specific good word about a family member each day. Read them together on Friday.

youth.talk: Sometimes when we praise you, you say, “You’re just saying that.” That reminds us that vague praise has little power. Paul says to speak “what is good for building others up as the need may be”, which means saying sincere things about specific matters. So we want to practice being more specific, and we also want to hear from you: what kind of affirmation makes you feel truly seen?
ask: Do you like to be praised? Do you prefer to hear it privately, or to be affirmed in front of others?
Who in our family do you think most needs encouragement? Would you like to try it together?
youth.do: Parent and child do a “secret mission” together: this week each of you finds a family member or friend and tells them one of their strengths specifically, then share their reactions at the weekend.
