fam.pray: Lord Jesus, thank you for teaching us to speak good words. Help us today to see the good things our family members do, and to say so bravely, so that our home grows warmer and warmer. In Jesus’ name, amen.

lessons.title: Peel Off the Label, Call Out the New Name
lessons.theme: Review & Adjust: calling my children by God’s view of them

v: One of the two who heard John and followed him was Andrew, Simon Peter’s brother.
He first found his own brother, Simon, and said to him, “We have found the Messiah!” (which is, being interpreted, Christ).
He brought him to Jesus. Jesus looked at him and said, “You are Simon the son of Jonah. You shall be called Cephas” (which is by interpretation, Peter).
The LORD’s angel appeared to him, and said to him, “The LORD is with you, you mighty man of valor!”

lessons.still: Look back at the words you spoke this week, like leafing through a notebook of conversations. Ask the Holy Spirit to read it with you: which sentence was honey? Which was a knife? Don’t rush to blame yourself. Just look honestly, and then hand the notebook to the Lord.
teach: When Jesus first saw Simon, he looked at him and said, “You shall be called Cephas”, which means rock. At that time Simon was impulsive and changeable, and later even denied the Lord three times. He was nothing like a rock. But Jesus did not call him by what he was then. He called him by what God intended him to be. The new name became the direction in which Peter was called and shaped for the rest of his life. Later he fell, but the Lord never took the name back.

Gideon was hiding in the winepress, threshing wheat in secret for fear of the enemy. But the angel said to him, “The LORD is with you, you mighty man of valor!” Gideon’s own answer was: my family is the poorest, and I am the least. He saw himself as a coward, but God called him a mighty man. God’s words do not describe the past, but call out the future. Gideon did go on to save Israel, because God’s words carried power.

This week we have learned the power of words, admitted old labels, received the identity of “beloved son” and practiced specific good words. Today we review: do my words sound more like describing my child’s past, or calling out the future God has placed in him? The way to adjust is to replace every negative label with one of God’s names. “Cry-baby” can become “a tender-hearted child”. “Stubborn” can become “a child with conviction, who is learning gentleness”.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Review and adjustment is a practice of humility. The proud parent sees only the child’s faults and will not take words back; the humble parent is willing to say, “I was wrong,” and to call the child by God’s view. When we turn from a temporary view to an eternal view, children will hear God’s calling in their parents’ words.
q: Who is God? — God names people by his purpose, calling into being what does not yet exist and making the timid into mighty warriors.
Who am I? — This week, were my words describing my child’s past, or calling out his future?
How should I respond? — What old label will I replace for each child? How will I call him by the new name next week?
lessons.jesus: Zacchaeus was the chief tax collector, spat on by everyone and called only “sinner”. But Jesus went to stay at his house and declared, “he also is a son of Abraham.” One sentence restored his identity, and Zacchaeus became willing to share his wealth with the poor. When Jesus gives people a new name first, life follows.
lessons.pray: Lord, thank you for walking back through this week’s words with me. Some words built my children up, and that was your grace. Some still hurt them, and I ask you to forgive me and heal their hearts. Give me your eyes. As you called Simon a rock and Gideon a mighty man, let me call my children by new names and call out the future you have put in them. Amen.
acts: Talk with your spouse: what are the good words we have said most often this week? Which labels still need to be peeled off?
Ask your child, “This week, which of Mom’s or Dad’s words made you happiest? Which still made you sad?”
Write down a “new name from God” for each child, and use it once a day next week
lessons.noon: “The LORD is with you, you mighty man of valor!” — Lord, help me too to see with your eyes, and call out the mighty one inside my child.

fam.key: God gives me a new name.

lamb.do: Make up a gentle little name song for your baby, setting his name to words of blessing, such as “brave little ___”, and sing it softly as you hold him.
lamb.say: You are God’s treasure, and you are brave little ___.

sprout.story: There was a man named Simon who spoke quickly and acted on impulse. One day he met Jesus for the first time. Jesus looked at him, smiled and gave him a new name: Peter, which means a big rock. Simon was startled: “Me? A big rock?” Jesus knew that one day Simon would become as steady as a big rock. Jesus will give you a good name too!
sprout.ask: If Jesus gave you a new name, what would you like it to be?
sprout.do: Each person sticks a label on a small stone saying “my good name from God”, such as “brave”, “gentle” or “helpful”, and puts it by their bed.

soldier.story: Siying in Vancouver lives with her grandpa. She was very afraid of speaking in front of people, and classmates called her “scaredy-cat”. When Grandpa found out, he told her the story of Gideon: Gideon was hiding, threshing wheat in secret, but God’s messenger called him a “mighty man of valor”. Later Gideon really did defeat a great army with three hundred men. Grandpa told Siying, “They call you scaredy-cat, but Grandpa sees someone very careful and considerate, and God will make you brave.” That term, Siying put up her hand for the first time and read a passage aloud to the class.
ask: What labels have people stuck on you? What would God call you?
What “new name” could you give to a family member?
soldier.do: Make “new name cards” as a family: each person writes for another family member a good name that God would give him, and writes down one piece of evidence you have seen in him.

youth.talk: All this week we have been learning how to speak. Honestly, Mom and Dad said some good words, but there were still several times when criticism burst out. Jesus called impulsive Simon “rock” and called hiding Gideon “mighty man”, and the way he looks at people is very different from ours. We want to learn to see you through God’s eyes, and not define you by the past. We also want to hear from you: how do you want us to see you?
ask: Was there a sentence this week that made you feel seen? Was there one that still made you sad?
If you could peel off one label someone has stuck on you, which would it be?
youth.do: Parents tell their child one thing: “the future we see God has in you”, and ask the child in turn to name one speaking habit they would like their parents to improve.

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for giving us new names. Help us not to call people by bad names, but to bless one another with the good names you give. In Jesus’ name, amen.

33.memT: Pleasant words are a honeycomb, sweet to the soul, and health to the bones.

mem.t: For everything there is a season, and a time for every purpose under heaven:

sat.d: Today every child gets a stretch of “special time”. The night before, let each child choose what they would like to do with Dad or Mom. It could be a bowl of noodles, browsing a bookshop, ball games, a bike ride, or just swinging in the park. Each date lasts thirty minutes to an hour, with the phone tucked away in a bag, giving all your attention to this one child. In families with many children, you can split the day into morning and afternoon, with the other adult looking after the rest. In the evening, share as a family: “My happiest moment with Dad / Mom today was…”, and put the photos in the family album.

sun: Think back to your childhood. Is there a time alone with your parents that you still remember? What did it mean to you?
This week, what did you notice you most often use to replace “being with” your children: busyness, your phone, or arranging more activities for them?
What “season that won’t come again” is your child in right now? Which child will you arrange one-on-one time with next week?

lessons.title: For Everything There Is a Season
lessons.theme: There is a season for being with your children, and once it passes it will not return

v: For everything there is a season, and a time for every purpose under heaven:
a time to be born, and a time to die; a time to plant, and a time to pluck up that which is planted;
a time to kill, and a time to heal; a time to break down, and a time to build up;
a time to weep, and a time to laugh; a time to mourn, and a time to dance;
He has made everything beautiful in its time. He has also set eternity in their hearts, yet so that man can’t find out the work that God has done from the beginning even to the end.

lessons.still: Look at a photo of one of your children, or think of how he looked this morning. How much taller is he than last year? Say to the Lord, “Lord, thank you for giving me this stretch of days walking beside my child. Teach me to treasure today.”
teach: The Teacher says, “For everything there is a season, and a time for every purpose under heaven.” A time to be born, and a time to die; a time to weep, and a time to laugh. At home this is especially true: there is a season when your child wants to be held, a season when he follows you around asking “why?”, and a season when he is willing to hold your hand to cross the road. These seasons do not come again. Many parents say, “Once I’m past this busy patch,” and when they look back, the child no longer needs to be held.

Being together needs quality, and it also needs quantity. Some say that as long as the time is high quality, there can be less of it. But a child’s heart is not like a restaurant where you can book a slot. The moments when he is willing to tell the truth are often the few minutes when you happen to be at home, happen to be free, and happen to be beside him as he brushes his teeth. Enough time is the soil in which quality moments can grow. It is like fishing: only if you sit long enough will the fish bite.

“He has made everything beautiful in its time.” God does not ask parents to be superheroes on call twenty-four hours a day. He asks us to do the right thing at the right time. When children are babies and toddlers, being with them means holding and caring for them. At school age, it means playing and doing things together. For teenagers, it means being there at the moment they are willing to talk. When we understand the season, we know what is most needed today.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Turn from an earthly view to a heavenly view, from the temporary to the eternal. Work opportunities will come again; a child’s childhood will not. People matter more than tasks, and relationships matter more than things: however many things we give our children, they cannot match a parent who is present. Where our time goes, our heart goes.
q: Who is God? — God rules over time, and he makes everything beautiful in its time.
Who am I? — What season is my child in now? Is the companionship I give what this season needs most?
How should I respond? — Today, for which child can I set aside fifteen minutes that belong wholly to him?
lessons.jesus: When Jesus appointed the twelve, his first purpose was not to send them off to work, but “that they might be with him”. For three years he walked, ate, sailed and spent nights with them. Jesus built his disciples with time, and changed their whole lives through his presence.
lessons.pray: Lord who rules over time, thank you for giving me this season of walking beside my children. I admit that I often say, “When I’m finished,” yet give my best time to other things. Teach me to read my children’s seasons, to give the right companionship at the right time, and remind me that today is the appointed time you have given. In the name of the Lord Jesus, amen.
acts: Write down each child’s age now, and one thing for which “in a few years he won’t…”
Today set aside fifteen minutes for one child, with no housework and no phone, just being with him
Open next week’s calendar and put a block of family time in first, then schedule everything else
lessons.noon: “For everything there is a season, and a time for every purpose under heaven.” — Lord, help me recognize that today is the time to be with my children.

fam.key: Mom and Dad being with me is how they love me.

lamb.do: Find a stretch of time today to lie on the floor and let your baby climb on you and play beside you, doing nothing else, just watching and responding to him.
lamb.say: Mommy is here with you, and I’m not going anywhere.

sprout.story: There is a big clock in Xiaoyou’s living room, tick-tock, tick-tock. Xiaoyou asked, “Mommy, why does the clock keep going?” Mommy said, “Because time keeps going and never stops. You grow bigger day by day, and Mommy can hardly bear it.” Xiaoyou thought for a moment and said, “Then if Mommy plays with me now, the time becomes ours!” Mommy smiled, put down the laundry and played with building blocks with Xiaoyou.
sprout.ask: What do you like best to do with Mom and Dad?
sprout.do: Set a timer for ten minutes and let your child decide what the whole family plays for those ten minutes. When time is up, say together, “Thank you, God, for giving us time!”

soldier.story: Weilun’s dad works in Singapore and comes home to Johor Bahru only at weekends. In the past, as soon as Dad got home he would lie on the sofa scrolling on his phone, and Weilun could only play by himself. Later Dad read “For everything there is a season” and was deeply moved. Weilun was ten, and in a few more years he might not want to go out with Dad. From that weekend, Dad took Weilun to play badminton every Saturday morning, and afterward they had breakfast together. Weilun said, “Saturday is what I look forward to most.”
ask: If you could have a regular time just for you with Dad or Mom every week, what would you like to do?
When Mom and Dad are with you, are they really “there”? How can you tell?
soldier.do: Make a “together timetable” with Mom and Dad, writing down which day and which time slot this week are for the whole family or one-on-one time, and stick it on the fridge.

youth.talk: Recently we read “For everything there is a season” and felt a bit sad and a bit awakened. When you were little you often pulled us to play with you, and we often said, “In a minute,” or “Another day.” Now you are older, with your own friends and schedule, and it is we who want to chat with you. We know time can’t be turned back, but from now on we don’t want to put you after everything else.
ask: Do you remember one thing we did together when you were small that left the deepest impression?
With your life as it is now, in what way would you feel most at ease having us spend time with you?
youth.do: Ask your child to choose something he enjoys but that his parents don’t really understand (a game, a song, a video), and let him take his parents through it for thirty minutes, while the parents only learn and don’t comment.

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for giving us every day. Help Mom and Dad have time to be with us, and help us treasure the time we have together. In Jesus’ name, amen.

lessons.title: Martha’s Kitchen
lessons.theme: There was much serving, but the good part was missed

v: As they went on their way, he entered into a certain village, and a certain woman named Martha received him into her house.
She had a sister called Mary, who also sat at Jesus’ feet and heard his word.
But Martha was distracted with much serving, and she came up to him, and said, “Lord, don’t you care that my sister left me to serve alone? Ask her therefore to help me.”
Jesus answered her, “Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things,
but one thing is needed. Mary has chosen the good part, which will not be taken away from her.”

lessons.still: Ask the Holy Spirit to take you back to your home last night. Where were you? In the kitchen, at the computer, by the washing machine? Where were your children? Ask quietly, “Lord, was I being with my children, or just taking care of them?”
teach: Jesus came to Bethany. Martha was busy preparing the meal, while Mary sat at Jesus’ feet and listened to his word. Martha was so busy she couldn’t stand it, and came to complain: “Lord, don’t you care that my sister left me to serve alone?” Jesus gently said, “Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things, but one thing is needed.” Martha was not doing something wrong. She was serving Jesus. But she was so busy that she forgot Jesus had come to be with her.

Many parents are Marthas. We cook, do laundry, drive the children, check homework and arrange tutoring, rushing around for our children all day, yet seldom really “being with them”. Caring for and being with are different. Caring is doing things for the child; being with is being present with the child. A child can be well fed, warmly dressed and have every activity packed in, and still feel in his heart, “Mom and Dad are busy and have no time for me.”

Today, ask the Holy Spirit to show you: what kind of parent am I? The busy carer, who finishes the tasks but is never seen? The head-down parent, who sits beside the child but keeps looking at a screen? The outsourcer, who fills the child’s time with classes and childminders? Or the postponer, who often says, “In a minute”? There is no shame in admitting you are Martha. Jesus called her name twice, and his tone was full of tenderness.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Self-ruled busyness is often about proving that I am a good parent; self-emptied presence puts down the need to prove and simply is with the child. Life first, then relationships, then ministry: if parents are too busy to be with God, it is hard for them to have the heart to be with their children. Relationship matters more than tasks, and presence matters more than achievement.
q: Who is God? — Jesus called out “Martha, Martha!” He cares about Martha herself, not how much she did.
Who am I? — The carer, the head-down, the outsourcer or the postponer: which am I most like?
How should I respond? — What “serving” task am I willing to put down, to choose the good part?
lessons.jesus: In the garden of Gethsemane, Jesus was deeply grieved and said to his disciples, “My soul is exceedingly sorrowful, even to death. Stay here and watch with me.” In his most painful hour, the Son of God longed to have someone beside him. He understands how much it matters to be accompanied, because he needed it himself.
lessons.pray: Lord, I admit that I am often Martha. I have been busy for my children all day without really being with them. I have taken caring to be the whole of love, and put off being with them until tomorrow. Gently call my name, and make me stop and choose the good part: first to sit at your feet, and then to sit beside my children. In the name of the Lord Jesus, amen.
acts: Record your time with your children today in two columns, “caring” and “being with”, and see the proportions
Choose one household task today that can wait until later, put it down, and spend ten minutes with your child
Say to your child, “Mom / Dad has been too busy lately and often hasn’t really been with you. I’m sorry.”
lessons.noon: “but one thing is needed” — Lord, help me put down my anxiety right now and choose the good part.

fam.key: Being together matters more than doing many things.

lamb.do: When you hold your baby today, don’t do other things as you hold him. Sit down and hold him for the length of a song, gently patting his back.
lamb.say: Right now Mommy is only holding you, and doing nothing else.

sprout.story: Mommy Penguin was so busy every day: catching fish, tidying the nest, chasing off the seagulls. Little Bobo followed her around saying, “Mommy, play ice-sliding with me!” Mommy said, “In a minute, Mommy’s busy.” Bobo waited and waited, until he fell asleep. The next day, Mommy Penguin put down her fish and said, “Bobo, today Mommy will play ice-sliding with you first!” Bobo was so happy that he spun round and round on the ice.
sprout.ask: Have you ever waited a long time for Mom and Dad to finish “in a minute”?
sprout.do: Play the “Pause Game” as a family: each person says one thing they are busy with, and then everyone shouts “Pause!”, puts down whatever is in their hands and has a big hug together.

soldier.story: Ziqing in Taipei has a mom who is a very good cook. Every evening Mom cooks four dishes and a soup in the kitchen, then washes up and wipes the table. Ziqing had so much to tell Mom, but Mom always said, “Mom’s busy. Go and do your homework first.” One day Ziqing wrote in a composition, “I wish Mom wouldn’t cook so many dishes, and could chat with me.” When Mom read it, tears fell. From that day on, Mom cooked one dish fewer, and after dinner she washed up with Ziqing and chatted with her.
ask: What do you think Ziqing wanted?
In our family, is there anything that keeps Mom and Dad so busy that they can’t be with you?
soldier.do: After dinner tonight, invite Dad or Mom to do a household job with you (washing up, hanging out the laundry), and chat while you work, so that the chore becomes time together.

youth.talk: Martha’s story has moved us deeply. We often feel that preparing your meals, paying for tutoring and driving you around is how we love you. Of course these are love too, but we have found that we are so busy that we are seldom really with you. Sometimes you are in your room and we are in the living room, each scrolling on our phones, under the same roof but living in two different worlds.
ask: Who do you think is the most “Martha” in our family? Why?
If we could do one thing less and have more time together, what would you want us to put down?
youth.do: Parents and child each name one thing that can be done less, and this week try using the saved time to have a late-night snack together or go for a walk.

fam.pray: Lord Jesus, thank you for loving to be with us. Help our family not to be too busy, and to stop often to be with one another. In Jesus’ name, amen.

lessons.title: Count Our Days
lessons.theme: I believe: this season of being with my children will not return, and today is the opportunity God has given

v: So teach us to count our days, that we may gain a heart of wisdom.
Yet you don’t know what your life will be like tomorrow. For what is your life? For you are a vapor that appears for a little time and then vanishes away.

lessons.still: Slowly work it out: how many years until your child is eighteen? About how many summer vacations, birthdays and Lunar New Years living with you are left? Don’t be frightened by the numbers. Just let them sink quietly into your heart, then say to the Lord, “Teach me.”
teach: In Psalm 90, Moses prayed, “So teach us to count our days, that we may gain a heart of wisdom.” We count our days not to become anxious but to gain wisdom. One father worked out that before his child left home at eighteen, there are only about nine hundred weekends. When he realized his child was already ten and fewer than half the weekends were left, he canceled his weekend social engagements.

James is even plainer: “you are a vapor that appears for a little time and then vanishes away.” This is true of our lives, and even more so of our children’s childhood. The little hands that are too noisy today will grow into big hands that ask you to let go tomorrow; the child who falls asleep in your arms today will one day wave goodbye to you at the airport. This is not sadness but a reminder: the child in front of you right now is God’s gift to you today.

Today we make a change of perspective: from “there will be other chances” to “today is the chance”; from temporary things, such as promotion, savings and a house, to eternal things, a child who knows God and has been loved. The most precious thing parents leave their children is not property but the memories of walking together, and the God they saw in those memories. I believe that being with my children is an investment in eternity.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Conviction lets truth reorder our priorities. A change of perspective: earth to heaven, temporary to eternal. When we really believe that being with our children has eternal value, our calendars change. We don’t spend time with our children only when we are free; we put them first, and arrange everything else around them. Letting Jesus reign includes letting him rule our time.
q: Who is God? — He is God from everlasting to everlasting, and his view of time differs from ours. How does he see my busyness right now?
Who am I? — Of the things I keep saying “there will be other chances” about, which one have I nearly missed?
How should I respond? — Write your “I believe”: I believe being with my children is…; I believe today…; so I will…
lessons.jesus: Jesus said, “I must work the works of him who sent me while it is day. The night is coming, when no one can work.” He had only a little over thirty years on earth, yet he was never frantic and never wasted time. He knew time was limited, so he gave it to the people and things that mattered most.
lessons.pray: Eternal God, teach me to count my days. I believe the season of my children beside me is your gift and will not come again; I believe today is the opportunity you have given me to be with them. Change my priorities, so that I no longer give my best time to lesser things, but invest in eternity by walking with my children to know you. Amen.
acts: Work out how many years each child has until eighteen, and about how many summer vacations, and write it in your prayer notebook
Write three “I believe” statements: I believe being with my children is…; I believe today…; I believe God will…
Today cancel or shorten one non-urgent thing and give that time to your child
lessons.noon: “So teach us to count our days, that we may gain a heart of wisdom.” — Lord, help me use my time with my children wisely today.

fam.key: Being together today is a gift from God.

lamb.do: Measure your baby’s hand, trace it on paper, write the date, and press your palm against his little palm.
lamb.say: Your little hands will grow, but Mommy and Daddy will always love you.

sprout.story: When the little sapling was first planted, it was only as tall as a little finger. Grandpa went to see it every day, watered it and talked to it. In spring the little tree put out new leaves, and in summer it grew taller than his knee. Grandpa said, “Time goes so fast, and the little tree has grown up in no time. So I come to see it every day. I don’t want to miss watching it grow.” Mom and Dad are like that too. Every day we want to be with you as you grow.
sprout.ask: In what ways do you think you have grown since last year?
sprout.do: Measure your heights against the door frame, draw a line and write the date, then say together, “Thank you, God, for letting us grow together!”

soldier.story: Peixin in Singapore has a Grandma who is a wonderful storyteller. Grandma often says, “When your mom was little, I was too busy and didn’t really spend time with her. In the blink of an eye she grew up and got married.” So now, every Wednesday afternoon, Grandma comes to pick Peixin up from school, takes her to eat tau huay and listens to her stories about school. Peixin asked, “Grandma, why do you come every week?” Grandma said, “Because time is like a mist that vanishes in an instant. I don’t want to miss it again.”
ask: Do you think time goes fast or slowly? Why?
If time passes quickly, what do you most want to do with your family?
soldier.do: As a family, write a “wish list for our family”: ten things you want to do together before the children grow up. Choose one to do this month.

youth.talk: One day we worked it out: there are only a few years until you are eighteen, and after that you may go to university or work, and the days you spend at home will get fewer and fewer. This frightened us a little, and we felt a bit of regret that we didn’t spend more time with you in the past. We don’t want to put pressure on you. We just want to tell you that time with you is very precious to us, more important than work and many other things.
ask: Before you leave home, is there anything you’d like to do with Mom and Dad?
Does time seem to go very fast to you? Is there anything you don’t want to miss?
youth.do: Parent and child make a list of “five things to do together before you leave home” and pick one to arrange this month.

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for giving us today, so that we can be together. Help us treasure every day and not waste our time with family. In Jesus’ name, amen.

lessons.title: Come Away and Rest Awhile
lessons.theme: One-on-one time lets a child know: you are my only focus

v: The apostles gathered themselves together to Jesus, and they told him all things, whatever they had done, and whatever they had taught.
He said to them, “Come away into a deserted place, and rest awhile.” For there were many coming and going, and they had no leisure so much as to eat.
They went away in the boat to a deserted place by themselves.

lessons.still: Imagine Jesus personally inviting you to come away with him to a quiet place to rest awhile. Spend a while alone with him first, doing nothing, simply being accompanied by him. Then think: today, which child can I invite in this way?
teach: The apostles returned from their mission and excitedly told Jesus everything. There were so many people coming and going that they had no time even to eat. Jesus said, “Come away into a deserted place, and rest awhile.” He took the disciples out of the crowd to be alone with them. In the busiest of times, what Jesus chose was not to do more but to be alone with his people, so that they could eat, rest and be heard.

One-on-one time matters especially to children, particularly in families with several of them. Family outings are good, but in a group a child is often just “one of them”. Only in one-on-one time does he feel, “I am Mom and Dad’s only focus.” The eldest no longer has to give way, the youngest no longer has to compete, and the one in the middle is no longer overlooked. Many children’s true words are spoken at moments like this.

A one-on-one date doesn’t need to cost much. The key is three things. Exclusive: only you and this child. Focused: phone away, eyes on him. Child-led: let him choose what to do, and parents gladly follow. It might be a fifteen-minute chat at bedtime, or a monthly breakfast date. At first the child may not be used to it, but if you keep going, this time will become the safest place in his heart.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Practice is turning conviction into action. A 920 life begins with the “2” beside us, and our child is the closest “2” we have. One-on-one time lets a child experience, in his parents, God’s love for him personally: God does not love only “all humanity”, he also loves him alone.
q: Who is God? — In his busiest time, Jesus still took his disciples aside to rest awhile. He invites me in the same way.
Who am I? — When was the last time I spent one-on-one time with each of my children?
How should I respond? — Which child will I invite today, to do what, and when?
lessons.jesus: When two of John’s disciples asked Jesus where he was staying, Jesus said, “Come and see.” They went, and “they stayed with him that day”. Jesus did not give them a handout. He gave them a whole day. The disciples’ lives began in time spent with Jesus.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, thank you for inviting me to come away with you and rest awhile. You love me alone, and you are willing to be alone with me. Today help me invite my children in the same way. Let me put down my phone and my to-do list, and look only at him; let him sense in our time together your love for him personally. Amen.
acts: Today arrange fifteen minutes or more of one-on-one time with one child, and let him decide what to do
On the date, set your phone to silent and put it in a bag
In your calendar, schedule a one-on-one slot this month for each child
lessons.noon: “Come away into a deserted place, and rest awhile.” — Lord, I come to you now, and I am willing to invite my children in the same way.

fam.key: I am Mom and Dad’s treasure.

lamb.do: Today give this child ten minutes alone with you: roll around on the bed, play peekaboo, and keep looking at him and smiling.
lamb.say: Right now it’s just the two of us, and you are my treasure.

sprout.story: Enen has two older siblings, and she is the youngest. One day Dad said, “Enen, today Daddy is taking only you out for ice cream!” Enen couldn’t believe it: “Only me? What about my brother and sister?” Dad said, “Today is Enen Day!” All the way there, Enen talked and talked, and Dad listened with a smile. When they got home, Enen hugged Dad and said, “Daddy, I feel so important!”
sprout.ask: If there were a day that was “your day”, what would you like to do with Dad or Mom?
sprout.do: Help your child make a “date invitation card”, drawing what he wants to do with Dad or Mom, and the parent signs to say yes.

soldier.story: The Chen family in Johor has four children, and the house is lively every day. Jiaming, third in the line, often felt forgotten. One day Mom wrote each child’s “special day” on the calendar. On Jiaming’s day, Mom took only him for a bike ride, and then to eat his favorite fried kway teow. As he ate, Jiaming told her about being left out by classmates at school, something he had never told anyone. Mom said, “Thank you for telling me. Let’s think of a way together.”
ask: Why do you think Jiaming told her what was on his heart only on his special day?
What would you like to do on your “special day”?
soldier.do: Plan this month’s “special day” with Dad or Mom: the place, what you will do and one question to talk about. Write it down and stick it on your bedroom door.

youth.talk: We have noticed that when the whole family goes out, everyone talks over each other and we rarely get a chance to really chat with you alone. So we want to invite you: each month, pick a time to go out alone with Dad or Mom and do what you want to do, with no talk about grades and no lectures. You can try it once first, and if it feels awkward you can tell us.
ask: If it were up to you, where would you want to go and what would you want to do?
Would you rather go out alone with Dad or with Mom? Or both?
youth.do: Let your child lead the planning of a one-on-one date, and the parent is responsible for showing up, paying and giving full attention, without planning any issue to “talk about while we’re there”.

fam.pray: Lord Jesus, thank you for loving each one of us and for loving to be alone with us. Let our time with Mom and Dad become our happiest time. In Jesus’ name, amen.

lessons.title: Let the Little Children Come to Me
lessons.theme: Review & Adjust: Jesus stopped, held the children and blessed them

v: They were bringing to him little children, that he should touch them, but the disciples rebuked those who were bringing them.
But when Jesus saw it, he was moved with indignation and said to them, “Allow the little children to come to me! Don’t forbid them, for God’s Kingdom belongs to such as these.
Most certainly I tell you, whoever will not receive God’s Kingdom like a little child, he will in no way enter into it.”
He took them in his arms and blessed them, laying his hands on them.

lessons.still: Look back over each day of this week, like leafing through a calendar. On which day were you with your children? Which day did you miss? Ask the Holy Spirit to look with you, not to blame you, but to honestly hand every day over to the Lord.
teach: Some people brought little children to Jesus, but the disciples thought Jesus was too busy and the children unimportant, so they rebuked those who brought them. When Jesus saw it, he was moved with indignation and said, “Allow the little children to come to me! Don’t forbid them.” Then he did three things: he took them in his arms, laid his hands on them and blessed them. At his busiest, with the crowds at their largest, Jesus put the children first.

This week we have learned that the season of being with our children will not return, seen ourselves as Martha, declared that “today is the opportunity” and practiced one-on-one time. Today we review: was there a moment this week when I was like those disciples, feeling that my child was interrupting “something more important”? And a moment when, like Jesus, I stopped and held my child? Write down both kinds of moment honestly, and God’s grace is in both.

Adjustment needs no grand plan. Just start with Jesus’ three actions. Holding: physical presence, a hug or a hand on the shoulder. Laying on hands: focused presence, with your eyes on him and your mind on him too. Blessing: presence in words, telling him, “God loves you, and I love you.” Next week, choose a fixed moment, such as every night at bedtime, and let these three things become a habit.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Review, adjustment and repetition are how being together becomes a family culture. The proud parent expects children to fit in with adults’ time; the humble parent learns from Jesus to stop for the child. Jesus is my example. He did not treat children as a disturbance to his ministry, but as a picture of the Kingdom.
q: Who is God? — Jesus was indignant when the disciples blocked the children. How much he values them!
Who am I? — This week, when was I like the disciples, blocking the children? When was I like Jesus, taking them in my arms?
How should I respond? — At which fixed moment next week will I give my child “holding, laying on hands and blessing”?
lessons.jesus: As Jesus hung on the cross, in his greatest agony, he still saw his mother standing nearby and said to her, “Woman, behold, your son!” and entrusted her to the disciple. Even in the last moments of his life, he cared for his family. Jesus’ companionship never stopped because of busyness or pain.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, thank you for walking back through this week with me. The few times I stopped to be with my children were your grace; and the several times I treated them as an interruption, please forgive me. Teach me your way: to hold my child, look at him attentively and bless him, so that our home becomes the place my children most want to come back to. Amen.
acts: Talk with your spouse: how much time did each of us spend with each child this week? Which time had the most quality?
Ask your child, “This week, did you feel Mom / Dad was with you more? Which time did you like best?”
Write down next week’s adjustment, for example: “Every night at bedtime, hold the child and bless him for three minutes.”
lessons.noon: “Allow the little children to come to me! Don’t forbid them” — Lord, today let me not block my children but welcome them.

fam.key: Jesus loves little children.

lamb.do: At bedtime, hold your baby in your arms, gently rest your hand on his head and say a short blessing over him.
lamb.say: Jesus loves you so much, and he wants to hold you and bless you.

sprout.story: A crowd of people lined up to see Jesus, and some moms and dads brought their children too. But Jesus’ friends told them to go away, saying Jesus was busy. The children were so sad. But Jesus said, “Let the little children come to me!” Jesus opened his arms and picked up the children one by one, stroked their heads and blessed them. The children all smiled.
sprout.ask: If you met Jesus, what would you like to say to him?
sprout.do: Act out the story: one person plays Jesus, opens his arms and says, “Let the little children come to me.” The others run over to be hugged and blessed.

soldier.story: Yuheng in Auckland lives alone with his mom. Mom works in the day and has a part-time job in the evening, and is often too tired to speak. This week Mom learned “Let the little children come to me” at church and decided that, however tired she was, she would sit beside Yuheng’s bed for five minutes every bedtime: first a hug, then listening to one thing from his day, and finally putting her hand on his head to pray. By Friday Yuheng said, “Mom, I feel like you’ve been more at home this week.” Mom smiled and hugged him tight.
ask: This week, which time with Mom and Dad made you happiest?
What would you like Mom and Dad to do with you next week?
soldier.do: Family meeting: each person says “my favorite time together this week”, then decide together on a fixed family time for next week.

youth.talk: This week we tried to spend more time with you, and perhaps at times it felt a bit forced, or even annoying. We also found that we were still sometimes busy and tired, and fell back into our old ways. That Jesus stopped to hold the children even when he was busy has encouraged us a lot. We want to ask how you feel, and we want to find together a way of being with you that you feel comfortable with.
ask: This week, did you feel we were around more? Which time did you like?
Is there anything about how we spend time with you that you would like us to change?
youth.do: Parents apologize to their child for one time that busyness replaced being together, and set one regular time for next week together with the child.

fam.pray: Lord Jesus, thank you for loving little children, and for loving us. Hold us and bless us, and let our family be together often. In Jesus’ name, amen.

34.memT: For everything there is a season, and a time for every purpose under heaven:

mem.t: Let all that you do be done in love.

sat.t: Family Day: Five Colors of Love
sat.d: Prepare cards in five colors, each standing for one way of expressing love: kind words, quality time, small gifts, helping hands and hugs and touch. Each person draws a family member’s name and does something for them with one of the colors: write an encouraging card, play with them for twenty minutes, make a small handmade gift, help tidy their room, or give them a great big hug. Afterward, let the receiver say, “Which one made me feel most loved?” Parents note down each child’s answer, as a map for loving them this season.

sun: In what way do you most easily feel loved yourself? Is it the same for your spouse and your children?
This week, which child did you notice receiving love differently from what you had assumed?
How could you bring “loving someone in a way they can understand” into your marriage, workplace or group? Which child will you do something for next week, in his way?

lessons.title: Let All You Do Be Done in Love
lessons.theme: Love must be translated into a language the child understands

v: Watch! Stand firm in the faith! Be courageous! Be strong!
Let all that you do be done in love.
My little children, let’s not love in word only, or with the tongue only, but in deed and truth.

lessons.still: Think of the person you love most. The first time you felt “I am truly loved”, what did they say, or what did they do? Quietly savor that moment, then say to the Lord, “Lord, teach me to love my child in a way he can feel.”
teach: At the end of 1 Corinthians, Paul sums up all his exhortations in one sentence: “Let all that you do be done in love.” It is a simple sentence, but not easy to live out. Many parents love their children deeply in their hearts, yet the children say, “I can’t feel it.” The problem is not that there isn’t enough love, but that the love has not been “translated”. Just as a radio must be tuned to the right frequency, love must be tuned to the child’s frequency before he can receive it.

There are roughly five ways of expressing love, often called the five “love languages”: words of affirmation, focused time, thoughtful gifts, acts of service and physical touch. Everyone needs all five, but one or two often reach the heart in a special way. One child breaks into a smile after a quick hug. Another needs you to sit with him until the jigsaw is finished. Another treasures a sticker you gave him for years. Another feels that you fixing his bicycle is the greatest love.

John says, “let’s not love in word only, or with the tongue only, but in deed and truth.” To do all in love is not to love people in the way I am used to, but in a way they can receive. This takes humility: letting go of the feeling that “I already love you so much”, and bending down to learn the child’s language. This week, we will learn to watch each child and find the key God has placed in his heart.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Love is not for making ourselves feel we have done our duty, but for the other person to be truly loved. Self-ruled love is centered on my way; self-emptied love is centered on the other person’s need. To do all in love is to let Jesus reign even in the way we express love, so that children can touch God’s love in their parents.
q: Who is God? — Through the incarnation, God translated his love into something people can see and touch.
Who am I? — Which way of expressing love do I use most? Is my child receiving it?
How should I respond? — Today I will express love to my child in a way that is “not my habit”.
lessons.jesus: Jesus loved people in many different ways. To the man with leprosy, he was “moved with compassion” and “stretched out his hand, and touched him”. To the hungry crowd, he shared bread. To Nicodemus, he talked patiently at night. To Zacchaeus, he went as a guest to his home. It was the same love, which Jesus spoke in a way each person could understand.
lessons.pray: Lord, thank you for loving me in a way I can understand, even becoming flesh for me. I admit that I often love my children in my own familiar way without asking whether they have received it. Give me a humble heart and sharp eyes, so that I learn each child’s love language and do all I do in love. In the name of the Lord Jesus, amen.
acts: Write down the five ways of expressing love, circle the one you use most and the one you use least
Today, express love to each child once in the way you use least
Ask yourself: what does each child most often ask of me? Write down the answers
lessons.noon: “Let all that you do be done in love.” — Lord, let every small thing I do right now carry your love.

fam.key: We love one another from the heart.

lamb.do: Today love your baby in each of the five ways once: say a kind word, play with him, give him a little toy, wipe his hands, hold him. Watch which one makes him smile the most.
lamb.say: Mommy and Daddy have so many, many ways of loving you.

sprout.story: The bear family had three children. Big brother Teddy liked Mommy’s hugs best. Middle sister Flora liked Mommy to say, “What a beautiful drawing!” Little brother Ballie liked Mommy to play ball with him. One day Mommy Bear only praised, and Teddy was gloomy. Mommy Bear thought for a moment, opened her arms and hugged Teddy, and Teddy smiled at once. Mommy Bear said, “So every child likes to be loved in a different way!”
sprout.ask: What do Mom and Dad do that makes you feel most loved?
sprout.do: Play “Guess the Love”: Mom and Dad act out five things (hugging, a kind word, playing together, giving a little thing, helping), and the child picks the one he likes best.

soldier.story: The Lin family in Kuala Lumpur has three children. Dad is good at buying gifts and brings back toys every time he returns from a business trip. But his eldest daughter Xinyi said, “Dad, I don’t want a gift. I want you to come to the library with me.” His second son Junxian likes it best when Dad says, “You played really well today.” His youngest, Zihao, rushes at Dad for a hug the moment he sees him. Only then did Dad realize that he had been loving his children the way he liked, and had never asked what they liked.
ask: Do you think you are more like Xinyi, Junxian or Zihao?
What kind of being loved do you think each person in our family likes best?
soldier.do: Each person writes “the way I like to be loved best” and “the way I think Dad / Mom likes best”, and at dinner you compare answers together.

youth.talk: You may feel that the way Mom and Dad show love is a little strange: always telling you to eat more, to wear one more layer, nagging you about homework. To us, that is love, but we know you may not always receive it. Paul says to do everything in love, and what we want to learn is not “I feel I love you so much” but “you truly feel loved”. So we want to ask you, and we are willing to change.
ask: Which things we do do you know are love, but actually put pressure on you?
Which makes you feel most loved: kind words, time together, gifts, help or a hug and a pat on the shoulder?
youth.do: Ask your child to rank the five ways in order, and parents rank theirs too. Swap, and this week each of you uses the other’s favorite way to show love once.

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for loving us in so many ways. Help everyone in our family to love one another in the way the other person likes. In Jesus’ name, amen.

lessons.title: Isaac Loved Esau, Rebekah Loved Jacob
lessons.theme: A parent’s favouritism leaves wounds among the children

v: The boys grew. Esau was a skillful hunter, a man of the field. Jacob was a quiet man, living in tents.
Now Isaac loved Esau, because he ate his venison. Rebekah loved Jacob.
Now Israel loved Joseph more than all his children, because he was the son of his old age, and he made him a tunic of many colors.
His brothers saw that their father loved him more than all his brothers, and they hated him, and couldn’t speak peaceably to him.

lessons.still: Before the Lord, think of your children one by one. When you think of which one does your heart feel lightest? When you think of which one does your heart feel a little weary? Don’t rush to deny it. Ask the Holy Spirit to let you gently see your own heart.
teach: Esau and Jacob were twins, but their personalities were completely different: one was a skillful hunter, a man of the field; the other was a quiet man, living in tents. The Bible says, “Isaac loved Esau, because he ate his venison. Rebekah loved Jacob.” Each parent favored the child who suited their own taste, and this family went on to deception, flight and twenty years of separation. The seed of favouritism bore bitter fruit.

In the next generation, Jacob repeated his parents’ mistake: “Israel loved Joseph more than all his children”, and made him a tunic of many colors. His brothers saw it and hated Joseph, and “couldn’t speak peaceably to him.” Parents may not feel they are playing favorites, but children’s eyes see most clearly: who has more photos taken, who is scolded more lightly for mistakes, whose words Mom and Dad are more willing to listen to.

Favouritism is often not deliberate. We naturally like the child who is “easy to talk with”, “like me” or “better behaved”. Sometimes we love in the way we are most used to, and one child happens to receive it while another doesn’t, and we assume the other is “harder to love”. Today, ask the Holy Spirit to show you: what kind of parent am I? Do I favor the child who is like me, the child who obeys, or do I love all the children in only one way?
lessons.light: 321 Light: Self-ruled love loves the one who makes me comfortable, the one who is like me; self-emptied love is willing to learn a new language for each child. Parents are not the king of the home. Jesus is. Each child is an inheritance entrusted by God, not a work chosen by the parents. A steward has no right to favorites, only the duty to be faithful.
q: Who is God? — God loves everyone and shows no partiality. How does he see the child I find hardest to love?
Who am I? — In my family, is there a child who is praised and heard more often? Is there one who is more often overlooked?
How should I respond? — In what way will I make a special effort today to love the child I am less close to?
lessons.jesus: The Bible says, “Now Jesus loved Martha, and her sister, and Lazarus.” The three had very different personalities, yet Jesus loved them all. After Lazarus died, he spoke to Martha about the resurrection, but with Mary he wept. It was the same love, which Jesus gave according to who each person was, favoring none.
lessons.pray: Lord, shine your light on my heart. I admit that I often, without realizing it, favor the child who is like me and makes things easy, and have less patience and warmth for another. Forgive me, and heal the wounds in my children’s hearts from being compared or overlooked. Give me your heart, so that I can love each of my children equally, in the way each can understand. In the name of the Lord Jesus, amen.
acts: Honestly write down: which child am I closest to? Which child do I feel most distant from? Why?
Today, seek out the child you are less close to, and love him once in the way he likes
Ask your spouse, “Do you think I favor one of the children?”
lessons.noon: “Now Jesus loved Martha, and her sister, and Lazarus.” — Lord, let me love every child as you do.

fam.key: Mom and Dad love every child.

lamb.do: If you have more than one child, take turns today holding each child on your lap for the same length of time, calling him by name and saying you love him.
lamb.say: You are our treasure, every one of you is a treasure.

sprout.story: On the farm there were two puppies: Yellow loved to run, and White loved to sleep. The farmer took Yellow for a walk every day, but seldom stroked White. White lay in the corner feeling so sad: “Doesn’t the farmer like me?” One day the farmer noticed. He sat down beside White, gently stroked his head and sat with him in the sun. White wagged his tail and said, “So the farmer loves me too!”
sprout.ask: Have you ever felt that you were loved less?
sprout.do: Each person names one “time when Mom and Dad love me”, and Mom and Dad say to each child, “I love you because you are you.”

soldier.story: Joseph had eleven brothers, but his father Jacob loved him best and made him a beautiful coat of many colors. His brothers saw it and were so jealous that they would not even speak kindly to Joseph. Later they even sold Joseph to faraway Egypt. His father’s favouritism had opened a deep crack between the brothers. Many years later, God himself healed this family, Joseph forgave his brothers, and the whole family was reunited.
ask: Have you ever felt that Mom and Dad love one of your brothers or sisters more? How did it feel?
If you were one of Joseph’s brothers, what would you wish your father had done?
soldier.do: Invite your child to write a short, honest note, “Sometimes I feel…”, and give it to Dad or Mom. The parents just say thank you, without defending themselves, and then find a time to talk one on one.

youth.talk: There are several families in the Bible who ran into big trouble because parents played favorites: Isaac favored Esau, Rebekah favored Jacob, and later Jacob favored Joseph. We read it with unease, because we too may favor one child without realizing it, or love all our children in only one way. We want to hear your most honest feelings, and even if it is hard to hear, we are willing.
ask: In our family, do you feel someone is favored? What makes you think so?
In which matter do you think we are most unfair between you and your brothers and sisters?
youth.do: Parents listen carefully to the child’s answer, choose one thing the child feels is unfair and correct it concretely this week, then tell the child what you changed.

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for loving everyone in our family without favouritism. Help Mom and Dad love every child well, and help us brothers and sisters love one another. In Jesus’ name, amen.

lessons.title: Fearfully and Wonderfully Made
lessons.theme: I believe: every child is God’s unique handiwork, worthy of being loved uniquely

v: For you formed my inmost being. You knit me together in my mother’s womb.
I will give thanks to you, for I am fearfully and wonderfully made. Your works are wonderful. My soul knows that very well.
My frame wasn’t hidden from you, when I was made in secret, woven together in the depths of the earth.
Your eyes saw my body. In your book they were all written, the days that were ordained for me, when as yet there were none of them.

lessons.still: Imagine God knitting your child together in the womb: each hair and each fingerprint made by his own hands. Meditate quietly: before this child was born, God already knew him and loved him.
teach: David said, “For you formed my inmost being. You knit me together in my mother’s womb. I will give thanks to you, for I am fearfully and wonderfully made.” No two snowflakes are alike, and no two children are alike. God does not mass-produce his children from a mold; he weaves them one by one with his own hands. Each child’s personality, feelings, and way of expressing and receiving love are all part of God’s handiwork.

So discovering a child’s love language is not a parenting technique but a spiritual kind of respect: I acknowledge that this child is God’s unique work, not a copy of me and not a repeat of his older brother or sister. The mistake parents make most often is trying to shape a child into what we want; God invites us first to know what he has made, and then to walk beside the child as he grows into what God intends.

Today we make a change of perspective, from the human view, “Why is this child so difficult?”, to God’s view, “This child is fearfully and wonderfully made.” From “he should be like me” to “I will learn his language.” Different children are not trouble but the many-colored glory of God. Let us say from the heart: I believe every child is God’s unique handiwork, worthy of being loved uniquely.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Conviction lets God’s word change the way I see people. When God’s view replaces the human view, a child is no longer a problem to be corrected but a treasure to be known. Let God be God: he is the designer of the child. Let man be man: I am the steward who is learning to love this work.
q: Who is God? — He is the God who knits each child together in secret with his own hands, and who wrote all his days in his book.
Who am I? — Do I often try to mold my child into my own image rather than first getting to know how God made him?
How should I respond? — Write your “I believe”: I believe my child ___ is made…; I believe the way he receives love is…; I will…
lessons.jesus: Jesus said the good shepherd “calls his own sheep by name”. He does not call a flock, but each one by name. He knows which one wanders easily and which one needs to be carried on his shoulders. Jesus’ love for each person is individual and unique, and he knows each of our children in this way.
lessons.pray: Creator Lord, I thank you because my children are fearfully and wonderfully made. I believe each one of them is your own handiwork, not a copy of me. Forgive me for wanting to turn my children into what I want. Open my eyes to know your purpose in each child, and to love him in a way he can receive. In the name of the Lord Jesus, amen.
acts: For each child, write down three things that make God’s making of him unique, including how he receives love
Write your “I believe” declaration, and read it once in prayer for each child
Today say to one child, “God made you special, and I love getting to know you.”
lessons.noon: “I will give thanks to you, for I am fearfully and wonderfully made.” — Lord, thank you for making my children with your own hands. Help me see them with your eyes.

fam.key: God made me special.

lamb.do: Hold your baby’s little hand and gently count his fingers one by one, then kiss his palm when you have finished.
lamb.say: God made every one of your little fingers himself. You are so special.

sprout.story: It was snowing! The little snowflakes floated down from the sky. One snowflake asked another, “Why don’t you look like me?” The other said, “Because God makes every snowflake different!” They landed on a child’s gloves, and the child said with delight, “Every one is so beautiful!” God makes every child different too, and every one is so beautiful.
sprout.ask: What do you think God made most special about you?
sprout.do: Each person makes a handprint on paper. Compare how everyone’s handprints are different, and say together, “God made me special!”

soldier.story: Bohan and Boyu in Tainan are twins who look almost exactly alike, but their personalities are very different. Bohan loves sport, and is happiest when Dad plays ball with him. Boyu loves drawing, and is happiest when Mom says, “Your drawing is so creative.” In the past the grown-ups often treated them as the same, buying them the same things and saying the same words to them. Later Mom and Dad read “fearfully and wonderfully made” and began to get to know them separately and to give each a different love. Both brothers said, “Now Mom and Dad understand me better.”
ask: What do you think is the biggest difference between you and your brother or sister (or friend)?
God made you very special. What do you think he wants you to do?
soldier.do: Make an “instruction manual for me”: write what I like, what I am afraid of and “the way I like to be loved best”, and give it to Mom and Dad to keep.

youth.talk: You may often feel that adults want to turn you into a certain kind of person: more outgoing, more hardworking, more like other people’s children. We admit that sometimes we have wanted you to be more like us. But David said that God knitted him together in the womb with his own hands, fearfully and wonderfully made. We want to learn to get to know how God made you first, rather than rushing to remake you.
ask: What do you think Mom and Dad understand least about you?
Is there a part of you that you wish we would appreciate more?
youth.do: Parents write down three “things I appreciate about how you’re different” and give them to their child by hand. Invite your child also to tell you one thing: “I wish you understood me better.”

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for making each one of us different, and all of us special. Help our family appreciate one another’s differences and love one another from the heart. In Jesus’ name, amen.

lessons.title: A Towel Around His Waist
lessons.theme: In deed and truth, actually loving with the child’s love language

v: Jesus, knowing that the Father had given all things into his hands, and that he came from God and was going to God,
arose from supper, and laid aside his outer garments. He took a towel and wrapped a towel around his waist.
Then he poured water into the basin, and began to wash the disciples’ feet and to wipe them with the towel that was wrapped around him.

lessons.still: Imagine Jesus crouching in front of you, drying your feet with a towel. He knows all your weaknesses, and still serves you with his own hands. Receive this love quietly, and then ask him, “Lord, how can I love my children like this today?”
teach: Jesus knew that the Father had given all things into his hands, and the next thing he did was to get up from the table, wrap a towel around his waist, pour water into a basin and wash his disciples’ feet with his own hands. In this scene, love speaks several languages. The time he spent crouching was companionship. The touch of his hands was touch. Washing the dust off people was service. Later he said, “You call me, ‘Teacher’ and ‘Lord.’ You say so correctly, for so I am.” That was affirmation, and a reminder of identity.

The key to practice is to be specific and deliberate. Think of each child’s love language, then do one thing today. For a child who likes words of affirmation, write a note and put it in his pencil case. For a child who likes time together, play a game of his choice with him for twenty minutes. For a child who likes gifts, give him something small and thoughtful, such as a pretty leaf picked up on the way home. For a child who likes service, help him with something he finds a nuisance. For a child who likes touch, give one more hug, a pat on the shoulder, or a back rub at bedtime.

But remember: a love language is not a bargaining chip, as in “If you’re good, I’ll hug you.” When a child has done wrong and is in his worst mood, loving him in his own language often opens his heart the most. With teenagers, touch may need to become a pat on the shoulder or a fist bump, and time together may be quiet presence on the drive. Love languages change with age, and parents must keep learning the new ways of saying it.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Practice is loving one another in deed and truth. Jesus is my example: he is Lord, yet wrapped a towel around his waist and washed feet. The self-emptied parent does not care which way saves face, but only whether the child has received love. Humble service brings out a humble response.
q: Who is God? — The Lord who has all things in his hands knelt to wash people’s feet.
Who am I? — Is my love a conditional exchange, or am I willing to give even when my child is hardest to love?
How should I respond? — What concrete thing will I do for each child today in his love language?
lessons.jesus: In the early morning after his resurrection, Jesus made a charcoal fire by the sea, cooked fish and bread, and said to the disciples who had caught nothing all night, “Come and eat breakfast!” He did not first blame anyone, but first prepared breakfast for the weary. The risen Lord still expresses his love through serving.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, thank you for wrapping a towel around your waist to wash my feet, and for loving me in a way I can receive. Today help me put down my pride and habits, and love each child concretely in his love language: a word, some time, a small gift, a helping hand, a hug. Let my children touch your love in our home. Amen.
acts: Today do one concrete thing for each child in his love language, and note his reaction in the evening
Choose a moment when a child has done wrong or is in a bad mood, love him first in his language, and talk about the matter afterward
Do something for your spouse too in his or her love language, where the children can see
lessons.noon: “let’s not love in word only, or with the tongue only, but in deed and truth.” — Lord, help me love my children with actions today.

fam.key: We love one another with actions.

lamb.do: At bath time, slowly wash your baby’s hands and feet, dry them gently with a towel, and sing as you dry.
lamb.say: Mommy is washing your feet, just as Jesus loves you.

sprout.story: Every day Xiaobao’s Grandpa picks him up from kindergarten. Today it rained and Xiaobao’s shoes were wet, and his feet were so cold. As soon as they got home, Grandpa heated a basin of warm water, crouched down to soak Xiaobao’s feet, and dried them with a towel. Xiaobao said, “Grandpa, you’re like Jesus!” Grandpa smiled and asked, “Why?” Xiaobao said, “Because Jesus washed his friends’ feet too!” Grandpa picked Xiaobao up and kissed him.
sprout.ask: How can you love your family with actions today?
sprout.do: Play “Serving Each Other” as a family: each person does one small thing for another family member, such as fetching slippers, pouring a glass of water or rubbing their back.

soldier.story: When Jesus ate the last supper with his disciples, nobody wanted to do the dirty, humble job of washing feet. So Jesus stood up, tied a towel round his waist, poured out a basin of water and crouched down to wash the disciples’ feet one by one. Peter was shocked and said the Lord should never wash his feet! Jesus told them: I am your Lord, and I serve you like this, so you should serve one another too. Real love is not only talk, but bending down and doing.
ask: What do you think the disciples thought when they saw Jesus washing their feet?
In our family, what is the job that is most like “foot washing”, which nobody wants to do?
soldier.do: This week be the “foot washer” of the house once: volunteer for a chore nobody wants to do, and don’t tell anyone it was you.

youth.talk: Jesus is Lord, yet he crouched down to wash his disciples’ feet. We have thought that the best way to love you may not be giving lots of big speeches, but doing something concrete in a way you can receive. Perhaps it is preparing the late-night snack you like, or driving you somewhere without asking lots of questions, or just a pat on the shoulder. We want to try, and you can tell us which one is right.
ask: Which thing we did recently made you feel “loved”?
Is there a kind of love you liked when you were little but find awkward now that you’re older?
youth.do: This week, parents do something for their child that he once mentioned but they never had time for. The child may also choose something to do for his parents as an act of service.

fam.pray: Lord Jesus, thank you for crouching down to wash your disciples’ feet. Help us today to love not only with our mouths but with actions, helping and serving one another. In Jesus’ name, amen.

lessons.title: Love Abounding More and More
lessons.theme: Review & Adjust: growing in knowledge and discernment of how to love my children

v: This I pray, that your love may abound yet more and more in knowledge and all discernment,
so that you may approve the things that are excellent, that you may be sincere and without offense to the day of Christ,
being filled with the fruits of righteousness which are through Jesus Christ, to the glory and praise of God.

lessons.still: Think back over this week: when was the brightest moment on each child’s face? What had you done just then? Ask the Holy Spirit to recall it with you slowly, without rushing to conclusions, simply letting the pictures come one by one.
teach: Paul prayed for the church in Philippi: “that your love may abound yet more and more in knowledge and all discernment.” Love is not a vague feeling, but something that can grow in knowledge and discernment. It is the same with a parent’s love for a child: not loving harder, but loving with more understanding of him. Today’s review lets our love abound more and more in knowing our children.

How do you discover a child’s love language? You can watch three things. First, how he loves others: a child who often draws cards for people may value gifts, and a child who often clings to you may value touch. Second, what he most often asks of you: “Play with me,” “Look at me,” “Help me.” Third, what he most often complains about: “You never listen,” “You never spend time with me.” The place of complaint is often where he longs most to be loved.

This week we learned to translate love into the child’s language, saw the harm of favouritism, declared that each child is fearfully and wonderfully made, and practiced loving with actions. Today, please work with your spouse on each child’s “map of love”, and note this week’s discoveries. Love languages change with age, so this map must often be updated. Love abounding more and more is a lifelong lesson.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Review, adjustment and repetition are the process by which love becomes more and more accurate. The proud parent says, “I already love you enough”; the humble parent asks, “Did you receive the way I love you?” Life first, then relationships: only parents filled with God’s love can pass that love accurately on to their children.
q: Who is God? — The more he knows us, the more deeply he loves us, and he is willing to make my love abound more and more.
Who am I? — This week, what new understanding did I gain of which child? Which child do I still not quite understand?
How should I respond? — Next week, how will I love my child more accurately in his love language?
lessons.jesus: Jesus knew that Peter would deny him three times, and told him in advance, “but I prayed for you, that your faith wouldn’t fail.” He knew Peter’s weakness and he knew what Peter needed. Jesus’ love was not only deep but accurate, reaching exactly where Peter needed it most.
lessons.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for walking back through this week with me. I am beginning to understand my children better, and that is your grace. There were also times when I still loved them my own way and did not notice their hearts. Make my love abound more and more in knowledge and discernment, so that I come to know each child you have made, and love them in ways they can receive. Amen.
acts: With your spouse, write a “map of love” for each child: his two favorite love languages, and the one thing that worked best this week
Ask your child, “This week, which thing Mom / Dad did made you feel most loved?”
Write down next week’s adjustment, for example: “Write a small note for my youngest daughter every day.”
lessons.noon: “that your love may abound yet more and more in knowledge and all discernment” — Lord, help me understand better today how to love my family.

fam.key: We are getting better at loving one another.

lamb.do: Remember your baby’s happiest moment this week, and do the same thing again today, smiling as you watch his reaction.
lamb.say: Mommy is getting to know you better and better. You’re so lovable.

sprout.story: Aji’s mom did an experiment this week: on Monday she hugged Aji, on Tuesday she said kind words, on Wednesday she played with him, on Thursday she gave him a pretty stone, and on Friday she helped him tidy his toys. On Saturday Mom asked, “Which day this week made you happiest?” Aji thought and said, “Wednesday! Mommy played dinosaurs with me!” Mom said, “Then I know. I’ll play with you often!”
sprout.ask: Which day this week did Mom and Dad make you happiest?
sprout.do: Draw a “love map of our family” together: each person draws a heart and, inside it, the way they like to be loved best.

soldier.story: Yijun, twelve, in Sydney, has been watched by her dad all week. Dad noticed that Yijun often helps her little brother pack his bag and helps Mom hang out the washing, so she must value “help”. One day Dad offered to fix her broken desk lamp, and Yijun happily said, “Thanks, Dad!” Dad said, “In the past I only knew how to buy you things. Now I know that what you like best is someone giving you a hand.” Yijun smiled and said, “Dad, you understand me better and better.”
ask: This week, what did a family member do that made you feel most loved?
Have you discovered which way of being loved each person in the family likes best?
soldier.do: Family meeting: each person says “the moment I felt most loved this week”, and guesses a family member’s love language and asks if it is right.

youth.talk: This week we tried to watch you and tried to love you in different ways. Some may have felt natural to you, and some may have felt a bit forced. Paul says to let love abound more and more in knowledge and discernment, and what we want is not to do it perfectly but to understand you better and better. So we really need your feedback, even if it is “that was a bit awkward”.
ask: Which thing we did this week made you feel most loved? Which was a bit awkward?
What do you think each person in our family needs most in the way of being loved?
youth.do: Parents and child write down “our family’s map of love”, including each person’s favorite love language, and stick it up at home, then update it again in three months.

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for helping us learn to love one another this week. Help us understand better and better how to love everyone in our family, and let our love grow more and more. In Jesus’ name, amen.

35.memT: Let all that you do be done in love.

mem.t: All chastening seems for the present to be not joyous but grievous; yet afterward it yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness to those who have been trained by it.

sat.t: Family Day: Planting the Fruit of Peace
sat.d: Go together to a flower market or supermarket and buy a small potted plant or a few seeds, then plant them at home as a family. As you plant, let the children help trim away dead leaves and tie the plant to a stake. Explain: trimming and staking may look like “holding the plant back” at the time, but they help it grow straighter and stronger. Then, together, write three “love boundaries for our family” on a card and stand it beside the pot. Finish with a prayer, asking God to make your home like this plant, bearing the fruit of peace.

sun: Think back to how you were disciplined as a child. Did it leave you with the fruit of peace, or with wounds? How does that shape the way you discipline your children today?
This week, when did you notice a moment that was truly “discipline,” and a moment that was really “letting off steam”?
How could you help the younger parents around you discipline with love rather than anger? Which one discipline habit of your own will you correct first next week?

lessons.title: Discipline for Our Good
lessons.theme: The Father of spirits disciplines us for our good, so that we bear the peaceful fruit of righteousness

v: For they indeed for a few days disciplined us as seemed good to them, but he for our profit, that we may be partakers of his holiness.
All chastening seems for the present to be not joyous but grievous; yet afterward it yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness to those who have been trained by it.
My son, don’t despise the LORD’s discipline, neither be weary of his correction;
for whom the LORD loves, he corrects, even as a father reproves the son in whom he delights.

lessons.still: Set your children’s problems aside for a moment. Quietly place yourself before your heavenly Father and remember how he has pruned you, waited for you and lifted you up. Say to him, “Father, the way you discipline me is my first lesson in disciplining my children.”
teach: The writer of Hebrews says that earthly fathers “for a few days disciplined us as seemed good to them, but he for our profit, that we may be partakers of his holiness.” Two kinds of discipline appear here. One is “as seemed good to them”: shaped by mood, by pride, by the anger of the moment. The other is “for our profit”: it looks to the child’s long-term good and to his very life. The discipline of our heavenly Father always belongs to the second kind.

In the Bible, the word for discipline is closer to training, nurturing and teaching, like a coach with an athlete or a gardener with a fruit tree. Its goal is not to make the child pay, but to help him learn. That is why the writer says, “All chastening seems for the present to be not joyous but grievous; yet afterward it yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness to those who have been trained by it.” Good discipline has a process and requires waiting, and what it finally bears is peace, not fear.

Proverbs says, “for whom the LORD loves, he corrects, even as a father reproves the son in whom he delights.” Discipline begins with love. Because we delight in our children, we do not let them run wild. Letting a child do anything is not love; it is a parent avoiding trouble. Hitting, shaming and threatening a child into fear is not love either; it is a parent who has lost control. In this unit we will learn a third way: setting boundaries in love, and holding on to love within those boundaries.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Move from a human point of view to God’s. Human discipline often aims to show a child who is boss, but God disciplines so that we may “be partakers of his holiness.” Parents are not the king of the home; Jesus is. Discipline is not parents exercising power; it is parents standing in for God, faithfully nurturing the inheritance he has entrusted to them.
q: Who is God? — The Father of spirits disciplines me for my good. Remember how he has disciplined you: what kind of Father is he?
Who am I? — When I discipline my children, is it more often “as seems good to me” or “for their profit”?
How should I respond? — The next time I need to discipline my child, what question will I ask myself first?
