lessons.jesus: The Bible says that Jesus, “though he was a Son, yet learned obedience by the things which he suffered.” The Son of God himself was trained by his heavenly Father and learned to obey. He knows what it is to be disciplined, so his teaching carries both truth and compassion, and he never looks down on our weakness.
lessons.pray: Father of spirits, thank you for disciplining me, not as seems good to you in a passing mood, but for my good. I confess that when I discipline my children I often bring my own anger, pride and moods, and sometimes even hurtful words and ways. Forgive me, and teach me to be like you: to set boundaries in love and to hold on to love within them, so that my home bears the fruit of peace. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Draw two columns: “discipline as it seemed good to me” and “discipline for my child’s good.” Write down recent examples of each.
Before you discipline your child today, pause for three seconds and ask, “Am I doing this for his good, or for myself?”
Share with your spouse: which part of the way you were disciplined as a child do you want to pass on, and which part do you want to stop?
lessons.noon: “All chastening seems for the present to be not joyous but grievous; yet afterward it yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness to those who have been trained by it.” — Lord, let my discipline today be for my child’s peace tomorrow. Amen.

fam.key: Mom and Dad discipline me because they love me.

lamb.do: When your child reaches for something dangerous, gently but firmly take his hand, lead him away, and give him something safe to play with.
lamb.say: Not that one, it will hurt you. Mommy loves you, so Mommy keeps you safe.

sprout.story: Mother Duck was leading her ducklings across the road. One little duck, Quack, would not listen and tried to run off onto the big road by himself. Mother Duck quickly spread her wings to block him. “Quack, no! The cars are dangerous!” Quack was a little cross. But a moment later a big truck whooshed past, and Quack jumped and hid under his mother’s wing. “Mommy,” he said, “thank you for stopping me.”
sprout.ask: When Mom and Dad say “no,” why do they say it?
sprout.do: Play “red light, green light”: when Mom or Dad says green, you go; when they say red, you stop. At the end, say together, “When Mom and Dad say stop, it’s because they love me!”

soldier.story: Ziyang from Ipoh loved basketball. His coach made him practice dribbling and shooting for an hour every day, and Ziyang often felt so tired he wanted to give up. He thought the coach was too strict. Then came a match in which he sank the key shot in the very last second, and the whole team cheered. The coach patted his shoulder and said, “See? That is the fruit of all your practice.” The Bible says discipline is not joyful at the time, but later it bears the fruit of peace. Your parents discipline you the way a coach trains you: so that your future will be better.
ask: What do you think is the difference between “discipline” and “punishment”?
Is there something you didn’t like being asked to do before, but are thankful for now?
soldier.do: Make a “family boundary card” together. Write down three family rules, and beside each one write, “This rule is here to protect…”

youth.talk: This week we begin to learn about discipline. Honestly, Mom and Dad are a bit nervous, because we know that in the past, some of the times we said we were disciplining you, we were really letting off steam: shouting, saying hurtful things, even making threats. The Bible says our heavenly Father disciplines us for our good, not according to his mood. We want to learn again, and we would like to hear how you feel first.
ask: Which of the ways we have disciplined you do you feel really helped you? Which only made you afraid or angry?
If you were the parent, how would you discipline a child your age?
youth.do: Parents honestly apologize to the child for one time they disciplined “as seemed good to them,” and invite the child to think together: when conflict comes, what can our family do next time?

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for disciplining us like a good dad, because you love us. Help us to listen to Mom and Dad, and help Mom and Dad to teach us with love. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

lessons.title: Discipline or Venting?
lessons.theme: Restore him in a spirit of gentleness, and watch yourself

v: Brothers, even if a man is caught in some fault, you who are spiritual must restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness, looking to yourself so that you also aren’t tempted.

lessons.still: Ask the Holy Spirit to take you back to the last time you were angry with your child. How loud was your voice? How fast was your heart beating? What did you really care about in that moment? Don’t rush to defend yourself. Just look honestly, and then hand that moment over to the Lord.
teach: Paul says, “Brothers, even if a man is caught in some fault, you who are spiritual must restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness, looking to yourself so that you also aren’t tempted.” This verse gives discipline two key words. The first is “restore”: the aim of discipline is to bring a person back, not to knock him down. The second is “looking to yourself”: the one who corrects may stumble too, and the most common stumble is being overcome by anger.

Punishment and discipline look alike but point in opposite directions. Punishment looks backwards: you did wrong, so you must pay. Discipline looks forwards: you did wrong, so let us learn together. Punishment is often driven by the parent’s anger; discipline is driven by the parent’s love. Punishment makes a child afraid, makes him hide and lie; discipline helps him understand, take responsibility and turn around. A shout, a humiliation or the silent treatment may quieten a child for now, but it sows fear and distance in his heart.

Today, ask the Holy Spirit to shine his light: what kind of parent am I? The exploder, who raises his voice the moment he is angry? The threatener, who loves to say, “If you do that again, I will…”? The silent one, who goes cold and leaves the child guessing? Or the avoider, who fears conflict and lets everything go? Admitting it is the beginning of change. If there is already physical or verbal harm in your home, please seek help from your church pastor and a professional counselor. Do not carry it alone.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win. A parent who disciplines in anger has the self on the throne; a parent who first deals with his own heart and then with the child’s behavior is letting Jesus reign. Govern yourself first, and then you can restore your child.
q: Who is God? — God restores the fallen with gentleness. He has never disciplined me with fear.
Who am I? — Exploder, threatener, silent one or avoider: which am I most often? What did I really care about in that moment?
How should I respond? — The next time anger rises, what specific method will I use to calm myself first?
lessons.jesus: When a Samaritan village refused to welcome Jesus, James and John were so angry that they asked to call down fire from heaven to consume them. Jesus turned and rebuked them, saying, “The Son of Man didn’t come to destroy men’s lives, but to save them.” Jesus rebukes in order to save, not to destroy.
lessons.pray: Lord, shine your light on me. I confess that I often treat venting as discipline: I use loudness, threats and coldness to frighten my children, and I have not won back their hearts. Forgive me, and heal the wounds in my children’s hearts. Holy Spirit, when my anger rises, remind me to watch myself first and then to restore my child with a spirit of gentleness. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Write down the three situations in which you most often lose your temper, and the words you most often say then.
Choose a “calm-down signal” for yourself, for example, step away for a glass of water and come back to deal with it afterward.
Find a moment to tell your child, “Last time I was so harsh with you, that wasn’t discipline, it was me venting. I’m sorry.”
lessons.noon: “you who are spiritual must restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness, looking to yourself so that you also aren’t tempted.” — Lord, before I discipline today, first rule my heart. Amen.

fam.key: When I am angry, I stop first.

lamb.do: When your child cries or throws a tantrum, take three deep breaths first, crouch down, speak in a steady voice and gently pat his back until he slowly settles.
lamb.say: You’re angry. Mommy is here. Let’s take a big breath together.

sprout.story: Puff the little fire dragon had a problem: whenever he got angry, fire shot out of his mouth and burned everything black. One day his little brother took his toy, and Puff wanted to breathe fire again. Mommy said, “Puff, stop for a moment! Put your hands on your tummy. Breathe in… and breathe out…” Puff took three breaths, and the fire grew smaller and smaller. He said, “Brother, that’s mine. Could I have it back, please?” And his brother gave the toy back.
sprout.ask: When you are angry, how can you make your fire smaller?
sprout.do: Practice “fire-dragon breathing” together: hands on tummy, breathe in slowly, breathe out slowly, three times. From now on, whenever someone is angry, remind them to do one.

soldier.story: Pinyan in Kaohsiung broke her mom’s favorite cup. Mom took one look and shouted, “How can you be so careless!” Pinyan burst into tears and ran to her room. After a while, Mom calmed down and remembered what she had been learning. She knocked on Pinyan’s door, sat down beside her and said, “I was too harsh just now. I’m sorry. I’m sad the cup is broken, but you are much more precious than a cup. Shall we clean up the pieces together?” Pinyan nodded, and they tidied up together, and their hearts were mended too.
ask: What was different between Mom’s first reaction and her second?
If you did something wrong, how would you want Mom and Dad to speak to you?
soldier.do: Make a “family calm-down corner” with your parents. Whoever is angry can go and sit there for five minutes first, then come back and talk when calm.

youth.talk: We need to tell you something that is hard to say. Many times in the past we said we were disciplining you, but we were really venting. When we were tired from work, or felt embarrassed because you talked back, we raised our voices, said very hurtful things, and even used threats to make you obey. The Bible says to restore people in a spirit of gentleness and to watch ourselves. We didn’t do that, and we want to admit it to you first.
ask: Which time we disciplined you felt the most unfair, or hurt you the most?
When we are angry, what do you think we could do better? Would you be willing to remind us?
youth.do: Parents and children agree on a “pause agreement”: whenever either side feels an argument coming, they can say, “Pause,” and both go off to cool down for twenty minutes before talking again.

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, we are sorry. When we are angry we often say the wrong thing and do the wrong thing. Help everyone in our family to stop first when we are angry, and to speak to one another gently. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

lessons.title: Whom I Love
lessons.theme: I believe: God’s discipline comes from love, and ends in sitting down to eat together

v: As many as I love, I reprove and chasten. Be zealous therefore, and repent.
Behold, I stand at the door and knock. If anyone hears my voice and opens the door, then I will come in to him and will dine with him, and he with me.

lessons.still: Picture Jesus standing outside the door of your heart, knocking gently. He has just pointed out your problem, yet he has not turned away. He is waiting for you at the door. Listen quietly to his voice, then open the door and let him in.
teach: The church in Laodicea was lukewarm and thought itself rich, and the Lord spoke very strong words to them. Yet right after that he said, “As many as I love, I reprove and chasten.” The reason for the rebuke is love. Even lovelier is the next verse: “Behold, I stand at the door and knock. If anyone hears my voice and opens the door, then I will come in to him and will dine with him, and he with me.” The Lord’s discipline does not end with a closed door, but with a meal at the same table.

This gives parents a clear picture: the end of discipline is not the child being punished, but the relationship being restored. Many parents finish disciplining and then send the child off to “think about it,” and nobody speaks for the whole evening. What the child learns is not a lesson, but this: “When I do wrong, I lose Mom and Dad’s love.” God does not do this. He points out the problem, then knocks at the door and invites us to sit down together again.

Today we make a shift in viewpoint: from “discipline is making my child see he is wrong” to “discipline is bringing my child back into love”; from “I am the judge” to “I am the one who walks him home.” Let us declare from the heart: I believe God’s discipline comes from love. I believe I discipline my child because I love him. I believe every act of discipline should end in reconciliation and in sitting down together.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Conviction is letting God’s heart become my heart. Relationships matter more than events, and people matter more than tasks. Discipline deals with the matter, but its purpose is to win the person back. Always reconcile after discipline. This is God’s way, and it is how Jesus receives glory in our home. Discipline first, then sit down together, and no cold corner is left in the house.
q: Who is God? — God rebukes and disciplines me because he loves me, and he stands at the door knocking, waiting for me to come back and dine with him.
Who am I? — Does my discipline more often end in reconciliation, or in the silent treatment?
How should I respond? — Write your “I believe”: I believe God disciplines me because… ; I believe I discipline my child in order to… ; so after every discipline, I will…
lessons.jesus: When Peter denied the Lord three times, “the Lord turned and looked at Peter.” That look held no curse and no shame, yet it made Peter remember the Lord’s words, and he went out and wept bitterly. After the resurrection, Jesus prepared breakfast for him by the lake and restored him. Jesus’ discipline began with a look and ended with a breakfast.
lessons.pray: Lord who loves me, thank you for rebuking and disciplining me, and for standing at the door and knocking, waiting for me to open and dine with you. I believe your discipline comes from love. I believe I discipline my children because I love them. Help me to make sure every act of discipline ends not in coldness but in an embrace, in reconciliation, and in a shared meal. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Write three “I believe” declarations and stick them up where you most often discipline your children.
If you need to discipline your child today, always end with a gesture of reconciliation: a hug, a snack together, or a prayer together.
Recall a time when discipline ended in the silent treatment, and find a chance to go back and make it right.
lessons.noon: “As many as I love, I reprove and chasten.” — Lord, let my discipline come from love and end in reconciliation. Amen.

fam.key: After discipline, we make up.

lamb.do: Every time you say “no” to your child, wait until he is calm, then pick him up and kiss him, so he knows your love has not gone away.
lamb.say: Not that, just now. But Mommy still loves you so much.

sprout.story: Little lamb Baa ran to the edge of a cliff. The shepherd quickly hooked him back with his staff and said loudly, “Baa, that is dangerous!” Baa was frightened and hid behind a rock, afraid to come out. The shepherd did not walk away. He sat down nearby and said softly, “Baa, I’m not angry with you. I was afraid you would get hurt. I love you.” Baa slowly came out, and the shepherd held him close, and they went home together to eat grass.
sprout.ask: After Mom and Dad correct you, what could they do so that you feel, “We’re friends again”?
sprout.do: Invent a family “making-up signal,” such as hooking little fingers or touching noses. After every correction, use it to make up.

soldier.story: The night Jesus was arrested, Peter was warming himself by the fire in the courtyard. Someone said he was one of Jesus’ disciples. Peter was afraid, and three times he said he did not know Jesus. Just then the rooster crowed, and Jesus turned and looked at Peter. There was no scolding in that look, but it made Peter remember what Jesus had said, and he went out and wept bitterly. Later, after Jesus rose from the dead, he made breakfast for Peter by the lake and gave him a new job to do. Jesus let Peter know: I still love you.
ask: What kind of look do you think Jesus gave Peter?
After you do something wrong, what are you most afraid of? What do you most hope for?
soldier.do: This week, if someone in the family is corrected, everyone shares a small snack at the end, as a sign that “we are at the same table again.”

youth.talk: We have noticed that in the past, after disciplining you, we often let things go “cold” for hours, even days, barely speaking. We thought that was giving you time to reflect, but it may only have been punishing you, and punishing ourselves too. In Revelation, after the Lord rebukes people, he stands at the door and knocks, wanting to eat with them. We want to learn that kind of discipline: clear, and always followed by reconciliation.
ask: After you get told off, what do you most often think about?
How would you like us to show you that “it’s over, and we still love you”?
youth.do: Parents and children agree on a “reconciliation ritual,” such as going out for a drink together or taking a ten-minute walk, and use it to end every conflict from now on.

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you that you still love us even when we do wrong. Help our family to make up quickly after every quarrel or correction, and to sit down together again. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

lessons.title: Teaching, Reproof, Correction, Training
lessons.theme: Four biblical steps for disciplining in love

v: Every Scripture is God-breathed and profitable for teaching, for reproof, for correction, and for instruction in righteousness,
that each person who belongs to God may be complete, thoroughly equipped for every good work.

lessons.still: Think of a conflict that is very likely to happen at home today: getting up, homework, phones, siblings quarreling. Bring that situation to the Lord first, and ask him to give you a calm heart and wise words today.
teach: Paul says that Scripture is “profitable for teaching, for reproof, for correction, and for instruction in righteousness.” These four words are a road map for discipline. Teaching means making things clear in advance: letting the child know what the rule is and why. Many conflicts are not a child’s deliberate defiance, but adults who never made things clear. Reproof is pointing out calmly and clearly when a child crosses the line: “We agreed that the phone goes away at nine, and it is now half past nine.”

Correction is helping the child put the wrong right, not just making him suffer for it. If he made a mess, he tidies it up; if he broke something, you clean it up together and he shares the cost from his pocket money; if he hurt someone, he apologizes and makes amends. This is the wisdom of natural consequences, letting a child learn responsibility from results. Instruction in righteousness is teaching him the right way and giving him a chance to practice: “Next time you want to play with your brother’s toy, what could you say? Let’s try it once.”

Before these four steps comes the most important one: connect first, then correct. When a child’s emotions are at their peak, he cannot take in any reasoning. The parent crouches down first and names his feelings; once he is calm, the four steps begin. If you yourself are angry, you can say first, “I’m too angry right now. Let me calm down for ten minutes, and then we’ll deal with this.” That is not weakness. It is showing your child what self-control looks like.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Practice means turning God’s word into concrete steps. Scripture is my standard, not my feelings; the Holy Spirit is my guide, not my anger. The four steps of discipline mean we no longer rely on impulse, but follow God’s way, step by step, leading our children onto the path of righteousness.
q: Who is God? — God teaches, reproves, corrects and trains me with his word. He is a patient teacher.
Who am I? — Of the four steps, which do I skip most often? At which do I most often stop?
How should I respond? — When conflict comes today, how will I connect first and then take the four steps?
lessons.jesus: People brought Jesus a woman caught in adultery, wanting to stone her to death. Jesus first let her accusers leave one by one, then said to her, “Neither do I condemn you. Go your way. From now on, sin no more.” He did not shame her, and he did not make light of sin. In him, grace and truth appeared together.
lessons.pray: Lord, thank you for patiently teaching me, reproving me and setting me straight with your word. When conflict comes at home today, help me to calm down first and connect with my child’s heart first, and then to teach clearly, reprove calmly, correct gently and instruct patiently. Let my discipline be like yours, full of both grace and truth. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Choose one situation where conflict often arises, and explain the rule and the reason to your child beforehand (teaching).
When your child crosses a line, first name his feelings, then calmly point out the problem, and let him take part in putting it right.
After the discipline, rehearse once with your child, “What could you do next time?”
lessons.noon: “Every Scripture is God-breathed and profitable for teaching, for reproof, for correction, and for instruction in righteousness” — Lord, today let me lead my children step by step according to your word. Amen.

fam.key: When I do wrong, I can learn to do right.

lamb.do: When your child throws food, say calmly, “Food goes on the plate.” Show him once, hold his hand and put the food back together, and when he does it, smile and praise him.
lamb.say: Food on the plate. Yes! You learned it.

sprout.story: Xiaoqing and her little brother Xiaohong were fighting over blocks, and Xiaohong knocked down Xiaoqing’s castle. Mommy did not shout. She first held the two apart and said, “You are both very upset, aren’t you?” When they had stopped crying, Mommy said, “Knocking down someone else’s castle is not okay. Xiaohong, let’s help your sister build it up again.” After Xiaohong had helped, Mommy taught him, “Next time you want to play, you can say, ‘May I play too?’” Xiaohong said it once, and his sister let him join in.
sprout.ask: After doing something wrong, how can we make it better?
sprout.do: Act it out: one person pretends to grab a toy, and the others teach him a good way to ask, “May I play too?”

soldier.story: Haoyu lives with his dad in Melbourne. They had agreed that every night at nine o’clock Haoyu would hand his phone to Dad, but Haoyu often secretly played on until late. In the past, Dad would have shouted. This time Dad said calmly, “We agreed on nine, and tonight you went half an hour over. So, as we agreed, tomorrow you get half an hour less.” Haoyu was a little unhappy, but he knew it had been said beforehand. Dad also asked, “What do you think would help you hand over your phone on time?” Haoyu thought, and said he could set an alarm to remind himself.
ask: How was Haoyu’s dad’s way this time different from shouting?
What parts do you think a good rule needs?
soldier.do: Make a new family rule with your parents and write down clearly: what the rule is, why it is there, what the consequence is if it isn’t kept, and what will help you keep it.

youth.talk: We would like to set the rules at home again together with you, not decided by us alone, but discussed together. The Bible shows four steps in discipline: first teach clearly, then point out the problem, then put it right, and finally learn the right way. In the past we often skipped the first step and went straight to scolding, and we often stopped at scolding without helping you put things right. We want to change that, and we need your opinion.
ask: Which rule in our home do you think is the least clear or the least reasonable?
If you don’t keep an agreement, what do you think would be a fair consequence?
youth.do: Parents and child discuss one rule that needs updating (for example, phones or curfew), write down the rule, the reason and the consequence, both sign it, and review it in a month.

fam.pray: Lord Jesus, thank you for teaching us so patiently. When we do wrong, help us to be willing to change and to learn to do what is right. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

lessons.title: He Knows How We Are Made
lessons.theme: Review and adjust: as the Father has compassion on his children, so may I discipline mine

v: He has not dealt with us according to our sins, nor repaid us for our iniquities.
For as the heavens are high above the earth, so great is his loving kindness toward those who fear him.
As far as the east is from the west, so far has he removed our transgressions from us.
Like a father has compassion on his children, so the LORD has compassion on those who fear him.
For he knows how we are made. He remembers that we are dust.

lessons.still: Look back over every moment this week when you disciplined your children, and look back too at how God treated your own weaknesses this week. Hold the two pictures side by side. Don’t hurry to condemn yourself; simply let the Holy Spirit look with you.
teach: David says, “He has not dealt with us according to our sins, nor repaid us for our iniquities.” And he says, “Like a father has compassion on his children, so the LORD has compassion on those who fear him. For he knows how we are made. He remembers that we are dust.” God disciplines us, yet never forgets that we are made of dust. He knows our limits, so his requirements are fitting and his compassion lasts.

Many conflicts over discipline come from parents forgetting how the child is made. To expect a two-year-old to sit quietly for an hour is to forget he is two. To expect a child who is tired out from a whole day to concentrate on homework at once is to forget he gets tired too. To expect a teenager to do everything his parents’ way is to forget he is learning to become his own person. Discipline must look at age, temperament and state. Fitting expectations are where a child’s success begins.

This week we learned that discipline is for our good, we told discipline from venting, we declared that discipline should end in reconciliation, and we practiced the four steps. Today we review: this week, did my discipline “know how my child is made,” as the heavenly Father does? Did I repay my child according to his mistakes? Next week, which expectation that doesn’t suit his age will I adjust, and after which discipline will I go back and make things right?
lessons.light: 321 Light: Review, adjustment and repetition are the road every parent must walk in learning to discipline. A humble parent admits he too is dust and also needs compassion; only one who has received God’s compassion can have compassion on his child. Deal with your own heart first, and then with your child’s behavior: when the parent’s heart changes, the way he disciplines changes.
q: Who is God? — God has not dealt with me according to my sins. He knows how I am made, and has compassion on me like a father.
Who am I? — This week, which of my expectations of my child did not fit his age or state?
How should I respond? — Which discipline habit will I correct next week? How, specifically?
lessons.jesus: After Peter fell, Jesus asked him three times by the lake whether he loved him, and then said to him, “Feed my lambs.” Jesus did not bring up old accounts, nor make Peter pay first. He restored the relationship, and he restored Peter’s calling. This is where the heavenly Father’s discipline ends: restoration and entrusting.
lessons.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you that you have not dealt with me according to my sins. You know how I am made, and you have compassion on me like a father. I confess that this week some of my discipline was too hasty and too harsh, and that I made demands that did not suit my children’s ages. Forgive me, and comfort my children’s hearts. Give me your compassion and wisdom, so that when I discipline my children I remember they are dust too, and need time to grow. Amen.
acts: Talk with your spouse: this week, which act of discipline bore the fruit of peace? Which was more like venting?
Ask your child, “This week, when Mom or Dad disciplined you, was it fairer and gentler than before? What still needs to change?”
For each child, write down one expectation to adjust, and one corrective action for next week.
lessons.noon: “Like a father has compassion on his children, so the LORD has compassion on those who fear him.” — Father, today let me show the same compassion to my children. Amen.

fam.key: The Father has compassion on me, and I have compassion on others.

lamb.do: When your child cries because he can’t do something, crouch down and slowly help him finish it once, then let him try on his own, and clap for even the smallest success.
lamb.say: Take your time. You’re still little. Mommy will learn it with you.

sprout.story: Slowpoke the little tortoise wanted to learn to climb a tree, but he kept slipping down. Brother Squirrel laughed, “You’re too slow!” Slowpoke felt very sad. Grandfather Tortoise came along and said, “Slowpoke, you’re a tortoise, not a squirrel. God made you a wonderful swimmer. Shall we go and learn to swim?” Slowpoke jumped into the water and swam so fast and so happily. Grandfather said, “God knows who you are. He never asks you to do what you cannot do.”
sprout.ask: Is there something you find very hard to do?
sprout.do: Each person names one thing they are learning but haven’t mastered yet, and everyone else says an encouraging word: “Take your time, we’re with you!”

soldier.story: Jiaxin in Sibu lives with her grandmother. In the past, when Jiaxin did badly in an exam, Grandma would scold her all evening. This week at church Grandma learned the verse “he knows how we are made,” and she began to think: every day after school Jiaxin also helps look after her little cousin, and by evening she is already tired. So this time Grandma did not scold her. Instead she said, “Grandma knows you’re tired. Let’s think together: what is the best time of day for you to study?” For the first time Jiaxin felt that Grandma understood her, and she offered to get up a little earlier to revise.
ask: This week, did Mom and Dad seem to understand your feelings better when they disciplined you?
Is there something you wish Mom and Dad would give you a little more time to learn?
soldier.do: Hold a family meeting: each person shares one time this week when they felt they were treated fairly, then talk together about which family rules need adjusting next week.

youth.talk: This week we learned a lot about discipline, and we also found how much we still have to change. Sometimes we forget that you are no longer a little child and need more respect and more discussion; at other times we expect you to be perfect like an adult and forget that you are still growing. The heavenly Father knows how we are made, and we want to learn to understand how you really are, rather than demanding things by our own standards.
ask: This week, where do you feel our discipline was better than before? Where did it still feel unfair?
In which things could we give you more independence? In which things do you still need our help?
youth.do: Parents and child together list three “things we can let go of more” and three “things we still need to agree on,” as the starting point for next week’s adjustments.

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you that you know each one of us and love us so patiently. Help our family to understand one another, to be willing to change when we are wrong, and to give each other time. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

36.memT: All chastening seems for the present to be not joyous but grievous; yet afterward it yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness to those who have been trained by it.

mem.t: ‘You fathers, don’t provoke your children to wrath, but nurture them in the discipline and instruction of the Lord.

sat.t: Family Day: An Afternoon of Listening
sat.d: Take a pot of tea and a simple snack to a park or a corner of the living room, and give each child fifteen minutes of “their own time.” The child decides what to play and what to talk about; the parents only follow and listen, with no correcting and no lecturing. When everyone has had a turn, let each person finish the sentence, “I feel heard when…” Then the parents ask first, “Is there any rule in our home that feels unfair to you?” Write down the answers without defending yourselves on the spot, and that evening pray over them together as husband and wife.

sun: This week, in which moment did you notice you were “provoking your children to wrath”? What were you protecting in your heart at the time?
Unfairness, humiliation, double standards, not listening: which of these four shows up most often in your home? Where did you learn it?
Which provoking sentence will you swap for a building-up one next week? Also invite another parent in your small group to remind you.

lessons.title: Don’t Provoke Your Children
lessons.theme: A parent’s authority is for nurturing, not for pressing down

v: Children, obey your parents in the Lord, for this is right.
“Honor your father and mother,” which is the first commandment with a promise:
“that it may be well with you, and you may live long on the earth.”
You fathers, don’t provoke your children to wrath, but nurture them in the discipline and instruction of the Lord.

lessons.still: Put down what is in your hands and be quiet for a minute. Think of the time of day today when you are most likely to lose your temper, and say to the Lord, “Lord, before that moment comes, I give myself to you.”
teach: When Paul wrote Ephesians, Roman law gave a father enormous power: a child’s future, marriage and even life or death lay in a word from him. In that culture, teaching children to obey was nothing new. What was new was that Paul then turned to the fathers and said, “don’t provoke your children to wrath.” He called the most powerful person in the household before God and reminded him that authority exists to serve.

To provoke is like poking a bowl of embers with a stick until the sparks fly. Parents seldom spoil a child’s heart in one go. It builds up day by day: a “Why can’t you be like so-and-so?”, a hand raised to cut the child off before he finishes, a rule that binds the child but not the parent. Behind a child’s anger there is often hurt and disappointment.

Paul does not stop at a prohibition. He gives a way forward: “but nurture them in the discipline and instruction of the Lord.” “Nurture” is a word about feeding and cultivating, like a gardener tending seedlings, not a foreman watching workers. Both discipline and instruction are “of the Lord”: not according to my temper or my pride, but according to the Lord, who is both gentle and just.
lessons.light: 321 Light: When Jesus reigns, parents step down from being the “king” of the home and return to being stewards. A steward does not use power to prove he is right; he gives account to the true Master. When a parent’s focus shifts from “my child must listen to me” to “we listen to the Lord together,” the fire of provocation begins to cool.
q: Who is God? — God entrusts authority to parents, and personally reminds them not to provoke their children. What kind of heart do you see in him through this?
Who am I? — Do I more often use a parent’s authority to nurture, or to get myself obeyed?
How should I respond? — In which situation today will I stop first and ask, “What would the Lord’s instruction say?”
lessons.jesus: When the disciples rebuked those who were bringing children to Jesus, he was indignant and said, “Allow the little children to come to me! Don’t forbid them.” He took the children in his arms and blessed them. Jesus held all authority, yet he used it to embrace the smallest. He is the model for how a parent uses authority.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, thank you for entrusting my children to me, and for using your authority so gently. I confess that I often press my children down with my volume, my face and my position, just to get things over with quickly. Forgive me, and teach me to nurture them in your discipline and instruction, so that my authority becomes a blessing to my children and not a burden. Amen.
acts: Today, when your child doesn’t listen, take three deep breaths before you speak.
Notice how many times today you say, “Why do you always…”, and write the number down tonight.
At bedtime say to your child, “If I spoke too harshly today, I’m sorry. I’m learning.”
lessons.noon: “You fathers, don’t provoke your children to wrath, but nurture them in the discipline and instruction of the Lord.” — Lord, put out the fire in my heart right now, and help me nurture my children your way. Amen.

fam.key: Mom and Dad and the children listen to the Lord together.

lamb.do: When your child cries, crouch down to his height first, gently pat his back, and count slowly to five in a very slow voice.
lamb.say: You don’t feel well. Mommy is here. We’ll take it slowly.

sprout.story: One day many moms and dads brought their little ones to see Jesus. The disciples said, “Go away, go away, Jesus is busy!” The children were very sad. Jesus saw it and said, “Don’t send them away! Let the little children come to me!” Jesus opened his arms, lifted the children up one by one and blessed them. The children were so happy, because Jesus loves them most.
sprout.ask: If Jesus gave you a hug, what would you want to say to him?
sprout.do: Play “Jesus hugs”: your child runs over, Mom or Dad opens their arms and hugs him, saying, “Jesus loves you!”

soldier.story: The Bible says, “Children, obey your parents in the Lord.” But did you know that the Bible goes on to speak to Mom and Dad too: “don’t provoke your children to wrath”? It means God wants not only the children to learn, but the parents to learn as well. It is like a soccer match: the players must keep the rules, and the referee must be fair. If the referee is always unfair and keeps shouting at people, the players get very angry. In our home, children learn to listen, and Mom and Dad learn to be gentle and fair.
ask: Which do you find harder, “obey your parents” or “don’t provoke your children”?
What do Mom and Dad do that makes you angriest?
soldier.do: Make a “two-way family agreement.” On one side write “what the children will learn,” on the other “what Mom and Dad will learn,” two things each, and stick it on the fridge.

youth.talk: There is a part of Ephesians that is interesting: first it tells children to obey their parents, and then right away it tells fathers not to provoke their children. To be honest, I felt a bit stung when I read the second half. Sometimes when you get angry it is not because you are rebellious, but because the way I speak really is hard to take. I would like to treat this passage as a lesson we both need to learn.
ask: In what situations do you feel I “provoke you” most often?
If you could give me one piece of advice so that our arguments are not so bad, what would it be?
youth.do: Invite your child for a one-on-one twenty-minute walk and ask him to name one way of speaking he wishes you would change. As a parent, reply only, “Thank you for telling me.”

fam.pray: Dear Jesus, thank you that you love little children most of all. Help our family: the children to learn to listen, Mom and Dad to learn to be gentle, and all of us to listen to you together. Amen.

lessons.title: How Have I Provoked My Child?
lessons.theme: Seeing, in the light, the four fires I usually light

v: Fathers, don’t provoke your children, so that they won’t be discouraged.
So, then, my beloved brothers, let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger;
for the anger of man doesn’t produce the righteousness of God.

lessons.still: Ask the Holy Spirit to take you back to the last time you lost your temper with your child. Don’t rush to explain; just look: the child’s face, your voice, your gestures. Say to the Lord, “Lord, let me see what I haven’t seen.”
teach: The Colossians version adds a reason: “so that they won’t be discouraged.” The result of provoking is not only a child who talks back. The deeper wound is that the fire in the child’s heart goes out: he stops trying, stops sharing, stops believing he is loved. A child who is often provoked may be well behaved outside, yet shut his bedroom door tightly when he gets home.

Parents commonly provoke with four fires. The first is unfairness: the eldest must always give way, the youngest is always protected. The second is humiliation: scolding in front of relatives, or putting up report cards to compare. The third is double standards: telling a child to put down his phone while scrolling on your own until midnight. The fourth is not listening: before the child has finished speaking, we have already passed sentence. Proverbs says, “He who answers before he hears, that is folly and shame to him.”

James’ prescription is simple but hard: be “swift to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger.” Parents often do the reverse: slow to hear, quick to speak, quick to anger. James adds, “the anger of man doesn’t produce the righteousness of God.” Shouting may quieten a child for a while, but it cannot draw his heart closer to God. Seeing ourselves is the beginning of change.
lessons.light: 321 Light: In a conflict, the self-ruled parent protects his own face and authority; the self-emptied parent is willing to be searched by the Holy Spirit and admits, “I was wrong too.” Pride provokes pride: the harder the parent, the more the child pushes back. Humility draws out humility: when the parent softens first, the child’s heart has a road home.
q: Who is God? — God is slow to anger and willing to hear us out. When did you last feel his patience?
Who am I? — Unfairness, humiliation, double standards, not listening: which fire do I most often light?
How should I respond? — Am I willing to ask my child or my spouse what kind of parent I am in their eyes?
lessons.jesus: One of Jesus’ sharpest rebukes of the scribes and Pharisees was that “they say, and don’t do”: they bind heavy burdens on men’s shoulders, but will not lift a finger themselves. Jesus himself practiced before he taught; what he asked of his disciples, he did first. He shows us a life with no double standard.
lessons.pray: Holy Spirit, thank you for shining your light on me so gently. I confess that I have provoked my children through unfairness, humiliation, double standards and not listening, and have discouraged them. Forgive me, and mend the places in my children’s hearts that I have burned. Teach me to be swift to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger. Amen.
acts: Write the four fires on a sheet of paper and circle the one you use most.
Today, when your child speaks, wait until he has completely finished, then count two seconds before you answer.
Ask your spouse, “In what matter do you think I hold a double standard with the children?”
lessons.noon: “let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger.” — Lord, this afternoon let my ears move faster than my mouth. Amen.

fam.key: Quick to listen, slow to speak.

lamb.do: When your baby babbles, stop what you are doing and look into his eyes. Wait until he has finished “talking,” then answer by copying his sounds.
lamb.say: I’m listening to you. What you say matters.

sprout.story: Little Rabbit ran up to Mother Rabbit. “Mommy, I, I, I… my carrot…” Mother Rabbit was busy and said, “Lost it again, did you?” Little Rabbit began to cry. Mother Rabbit stopped, crouched down and said, “I’m sorry. You tell me, and I’ll listen.” Little Rabbit said, “I gave my carrot to the sick little deer!” Mother Rabbit gave him a big hug. “So that’s what happened. Thank you for telling me.”
sprout.ask: When Mom and Dad listen until you have finished, how does it feel inside?
sprout.do: Play the “long ears game”: one person tells something that happened today, and the listener puts a hand beside an ear like a rabbit ear and keeps it there until the story is done, and only then may answer.

soldier.story: Weijie came home from school wanting to tell Dad how a classmate had blamed him unfairly. He had only said, “Today the teacher said I…” when Dad cut in, “Have you been in trouble again?” Weijie shouted, “You never listen!” and ran to his room. Later Dad knocked at the door and said, “I didn’t let you finish just now. I’m sorry. Would you tell me again?” Weijie thought about it, then opened the door. The Bible says, “Be swift to hear, slow to speak.”
ask: Has anyone ever misunderstood you before you had finished speaking? How did that feel?
Who in our family is best at being “swift to hear”?
soldier.do: This week at dinner, take turns sharing one thing. Everyone else must first say, “What I heard you say is…” before they may give their opinion.

youth.talk: I have noticed lately that when I talk with you, I often start working out how to reply before you are halfway through, and I sometimes jump straight to a conclusion. I think that may make you feel there’s no point in saying anything, so you just stop. I am not trying to make excuses; I only want to admit that I listen too little and speak too quickly. If you are willing, I would like to learn again how to listen to you.
ask: On what kind of topic do you think I most often “reach a conclusion without hearing you out”?
When I am listening to you, what would you like me to do, or not do?
youth.do: Set aside twenty minutes of “listening only” time: the child says whatever he wants to say, and the parent may only ask, “What else?” and “How did that feel at the time?”

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for always listening to us. Help each of us to grow long ears: to listen quickly, speak slowly, and not get angry so fast. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

lessons.title: The Father Is Slow to Anger
lessons.theme: I believe: as God has compassion on me, I will have compassion on my children

v: The LORD is merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and abundant in loving kindness.
He will not always accuse; neither will he stay angry forever.
He has not dealt with us according to our sins, nor repaid us for our iniquities.
For as the heavens are high above the earth, so great is his loving kindness toward those who fear him.
As far as the east is from the west, so far has he removed our transgressions from us.
Like a father has compassion on his children, so the LORD has compassion on those who fear him.
For he knows how we are made. He remembers that we are dust.

lessons.still: Read slowly, once: “He has not dealt with us according to our sins.” Let that sentence rest on your heart. Think of your most failing moment today: how does God see you in it? Quietly receive his compassion.
teach: The God described in Psalm 103 is very different from the “disciplinarian” many parents carry in their minds: “The LORD is merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and abundant in loving kindness.” He is not an overseer holding a magnifying glass, waiting for us to slip, but a Father who “will not always accuse; neither will he stay angry forever.” Our attitude toward our children often reflects the God we believe in.

“Like a father has compassion on his children, so the LORD has compassion on those who fear him. For he knows how we are made. He remembers that we are dust.” God understands our limits. In the same way, when a three-year-old spills milk, he is not setting himself against his parents on purpose; when a fourteen-year-old forgets things again and again, his brain is often still developing. When we understand how a child is made, we stop mistaking childishness for rebellion.

Here is the change of viewpoint. From the human viewpoint, my child’s mistake challenges my authority. From God’s viewpoint, my child’s mistake is a chance to learn, and a moment for me to live out God’s compassion. We move from “I must win this fight” to “I want to win my child’s heart.” Today, write your own “I believe” declaration and let the truth take root in your heart.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Change the belief and you change the life. When we are convinced that God is a Father who is “slow to anger,” we no longer need anger to keep order at home. We must receive compassion before we can give it; we must be filled with God’s love first, or we will pour out anger from an empty cup.
q: Who is God? — He has not dealt with us according to our sins, and he knows we are only dust. How does a God like this make you feel?
Who am I? — Is the God in my heart more like the Father of Psalm 103, or like a stern overseer? How has that shaped the way I treat my children?
How should I respond? — Write your “I believe” declaration: I believe God is not quick to be angry with me, so I will…
lessons.jesus: When Peter denied the Lord three times, Jesus did not shame him after the resurrection. Instead he prepared a charcoal fire and breakfast for him by the lake and asked three times, “Do you love me?” He did not deal with Peter according to his sins; he entrusted him again with his calling. Jesus shows us the compassion of the heavenly Father.
lessons.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you that you have not dealt with me according to my sins and that you do not stay angry forever. I confess that I am often harsher with my children than you are with me, and I forget that they are only dust too. I believe your compassion is enough for me. Fill me, so that the loving kindness I receive from you flows on to my children. Amen.
acts: Write three “I believe” sentences: I believe God is not quick to be angry with me; I believe my child is someone who is learning; I believe God will lead him through my gentleness.
Write down one recent behavior of your child that made you angry and beside it write, “How he is made is…, what he needs is…”
Today when your child makes a mistake, start with one sentence: “It’s all right. Let’s work it out together.”
lessons.noon: “Like a father has compassion on his children, so the LORD has compassion on those who fear him.” — Father, let me receive your compassion first, and then bring it to my children. Amen.

fam.key: Our heavenly Father is slow to anger, and he loves me very much.

lamb.do: As you wipe up spilled water or food with your child, sing a gentle line, “Heavenly Father loves me,” while you wipe.
lamb.say: Never mind that it spilled. Let’s wipe it up together.

sprout.story: Little Bear Bobo wanted to help Dad pour the juice, but the whole cup tipped onto the floor. Bobo was so scared that he hid under the table, thinking Dad would shout at him. Instead, Papa Bear crouched down and said, “Bobo, I’m so glad you wanted to help. Come on, let’s wipe it up together and pour another cup.” The Bible says heavenly Father is just like that: slow to anger, and loving us very patiently.
sprout.ask: When you do something wrong, how do you most wish Mom and Dad would treat you?
sprout.do: Play “wipe it clean” with a small towel: spill a few drops of water on the table and wipe them up together, saying as you wipe, “Heavenly Father is so patient!”

soldier.story: The psalm says that as high as the heavens are above the earth, so great is God’s loving kindness; as far as the east is from the west, so far has he removed our sins from us. Did you know that if you keep walking north, one day you reach the North Pole and then start heading south? But if you keep walking east, you just go on east for ever and never turn west. God has thrown our wrongs that far away, which means he never brings them up again.
ask: What do you think “not bringing up old wrongs” means? Do we do that in our family?
Since God treats us this way, how can we treat each other at home?
soldier.do: Take out a globe or a map and find east and west, and say together, “God has thrown our wrongs that far!” Each person writes down one thing they want God to forgive, screws the paper into a ball and throws it in the bin.

youth.talk: When I was young, the God in my heart was a bit like a very strict teacher who took marks off for every mistake. So that is often how I have treated you. Lately I read in Psalm 103 that God is slow to anger and knows we are only dust, and I realized that what I demand of you is sometimes harsher than what God demands of me. I want to change, but I need your help.
ask: Is the God in your heart more like a strict teacher, a distant commander, or a loving father? Why?
Has my attitude toward you made it harder for you to believe God is loving?
youth.do: The parent writes a small card for the child, with the line “I believe that as God has compassion on me, I will have compassion on you,” and puts it on the child’s desk.

fam.pray: Daddy in heaven, thank you that you are slow to anger and love us so patiently. Help our family to love one another like this, and not bring up old wrongs. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

lessons.title: A Gentle Answer
lessons.theme: Swap out one provoking sentence today

v: A gentle answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger.
The tongue of the wise commends knowledge, but the mouths of fools gush out folly.
The LORD’s eyes are everywhere, keeping watch on the evil and the good.
A gentle tongue is a tree of life, but deceit in it crushes the spirit.

lessons.still: Think of the time of day when conflict is most likely to flare at home: getting up, leaving the house, homework, or bedtime? Ask the Lord to be with you before that time arrives, and say, “Lord, give me a gentle tongue.”
teach: “A gentle answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger.” This proverb reads like the instructions for a switch: in the very same scene, how the parent speaks decides whether the fire grows or shrinks. When a child screams, “I won’t!” and the parent answers with an even louder voice, it is like pouring oil on a fire. If the parent crouches down and slows his voice, the fire has nothing to burn.

Gentle does not mean weak, and it does not mean giving up boundaries. Gentle means saying a clear thing in a steady tone. For example, change “If you don’t finish that, forget about dinner!” into “When your homework is done, we’ll go and eat. I’ll sit beside you while you start the first question.” The first is a threat and the second is an invitation. Both have a boundary, but only the second does not provoke.

Try four steps today: stop, crouch, speak, listen. Stop: close your mouth for three seconds first. Crouch: bring your eyes to your child’s level. Speak: say “I see… I hope…” in place of “You always…” Listen: ask your child, “What do you think?” “A gentle tongue is a tree of life,” and every gentle word plants a tree in your child’s heart.
lessons.light: 321 Light: People matter more than tasks; don’t hurt a person for the sake of a task. Homework, tidiness and punctuality all matter, but none is worth paying for with a sentence that stabs your child. Use the heart and rely on the Holy Spirit; don’t use the head and rely on yourself. Asking the Spirit for help one second before you lose your temper is worth more than ten explanations afterward.
q: Who is God? — The LORD’s eyes are everywhere, and he hears every word in our home. Does that make you alert, or does it comfort you?
Who am I? — What is the “harsh word” I say most often? When does it usually pop out?
How should I respond? — Which gentle sentence will I use today in place of that provoking one?
lessons.jesus: When Jesus was cursed, he did not curse back; when he suffered, he did not threaten. Facing those who attacked him, he still spoke the truth clearly, without using words to wound. He said, “I am gentle and humble in heart,” and invites us to learn his way. His gentleness carries strength.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, you are gentle and humble in heart. I confess that my tongue often runs faster than my heart, and I speak harsh words that stir up my children’s anger. Today put a gentle answer in my mouth. In the most hectic moments, remind me to stop, crouch, speak and listen, so that my words become a tree of life for my children. Amen.
acts: Write “stop, crouch, speak, listen” on a sticky note and put it where you most often lose your temper.
Today change one “You always…” into “I see… I hope…”
At least once, give your child a boundary without a threat: say it clearly, give a choice, and sit with him as he starts.
lessons.noon: “A gentle answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger.” — Lord, this afternoon, guard my tongue. Amen.

fam.key: Gentle words are like a tree of life.

lamb.do: When your baby wriggles during a diaper change or getting dressed, don’t raise your voice. Hum softly instead, and tell him what comes next as you go.
lamb.say: Left arm first, then right arm. So gentle.

sprout.story: Two little birds were quarreling. The big bird said, “It’s my worm!” The small bird shouted, “It is not!” They got louder and louder. Then old Owl flew over and said, in a very, very soft voice, “You must both be hungry. There are plenty more worms here.” When the two little birds heard that, they stopped quarreling. The Bible says, “A gentle answer turns away wrath.” Gentle words can make anger smaller!
sprout.ask: When you are angry, which feels better: loud words or gentle words?
sprout.do: Play “loud voice, soft voice”: first say “I won’t!” loudly, then say “Let’s think of a way together” in your softest voice, and compare how each feels inside.

soldier.story: Jiahui in Singapore was lying in bed again this morning. In the past, Mom would shout from the doorway, “If you don’t get up, you’ll be late, and it’s your own fault!” and Jiahui would pull the covers up even harder. Today, Mom came in, sat on the edge of the bed, stroked her hair and said, “I can see you’re tired. I hope you can be up before seven, because the school bus won’t wait for us. Would you like to wash your face first or get dressed first?” Jiahui rubbed her eyes and sat up.
ask: How was Mom’s second way of speaking different from the first?
At school or at home, what “gentle answer” could you use to make an argument smaller?
soldier.do: Today the whole family becomes “tree of life detectives”: each time someone hears a gentle word, stick a leaf on the tree picture on the fridge, and count the leaves tonight.

youth.talk: I have noticed that when we argue, it is often not about what we are arguing about but about the tone. You roll your eyes, I raise my voice; I raise my voice, you get louder. Proverbs says a gentle answer turns away wrath. I want to try first: even if you are fierce, I will slow down and lower my voice. But I would also like us to agree on a signal that either of us can use to call a pause when one of us is about to explode.
ask: When we argue, who do you think lights the fire first? Which sentence is it usually?
What kind of pause signal could we agree on? How long a pause would be best?
youth.do: Agree with your child on a “pause signal”: whenever either side calls a pause, both cool down for ten minutes and then come back to talk properly.

fam.pray: Lord Jesus, thank you that you speak so gently. Help us to speak gently today, so that anger gets smaller and love gets bigger. Amen.

lessons.title: Search Me, and Ask My Child
lessons.theme: Review and adjust: let my child help me see my blind spots

v: Search me, God, and know my heart. Try me, and know my thoughts.
See if there is any wicked way in me, and lead me in the everlasting way.
There is one who speaks rashly like the piercing of a sword, but the tongue of the wise heals.

lessons.still: Play back the words spoken at home this week, like a recording, in your heart. Ask the Holy Spirit to listen with you: which sentence was like a sword, and which like medicine? No condemning, just honest listening.
teach: At the end of Psalm 139, David prays, “Search me, God, and know my heart. Try me, and know my thoughts. See if there is any wicked way in me.” This is a brave prayer. Most parents are very good at searching their children: they see the messy room, the missing homework, the bad attitude. Yet they seldom invite God to search their own tone, their own looks and their own motives.

Proverbs says, “There is one who speaks rashly like the piercing of a sword, but the tongue of the wise heals.” Sword and medicine may come from the same mouth, differing only in whether we stopped to think. This week we saw the four fires of provoking and learned the gentle answer. Today we look back: are my words mostly sword or medicine?

The best helper in a review is the child himself. Asking a child, “Did Mom and Dad make you feel anything was unfair this week?” takes courage, because the answer may be hard to hear. But when parents are willing to listen, the child learns that in this home, mistakes can be spoken about and can be put right. A parent who humbly receives feedback is himself the best discipline and instruction.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Review, adjustment and repetition are the rhythm of changed lives. A proud parent only searches his children; a humble parent first asks God to search himself. Relationships matter more than face: being shown a blind spot by your child does not cost you authority, it wins you trust.
q: Who is God? — God searches the heart in order to “lead me in the everlasting way,” not to condemn. Are you willing to be searched by a God like this?
Who am I? — What was the most sword-like sentence I spoke this week? What was the most medicine-like?
How should I respond? — Which sentence or habit will I correct next week? Write down a specific replacement.
lessons.jesus: At the Last Supper, Jesus took off his outer garment, tied a towel around himself and washed his disciples’ feet. The Teacher knelt at his students’ feet and turned the order of authority upside down. Only a parent willing to stoop can hear the voice in a child’s heart. Jesus is just such an example.
lessons.pray: God, search me and know my thoughts, and see if there is any wicked way in me. This week I spoke some words that pierced my children, and some words that healed. Thank you that you saw them all. Forgive my rashness, heal my children’s hearts, and give me the courage to hear my children’s honest words, and lead me in your way next week. Amen.
acts: Talk with your spouse for ten minutes: what was the most “medicine” moment in our home this week? What was the most “sword” moment?
Ask your child, “This week, was I more like Jesus? Where am I still not like him?” Only listen, don’t defend, and say thank you.
Write down next week’s corrective action: which sentence will you change into which sentence?
lessons.noon: “There is one who speaks rashly like the piercing of a sword, but the tongue of the wise heals.” — Lord, today let my words be healing for my family. Amen.

fam.key: My words should be like medicine, not like a sword.

lamb.do: When your child falls or cries, pick him up, and gently blow on the sore place and kiss it better.
lamb.say: Mommy’s words are to make you better. I love you.

sprout.story: Little Elephant Dodo said to Giraffe, “Your neck looks so funny!” Giraffe was very sad and hid behind a tree. Dodo’s mother said, “Dodo, those words were like a thorn, and they pricked Giraffe’s heart.” Dodo thought about it, then ran over and said, “I’m sorry. Your neck is amazing, because you can reach the very highest leaves!” Giraffe smiled. Kind words are like medicine and can make people feel better.
sprout.ask: Have you said any medicine words this week?
sprout.do: Prepare two boxes, one with a sword drawn on it and one with a medicine bottle. Each person writes or draws one kind word on a slip of paper and puts it in the medicine box, and tonight you open it and read them together.

soldier.story: Ajie’s family in Kuala Lumpur tried something new this week. On Friday evening Dad took out a sheet of paper and asked his three children, “This week, did Dad make you feel anything was unfair, or tell you off in a way that hurt?” Everyone was quiet for a moment. The second child said softly, “When you scolded my brother you scolded me too, but that time it wasn’t me.” Dad did not get angry. He wrote it down and said, “Thank you for telling me. I’m sorry. Next time I’ll ask first.” That night the house felt lighter.
ask: If Mom and Dad asked you this question, what would you want to say?
After someone tells the truth, how should the family respond so that it feels safe?
soldier.do: Hold a ten-minute family meeting. Each person shares “the kindest word I received this week” and “one word I want to stop saying next week.” Mom and Dad go first.

youth.talk: All this week I have been wondering whether the words I speak to you are more like a sword or like medicine. I want to ask you directly, even though I am a little nervous about the answer. I promise this time not to defend myself, not to bring up old wrongs, and not to use what you say against you later. What you say matters to me, and I want to know from your side where I have provoked you.
ask: This week, was there any sentence of mine that felt like a sword?
Is there any change in me that you have noticed, even a very small one?
youth.do: The parent first apologizes to the child for one specific thing this week, and then asks the child to help choose one “gentle replacement sentence” for the parent to practice next week.

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for being with us this week. Forgive us for the hurtful words we have said, and help us next week to speak more kind words that are like medicine. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

37.memT: ‘You fathers, don’t provoke your children to wrath, but nurture them in the discipline and instruction of the Lord.

mem.t: ‘Don’t be deceived. God is not mocked, for whatever a man sows, that he will also reap.

sat.t: Family Day: The Rules of Our Home Game
sat.d: Begin with a game that has no rules: take out a board game or a ball and announce that anyone may play however they like. Within a few minutes everyone will be quarreling. Stop and ask, “Why did it stop being fun?” Then together make three to five “rules for our family.” For each rule write clearly what to do, and what the natural consequence will be if it isn’t done. Parents keep the rules too. Everyone signs the rule sheet, you stick it up in the living room, and next month you review and adjust it together.

sun: Is your home more likely to have “no boundaries” or “boundaries that are too tight”? And which was the home you grew up in?
Recently, was there a time when you held back from cleaning up your child’s consequences, and then saw him learn his lesson?
Which family rule will you and your spouse set or change together next week? You might also invite a couple in your small group to share what they do.

lessons.title: You Reap What You Sow
lessons.theme: Natural consequences are a teacher God has placed in life

v: Don’t be deceived. God is not mocked, for whatever a man sows, that he will also reap.
For he who sows to his own flesh will from the flesh reap corruption. But he who sows to the Spirit will from the Spirit reap eternal life.
Let’s not be weary in doing good, for we will reap in due season if we don’t give up.

lessons.still: Think about what seeds you have sown in your child today: a word, a habit, a look. Say quietly to the Lord, “Lord, let what I sow be the seed of the Spirit.”
teach: “Don’t be deceived. God is not mocked, for whatever a man sows, that he will also reap.” Every farmer knows that if you plant sweet potatoes, you won’t harvest lychees. This is a law God built into creation, and it is a law of family life too. A child who goes to bed too late is tired the next day; a child who leaves homework to the last minute has to stay up to finish it. The consequence itself is a quiet but effective teacher.

Many parents, when they discipline, have a habit of adding on the spur of the moment: “If you do that again, no TV for a month!” That kind of punishment often has nothing to do with what the child did; it has only to do with the parent’s anger at that moment. Natural consequences are different. They don’t need the parent to lose his temper; they only need the parent not to step in, not to rescue and not to mock: “You forgot your jacket, so you’ll be a little cold. What would you like to do next time to remind yourself?”

Paul goes on, “Let’s not be weary in doing good, for we will reap in due season if we don’t give up.” Boundaries and consequences need time to sprout. A child will not change the first time he is told. Say it ten times, and carry it out gently and consistently ten times, and the child slowly comes to understand that the words of this home can be trusted. A parent who does not lose heart will see the harvest.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Let people be people, and let God be God. A parent does not have to play the angry enforcer at every consequence. We can let the laws God designed teach our children. Our place is to walk beside the child as he learns from consequences, not to bear everything for him or to manufacture pain with our anger.
q: Who is God? — God set the law of “you reap what you sow,” and the law is fair. Have you seen such a harvest in your own life?
Who am I? — Do I more often “rescue my child from consequences,” or “pile on punishments out of anger”?
How should I respond? — Today, in which small matter can I quietly let my child experience a natural consequence, and think it through with him?
lessons.jesus: A rich young man asked Jesus the way to eternal life, and Jesus, “looking at him, loved him,” and said plainly what he still lacked. The young man went away sad. Jesus did not run after him to lower the standard, and he did not scold him. Jesus’ love is both clear and respectful of a person’s choice.
lessons.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for setting fair laws in life. I confess that sometimes I rescue my children from everything, and sometimes I add to their punishment in anger. Neither is your way. Give me wisdom and patience, so that my children can meet consequences within safe limits and learn responsibility. Help me too not to be weary in doing good, but to wait for the harvest you have promised. Amen.
acts: Recall your child’s most recent mistake and ask yourself: what is the natural consequence? Did I step in too much?
Today when your child forgets some small thing, don’t fix it for him. Ask instead, “What would you like to do next time?”
Write down the punishment you most often add on the spur of the moment, and think of a natural consequence related to the behavior to replace it.
lessons.noon: “whatever a man sows, that he will also reap.” — Lord, today help me sow the seed of the Spirit in my children. Amen.

fam.key: What we plant is what we pick.

lamb.do: Together with your child, put a bean into damp cotton wool, and every day carry him over to look at it and touch it.
lamb.say: We planted a bean, so a bean will grow!

sprout.story: Little Squirrel Kiki played and played all autumn and would not store any pine cones. Mother Squirrel reminded him, “Winter is coming.” Kiki said, “I’ll do it tomorrow!” Then winter came with heavy snow, and Kiki’s hole was empty and his tummy rumbled. Mother shared a few of her pine cones with him and cuddled him. “Next autumn, shall we store them together?” Kiki nodded.
sprout.ask: Why did Kiki have no pine cones to eat in winter?
sprout.do: Put some soil in a cup, plant a few bean seeds together, stick on a label, “What we plant is what we pick,” and water and watch them every day.

soldier.story: Bohan in Taichung needed Mom to keep nagging him every morning before he would pack his school bag. One day Mom said, “From today the bag is your responsibility. I won’t check it for you any more.” On the third day, Bohan forgot his art supplies and could only watch in art class. He came home feeling low. Mom did not say, “I told you so.” Instead she sat with him and made a checklist. From then on, Bohan ticked it off himself every night.
ask: What did Bohan learn from this? What would have happened if Mom had brought his things to school every time?
Is there something you wish Mom and Dad would let you take charge of by yourself?
soldier.do: Each child chooses one thing of his own, such as packing his bag, preparing his water bottle or tidying his toys. Make an “I’m in charge” checklist and do it by yourself this week.

youth.talk: I notice I am sometimes torn. On the one hand I want you to be independent, and on the other I can’t help clearing things up for you, afraid you will lose out or be told off by a teacher. But the Bible says you reap what you sow, and if I keep reaping for you, you may never learn to sow. I would like to try stepping back, letting you make your own decisions and face the results yourself. But whenever you need help, I will always be here.
ask: Which things do you feel you can already take full responsibility for, without us stepping in?
Is there anything you would actually like us to help with, but feel shy to ask?
youth.do: Together with your child, make two lists, “Already yours” and “Let’s talk it over,” three things on each, and agree to adjust them after a month.

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you that we reap what we sow. Help us to sow good seed: listening, honesty and love for others. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

lessons.title: The Father Who Never Asked, “Why Have You Done So?”
lessons.theme: No boundaries is not love

v: Then Adonijah the son of Haggith exalted himself, saying, “I will be king.” Then he prepared him chariots and horsemen, and fifty men to run before him.
His father had not displeased him at any time in saying, “Why have you done so?” and he was also a very handsome man; and he was born after Absalom.
For I have told him that I will judge his house forever for the iniquity which he knew, because his sons brought a curse on themselves, and he didn’t restrain them.

lessons.still: Be still and ask the Holy Spirit to shine a light: in what matter do I actually know I should set a boundary, yet I have not spoken up because I fear conflict or fear my child’s displeasure? Let that picture slowly rise.
teach: The Bible records two very accomplished fathers who lost their footing at home. Eli was the high priest, and “his sons brought a curse on themselves, and he didn’t restrain them.” David was a king after God’s own heart, yet about his son Adonijah the Bible says in one quiet line, “His father had not displeased him at any time in saying, ‘Why have you done so?’” A child who was never once questioned later exalted himself and said, “I will be king,” and brought upheaval on the nation.

Last week we saw parents who provoke their children by being too harsh and too tight. This week we see another way of losing ground: being too soft and too loose. Some parents feel guilty over being busy at work and make up for it with permissiveness. Some were raised too strictly and vow never to be like their parents, and end up not governing anything. A home with no boundaries is like a mountain road with no guardrails: it looks free, but it is dangerous.

Boundaries are not the opposite of love; they are the shape of love. Saying “no” may make a child unhappy for a while, but a child who never hears “no” will find it hard, when grown, to say no to his own desires. Proverbs says, “Like a city that is broken down and without walls is a man whose spirit is without restraint.” The boundaries a parent gently sets today become the city walls in his child’s heart tomorrow.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The self-ruled life has two faces. One is control: the child must do as I say. The other is pleasing: I’m afraid my child won’t like me. In both, the focus is on self. A self-emptied parent keeps his focus on Jesus and is willing to bear being disliked for a while for the sake of the child’s good. That is love.
q: Who is God? — God cares whether parents “restrain” their children from doing evil. What does this show you about his concern for children?
Who am I? — Am I more like a parent who is too tight or too loose? In which matter am I afraid to say “no” to my child?
How should I respond? — What “unspoken boundary” do I need to confess to God?
lessons.jesus: Peter said, “You will never wash my feet!” Jesus did not give way just because his student was upset. He said gently and clearly, “If I don’t wash you, you have no part with me.” As he stooped to serve, he held firmly to the truth. Jesus shows us that humility and boundaries can exist together.
lessons.pray: Lord, thank you for shining your light on me. I confess that sometimes, from tiredness, guilt or fear of conflict, I have not said the “no” my child needed to hear. Forgive me, and give me courage and gentleness to set boundaries where they are needed. Let me stop pleasing my children and truly think of their good. Amen.
acts: Write down one thing about which you “should have said no and didn’t,” and pray over it.
Ask your spouse, “In what way do you think I am too loose or too tight with the children?”
Today give your child one gentle, clear “no,” with a short reason.
lessons.noon: “Like a city that is broken down and without walls is a man whose spirit is without restraint.” — Lord, help me build good walls in my children’s hearts. Amen.

fam.key: When Mom and Dad say “no,” that is love too.

lamb.do: When your child reaches for a socket or a hot pan, gently take his hand away, look into his eyes, shake your head, and then give him something he can play with.
lamb.say: Not that one, it will hurt you. This one is fine. Here you are.

sprout.story: Little lamb Baa saw some delicious grass beside the cliff and wanted to jump the fence to eat it. The shepherd had built the fence nice and high, and Baa was cross. “Why won’t you let me go over?” That night Baa saw a wolf prowling about outside the fence. Then she understood: the fence was not there to make her unhappy. It was there to protect her.
sprout.ask: Which “fences” in our home are protecting you?
sprout.do: Use chairs and string to make a “safety fence” in the living room and play “the wolf is coming.” When the wolf comes, everyone runs inside the fence and shouts, “The fence protects me!”

soldier.story: King David in the Bible was very capable. He defeated the giant Goliath and wrote many psalms. But the Bible says David never once asked his son Adonijah, “Why have you done so?” No matter what his son did, he didn’t say anything. So when Adonijah grew up, he announced that he would be king, and the whole country was thrown into chaos. His father not saying “no” seemed kind, but it actually harmed his son.
ask: Do you think a father who never says anything loves his child, or does not love him? Why?
Which rule in our home did you dislike at first, but later found was actually good for you?
soldier.do: Each person writes down one family rule they didn’t like before but now understand, shares it at dinner, and thanks Mom, Dad or whoever made it.

youth.talk: Honestly, sometimes I don’t quite dare to say “no” to you. I’m afraid you’ll be unhappy and our relationship will suffer, so I turn a blind eye. But when I read that David never once asked his son, “Why have you done so?”, I felt a little afraid.
