I don’t want to control you, but neither do I want to give up my responsibility as a parent just because I’m afraid you won’t like me. I think we need to find the balance together.
ask: Where do you think our family is too tight, and where too loose?
If I need to say “no” to you, how could I say it so that it is easier for you to take?
youth.do: Together with your child, discuss one matter that has no clear boundary at the moment, such as what time to be home at night or phone use. Each proposes a plan, and together you set a temporary rule.

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for giving us family rules that protect us like a fence. Help us to understand that when Mom and Dad say “no,” it is because they love us. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

lessons.title: God, the First Father to Set Boundaries
lessons.theme: I believe: boundaries bring freedom, and choices bring respect

v: The LORD God took the man, and put him into the garden of Eden to cultivate and keep it.
The LORD God commanded the man, saying, “You may freely eat of every tree of the garden;
but you shall not eat of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil; for in the day that you eat of it, you will surely die.”

lessons.still: Picture the Garden of Eden: a whole garden of fruit trees, with only one tree forbidden. Quietly feel how much room God gave humankind. Say to the Lord, “Lord, thank you for giving me freedom, and for giving me boundaries.”
teach: Eden is the first home in the Bible. God said to Adam, “You may freely eat of every tree of the garden; but you shall not eat of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil.” Notice the proportion: a whole garden of “you may,” and only one “you shall not.” God’s boundary is not a long list of tightly packed prohibitions, but a single clear line drawn within abundant freedom.

God also did three things: he explained the boundary clearly, he said beforehand what the consequence would be, and he let the man choose for himself. He did not build a high wall around the tree, and he did not stand under it watching every minute. God respects our freedom to choose, because obedience without choice is not love. After the man sinned, God did not take back all his love. He came into the garden and called, “Where are you?” and with his own hands “made garments of animal skins” and clothed them.

This brings a change of viewpoint. From the human viewpoint, discipline is “making my child do as I say.” From God’s viewpoint, discipline is “helping my child learn to make right choices himself.” In the end we do not want a child who obeys only when his parents are in the room, but a person who can choose before God when his parents are not there. Today, write your “I believe” declaration.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Change the belief and you change the life. The parent moves from “controller” to “trainer,” from “holding back the child’s hands” to “shaping the child’s heart.” “Out of it is the wellspring of life.” The ultimate aim of boundaries is that the child’s heart is won by God, not only that his behavior is held in check by his parents.
q: Who is God? — God gave a whole garden of freedom and also one clear boundary. What kind of father does this show you he is?
Who am I? — What is the proportion of “you may” to “you may not” in my home? Does my child feel freedom, or restriction?
How should I respond? — Write your “I believe” declaration: I believe boundaries are… ; I believe choices are… ; I believe God will, through…
lessons.jesus: When many disciples left Jesus, he did not hold them back. He turned and asked the twelve, “You don’t also want to go away, do you?” Jesus put the choice in their hands. Peter answered, “Lord, to whom would we go? You have the words of eternal life.” True following comes from a respected choice.
lessons.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you that in Eden you gave humankind a whole garden of freedom, and also a clear boundary. I believe your boundaries are love and the choices you give are respect. Help me to learn your way: to say “you may” often, to say “you may not” clearly, to name the consequence beforehand, and to let go so that my child can learn to choose. Let my aim be not only to hold my child in check, but to help his heart turn to you. Amen.
acts: Write three “I believe” sentences: I believe boundaries are the protection of love; I believe giving my child choices is respecting him; I believe God will teach him through consequences.
Count how many times today you say “no” to your child, and try to change half of them into “you may…”
For each child, think of one “a whole garden of yes, and one no” rule, for example: “You may play at the weekend, only no screens after nine at night.”
lessons.noon: “You may freely eat of every tree of the garden.” — Father, thank you for your abundance; teach me to give my children a love this wide and this clear. Amen.

fam.key: God gives us so many “yeses.”

lamb.do: Let your child crawl and play freely on a safe mat while you stay beside him, only gently carrying him back at the edge.
lamb.say: You can play anywhere here. Daddy is here to keep you safe.

sprout.story: God made a beautiful garden with lots and lots of fruit trees: apples, bananas, grapes, mangoes… God said to Adam, “You may eat all of these! Only the tree in the middle you may not eat.” Adam was so happy, because God had given him so many, many “yeses”! The rules God makes are because God loves us and wants to keep us safe.
sprout.ask: Why do you think God said only one “no”?
sprout.do: Draw a big garden on a sheet of paper with many trees. Write “yes” on every tree and “no” on only the middle one, and count how many “yeses” there are.

soldier.story: In the Garden of Eden God gave Adam a job and also a rule: he could eat from every tree except one, and eating from that one would bring death. God did not lock that tree in a cage; he let Adam choose for himself. Why? Because God wants children who love him, not robots. Sadly, Adam and Eve chose wrongly, but God still came looking for them, and even made clothes for them. God’s rule was clear, and God’s love never left.
ask: If God had locked up that tree, Adam would not have done wrong. Why didn’t God do that?
What choices in our home do you think you can make by yourself?
soldier.do: As a family, write “our family’s yes list” with at least ten things you may do, then two or three “no”s, and see which side is longer.

youth.talk: When I read Genesis chapter 2, I noticed that God gave Adam very few rules and a great deal of freedom. Looking at myself, I seem to do the opposite: a pile of rules and very little freedom. You have grown up, and I want to learn God’s way and hand more choices over to you. But I will also state clearly the few boundaries that really matter, together with the reasons behind them.
ask: Which of our family rules do you think are really important and can’t be given up? Which could be discussed?
If you could make more decisions yourself, where would you most like to start?
youth.do: Together with your child, sort the family rules into “core boundaries” and “negotiable,” with no more than five core boundaries, and explain the reason behind each one.

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for giving us so many “yeses,” and for the “no” that protects us. Help us to make right choices every day. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

lessons.title: Give Choices, Let Consequences Speak
lessons.theme: Gentle and firm: try it today

v: But let your ‘Yes’ be ‘Yes’ and your ‘No’ be ‘No.’ Whatever is more than these is of the evil one.
For even when we were with you, we commanded you this: “If anyone is not willing to work, don’t let him eat.”

lessons.still: There will be a moment today when you need to state a boundary clearly to your child. Wait quietly on the Lord, and ask him for a gentle tone and a firm heart at that time. Take a deep breath and say, “Lord, let my ‘Yes’ be ‘Yes.’”
teach: Jesus said, “let your ‘Yes’ be ‘Yes’ and your ‘No’ be ‘No.’” What children need most is for their parents’ words to be trustworthy. Today you say, “The TV goes off at nine,” tomorrow you extend it to ten because you are tired, and the day after you suddenly lose your temper and switch it off. What the child learns is not to keep rules, but that “it depends on Mom and Dad’s mood today.” Consistency is stronger than strictness.

Paul told the Thessalonians, “If anyone is not willing to work, don’t let him eat.” This is an example of a consequence tied to behavior. At home it can work the same way: toys that aren’t put away “rest” for a day; if a child keeps playing at the table, the bowl is cleared when dinner time is over; if homework drags on late, there is no time for cartoons. When the consequence is related to the behavior, explained beforehand and carried out gently, there is no need for shouting and no need for shaming.

Try three steps today. One, say it beforehand: “After dinner, toys go away first, and when they are tidied we can have a story.” Two, give a choice: “Would you like to put away the blocks first, or the cars?” Three, carry it out gently: if the child doesn’t tidy up, say calmly, “No story time today. We’ll try again tomorrow.” Remember: natural consequences are only for safe situations. Where safety is involved, the parent protects the child directly and does not let him “learn a lesson.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: People matter more than tasks. Giving choices treats the child as a person who can think and take responsibility; carrying out consequences without anger protects the relationship from being hurt by the matter. Gentleness is toward the child’s heart, firmness is toward God’s principle, and both depend on the Holy Spirit and not on the parent’s emotions.
q: Who is God? — God is faithful in what he says and never changes with moods. What sense of security does this give you before him?
Who am I? — Are my “yes” and “no” trustworthy in my child’s eyes? On which matter do I flip-flop most often?
How should I respond? — Today, what matter will I make clear beforehand, give a choice about, and carry out gently?
lessons.jesus: “It came to pass, when the days were near that he should be taken up, he intently set his face to go to Jerusalem.” His disciples tried to hold him back and the crowds misunderstood him, but he walked on, step by step, toward the cross. Jesus was not stubborn; he knew clearly the Father’s will. Gentle with people and firm about his mission, he is the example for parents who are gentle and firm.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, your word is faithful and reliable. I confess that, from tiredness or mood, I often turn “yes” into “no” and leave my children not knowing where they stand. Today help me to speak clearly, give choices and carry them out gently. When my child cries and makes a fuss, let me not be provoked and not give in too easily. Amen.
acts: Choose a fixed time each day, such as bedtime or leaving the house, and tell your child the rule and the consequence beforehand.
Today give your child at least two “either-or” choices, and make sure you can accept both options.
When you carry out a consequence, say it in the same calm tone, “That’s all right. We’ll try again tomorrow.” No scolding and no bringing up old wrongs.
lessons.noon: “let your ‘Yes’ be ‘Yes’ and your ‘No’ be ‘No.’” — Lord, today let my words be gentle and faithful. Amen.

fam.key: We do what we say, gently and clearly.

lamb.do: Hold two garments or two pieces of fruit, one in each hand, and let your child reach for one. When he has chosen, praise him.
lamb.say: You chose this one. Well done! You can choose by yourself.

sprout.story: Mom said to Xiaokai, “We’re going out. Would you like to wear your red shoes or your blue shoes?” Xiaokai thought, “Blue!” Mom said, “Good. When they’re on, we’ll go to the park.” Xiaokai slowly put his shoes on himself. But the next day Xiaokai didn’t want to put away his blocks. Mom said, “If the blocks aren’t put away, they will rest for a day tomorrow.” The next day the blocks really did rest. Xiaokai said, “I’ll put them away today!”
sprout.ask: If you could choose, what would you like to choose most?
sprout.do: Play the “this or that” game: Mom and Dad give two options, such as “three jumps or one spin,” the child chooses one and does it, and then the child gives Mom and Dad a choice.

soldier.story: Zixuan, who grew up in Johor Bahru, loved video games. Dad agreed with him: “After homework each day you may play for forty minutes, and when the time is up you turn it off. If you go over, you lose your game time tomorrow.” On the first day, Zixuan played for forty-five minutes. Dad didn’t scold. He just said calmly, “No games tomorrow.” Zixuan was very unhappy, but the next day Dad really didn’t give way, and he wasn’t angry either. From the third day, Zixuan set an alarm for himself.
ask: Dad didn’t scold, so why did Zixuan still learn?
Do you think we have any rules in our home that get “said but not done”?
soldier.do: Pick, together with Mom and Dad, the rule you most often forget. Write it clearly, what happens if you keep it and what happens if you don’t, and try it this week.

youth.talk: I want to admit to you that the rules in our home are often inconsistent. Sometimes I am very relaxed, and sometimes suddenly very strict, and even I find it confusing. That isn’t fair. So I would like us to spell out a few important things together, including what happens if they are not done. I would also like you to keep an eye on me: if I flip-flop myself, you can remind me.
ask: Which family rule do you think gets enforced most according to mood?
If you broke an agreement, what kind of consequence would you think reasonable?
youth.do: Together with your child, choose one family rule and write it down: the boundary, the reason, and the consequence if it is not kept. Both sign it, and review after a week whether it is fair.

fam.pray: Lord Jesus, thank you that you do what you say. Help everyone in our family to do what we say, and to keep the rules with gentle hearts. Amen.

lessons.title: Two Hearts Agreed, Letting Go Step by Step
lessons.theme: Review and adjust: husband and wife set the rules in unity, and let go as the child grows

v: Do two walk together, unless they have agreed?
And he went down with them and came to Nazareth. He was subject to them, and his mother kept all these sayings in her heart.
And Jesus increased in wisdom and stature, and in favor with God and men.

lessons.still: Look back over the rules at home this week: which held, and which slipped? Ask the Holy Spirit to go over them with you. Think also of your spouse, or the elders who help raise the children: are you standing on the same line?
teach: “Do two walk together, unless they have agreed?” In many homes boundaries fail, not because the rules are bad, but because Mom and Dad are out of step. Dad says no, so the child goes to Mom; Mom holds firm, and Grandma quietly lets it pass. Children soon learn to find the gaps between adults. Being united as a couple does not mean agreeing on everything; it means talking it over in private first, and standing on the same side in front of the child.

The same applies to single-parent households and to grandparents raising grandchildren: you need to find companions to support you, such as a former spouse, an elder, or the spiritual companions in your church. Ecclesiastes says, “Two are better than one.” When those raising the child support one another instead of undermining one another, the child grows up in consistent love.

Luke records the twelve-year-old Jesus, “he went down with them and came to Nazareth,” and “was subject to them,” and that he “increased in wisdom and stature.” Growth means letting go must change with it. At three you choose the child’s clothes for him; at eight you give two choices; at fifteen you let him decide, and talk it over together. Boundaries are like a kite string: held steady, and let out slowly as the kite climbs.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The order of relationships is first with God, then with yourself, then with others. Husband and wife come before God together first, and then face the children together. A review is not blaming one another, “You spoil him,” “You are too harsh.” It is humility drawing out humility, correcting together, and winning together.
q: Who is God? — God let Jesus be subject to his parents at home and grow, and also sent him out step by step. How do you see God “letting go”?
Who am I? — On setting the rules, am I united with my spouse (or whoever raises the children with me)? Have I ever undercut the other in front of the child?
How should I respond? — Which rule will we correct together next week? In what matter can I begin to let go and hand responsibility to my child?
lessons.jesus: Jesus trained his disciples by first letting them follow beside him and watch, then sending them out two by two, and when they returned, going over what they had experienced with them. Jesus’ letting go was not abandonment: it came with accompanying, sending and reviewing. This is just the pattern for parents letting go step by step.
lessons.pray: Lord, thank you for going back over this week with us. I confess that my spouse and I are sometimes out of step and leave the children unsure; I have also sometimes let go too fast, or held on too tight. Make us one in heart, united first before you, and then leading our children together. And teach me, as my children grow, to let go to you step by step. Amen.
acts: Talk for fifteen minutes with your spouse (or whoever raises the children with you): this week, which rule were we not in step on? How will we talk it over in private first next week?
Ask your child, “This week, did Mom and Dad do what they said? Were we more like Jesus?” Just listen, and say thank you.
For each child, write down one thing you can begin to let him take charge of next week.
lessons.noon: “Do two walk together, unless they have agreed?” — Lord, make my spouse and me one in heart, and let us lead this home together. Amen.

fam.key: Mom and Dad love us with one heart.

lamb.do: Mom and Dad hold the child together, one on each side, rock him gently, and sing a hymn together.
lamb.say: Mommy and Daddy love you together and keep you safe together.

sprout.story: A penguin dad and mom looked after their penguin chick together. Dad kept the egg warm on his feet while Mom went to find fish and came back. After the chick was born they took turns looking after it, and never quarreled, saying, “That’s your job!” The chick grew bigger every day. One day Dad and Mom walked him down to the sea together and said, “You can swim by yourself now!” With a splash the chick jumped into the sea.
sprout.ask: Why do you think the penguin chick grew up so well?
sprout.do: Play the “three-legged race” as a family: Dad and Mom are tied together, the child is the judge, and you see how they get along fastest by being in step. Then swap, and tie the child to a grown-up.

soldier.story: When Jesus was twelve, he went to Jerusalem for the festival with his parents, but he stayed behind in the temple, and his parents searched for three days before they found him. Jesus went back to Nazareth with them, and the Bible says he “was subject to them” and “increased in wisdom and stature.” Jesus grew up step by step too. So do you: when you were little Mom and Dad did lots of things for you, and as you grow older you can take charge of more.
ask: What can you do now that you couldn’t do a year ago?
What would you like Mom and Dad to let you try by yourself next week?
soldier.do: Hold a ten-minute family meeting: each person says one “thing I can do this week,” and Mom and Dad pick one thing for each child to take charge of next week and write it on the family whiteboard.

youth.talk: This week I talked with your other parent, and we found that in matters concerning you we often aren’t in step, so sometimes you don’t know whom to listen to. We’re sorry. We have decided that from now on we will talk important things over in private first, and then speak with you together. We also want to admit that you are growing up, and there are things we should be letting go of; we are still learning how to let go.
ask: In what matter do you think the two of us most often say different things?
Is there something you think we should trust you with more, and let you decide?
youth.do: Parents sit down together with the child and choose one thing to move from “parents decide” to “child decides, parents advise,” such as pocket money or weekend plans, and try it for a month.

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for giving us a home where Mom and Dad love us together. Help us to grow a little more each day and learn to take charge of ourselves. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

38.memT: ‘Don’t be deceived. God is not mocked, for whatever a man sows, that he will also reap.

mem.t: Confess your sins to one another and pray for one another, that you may be healed. The insistent prayer of a righteous person is powerfully effective.

sat.d: Find something broken in your home: a cracked flowerpot, a toy with a broken leg, a shirt with a hole. Mend it together as a family. Adults handle the broken pottery pieces, while the children brush on the glue, add the color or sew on the button. Once the flowerpot is mended, trace the cracks with gold paint. When it is done, look at it together: “The mended places have become the most special places.” Finally, Mom and Dad go first, each naming “one thing I want to repair” and saying one sincere apology to the family. Then pray together for your home.

sun: As a child, did you ever hear your parents apologize to you? What effect did it have on you?
This week, which part of apologizing to your child was hardest to say? How did your child respond?
Which step of “parents apologize first” will you share with another family next week, or invite your small group to practice together?

lessons.title: Confess to One Another and Be Healed
lessons.theme: When parents admit a fault they do not lose authority; they bring healing

v: Confess your sins to one another and pray for one another, that you may be healed. The insistent prayer of a righteous person is powerfully effective.
If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.
If we confess our sins, he is faithful and righteous to forgive us the sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.

lessons.still: Be still and let your heart slowly relax. Think of a recent unpleasant clash at home and ask the Lord, “Lord, in that matter, what part do I need to admit?” There is no hurry; let him show you gently.
teach: James says, “Confess your sins to one another and pray for one another, that you may be healed.” “One another” runs in both directions. It is not only children confessing to parents, but parents confessing to children as well. Many Chinese parents grew up hearing, “How could an adult be wrong?” and so admitting a fault feels like losing face and authority. But the Bible says confession brings not shame but healing.

John puts it even more directly: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.” When parents will not admit fault, children can see it anyway, and they learn two things: first, that people with power need never admit they are wrong; second, that when you are wrong you should cover it up. But when a parent says, “I was wrong just now. I’m sorry,” the child learns that in this home, mistakes can be spoken about and can be forgiven.

In Japan there is a craft for mending porcelain: the cracks are filled with gold lacquer, and the mended bowl becomes more special than it was before. Relationships at home are like this. No family never breaks, but the mending after the breaking matters more than pretending nothing happened. A child will forget many of his parents’ words, but he will remember for a long time that Mom and Dad once crouched down and said to him, “I’m sorry.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Pride leaves its place to grasp at power; humility lays down power and returns to its place. A parent’s apology is an admission that “I am not the king of this home; Jesus is.” Pride provokes pride, one side holding out and the other pushing back; humility draws out humility, and when the parent bows first, the child’s heart has a road back.
q: Who is God? — God is faithful and righteous, and will forgive those who confess. How have you experienced his forgiveness?
Who am I? — Do I still believe in my heart that “if a parent apologizes, he loses authority”? Where did that idea come from?
How should I respond? — What unspoken apology do I owe my child?
lessons.jesus: Jesus is the only one who never needed to apologize to anyone. He never sinned, yet he was willing to bear our sin and die on the cross. Because of him, when we confess we need not fear being cast out, for God is faithful and righteous to forgive. Jesus made confession the road to healing.
lessons.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for forgiving me when I confess, and never shaming me. I confess that I am often unwilling to admit fault to my children, afraid of losing face and authority. Take away my pride, and teach me to confess to one another and pray for one another. Let our home find healing in confession and forgiveness, and let my children see your grace in me. Amen.
acts: Write down one apology you owe your child, and confess it before God first.
If you say something wrong today, say within ten minutes, “I was wrong just now. I’m sorry.”
Intercede for one child, asking God to heal any wound you may have caused in his heart.
lessons.noon: “Confess your sins to one another and pray for one another, that you may be healed.” — Lord, give me courage to be the first to admit my fault at home. Amen.

fam.key: When we say sorry, love comes back.

lamb.do: If you have accidentally hurt your child or made him wait too long, pick him up, look into his eyes, say sorry gently, and kiss him.
lamb.say: I’m sorry, Mommy made you wait too long. I love you.

sprout.story: Papa Bear was very tired after work. When he got home, Little Bear ran over to ask him to play, and Papa Bear said loudly, “Go away, I’m tired!” Little Bear went off crying. Papa Bear sat in his chair, feeling very sad. Then he went to Little Bear, crouched down and said, “I’m sorry, Daddy was cross with you just now. Can you forgive me?” Little Bear hugged his dad, and the two bears played with blocks until bedtime.
sprout.ask: Do grown-ups say sorry too?
sprout.do: Play “Sorry, that’s okay”: one person says “I’m sorry,” and the other says “That’s okay, I forgive you,” then you hug. Everyone takes a turn, with Mom and Dad going first.

soldier.story: Siying in Penang did badly in an exam, and Mom said in front of the relatives, “She just doesn’t work hard.” Siying didn’t say a word all evening. At bedtime Mom came to her room and said, “What I said about you in front of everyone today was wrong. You must have felt so embarrassed and sad. I’m sorry. I won’t talk about your marks in front of other people again.” Siying’s eyes turned red, and she nodded and said, “I forgive you.” The Bible says that when we confess to one another, we are healed.
ask: After Mom said sorry, what do you think changed in Siying’s heart?
When a grown-up says sorry to a child, is it embarrassing or brave? Why?
soldier.do: Each person thinks of one “sorry” they want to say to a family member this week, writes it on a slip of paper, and hands it over after dinner. The other person answers, “I forgive you.”

youth.talk: When I was young I rarely heard an adult say sorry, so I always thought that if parents apologize, they lose their authority. Now I think that was wrong. Over these years I must have hurt you in many ways; some I know about, and some I may not have noticed at all. I don’t want to pretend I was always right. If you are willing, could you tell me one thing you have always wanted me to apologize for?
ask: When an adult says “I’m sorry,” do you respect him more, or less?
Is there something you have always wanted me to admit I got wrong?
youth.do: The parent first chooses one thing he knows he did wrong, and this week finds a quiet time to apologize to the child one-on-one, sincerely, without adding “but.”

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for always forgiving us. Help each person in our family to say sorry when we do wrong, and to be willing to say, “I forgive you.” In Jesus’ name, Amen.

lessons.title: “You Are the Man!”
lessons.theme: Only when we see ourselves can we truly apologize

v: Nathan said to David, “You are the man! This is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says: ‘I anointed you king over Israel, and I delivered you out of the hand of Saul.
David said to Nathan, “I have sinned against the LORD.” Nathan said to David, “The LORD also has put away your sin. You will not die.

lessons.still: Be still and ask the Holy Spirit to take you back to the most recent time you were quite sure that “the child was in the wrong.” Look again, this time from the child’s point of view. Say to the Lord, “Lord, let me see myself.”
teach: The prophet Nathan told David a story: a rich man had many flocks and herds, yet he took from a poor man his one little ewe lamb. David was furious and said the man deserved to die. Nathan said only one sentence: “You are the man!” David could see other people’s faults clearly, but not his own. Parents are often the same. When a child talks back, we see it perfectly; how sharp our own tone is, we cannot hear.

When the Holy Spirit shines his light, people respond differently. Some parents never apologize at all. Some give a “fake apology”: “I’m sorry, but you were wrong too”, apologizing in the first half and pushing the blame back onto the child in the second. Some use a toy or a big meal instead of saying sorry. And some sink into self-blame, saying, “I’m the worst mother,” and end up making the child comfort them. None of these is yet a true apology.

David’s response was very short: “I have sinned against the LORD.” No excuse, no explanation, no blaming Bathsheba. Proverbs says, “He who conceals his sins doesn’t prosper, but whoever confesses and renounces them finds mercy.” A true apology begins with seeing: seeing what I did and what it did to my child, and then simply admitting it.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The focus is on Jesus, not on others. The self-ruled parent is very good at seeing the child’s faults, because his focus is on others; the self-emptied parent first lets the Holy Spirit shine on himself, because his focus is on Jesus. The light is not to condemn, but to bring us out of darkness and back to our place.
q: Who is God? — God sent Nathan, not to destroy David, but to win him back. In God’s light, do you feel fear or grace?
Who am I? — Never apologizing, fake apology, replacing it with gifts, sinking into self-blame: which am I most often?
How should I respond? — In what matter is the Holy Spirit saying to me, “You are the man”?
lessons.jesus: Jesus told a parable: the Pharisee stood and boasted about himself, but the tax collector stood far away, beat his chest and said, “God, be merciful to me, a sinner!” Jesus said that the tax collector went down to his house justified. What Jesus values is not a perfect appearance but a heart that honestly admits.
lessons.pray: Holy Spirit, shine your light on me and let me see in myself what I cannot see in my child. I confess that I am very good at seeing my child’s faults, yet I often cover my own with excuses, with “but,” and with gifts. Forgive me, and give me a heart that simply admits, so that like David I make no excuses and simply say what I did wrong. Amen.
acts: Write down your most recent conflict in two columns, “the child’s fault” and “my fault,” and fill in mine first.
Notice whether you say “I’m sorry, but…” today, and swallow whatever comes after the “but.”
Ask your spouse, “Do you think I owe the children an apology?”
lessons.noon: “He who conceals his sins doesn’t prosper, but whoever confesses and renounces them finds mercy.” — Lord, I don’t want to cover up; have mercy on me. Amen.

fam.key: A brave person can see his own mistakes.

lamb.do: Hold your child in front of a mirror, point to the two of you in the mirror, and gently touch his nose and then your own.
lamb.say: This is you, and this is Mommy. We are both learning, and God loves us both.

sprout.story: Little Fox saw Little Rabbit spill the juice and laughed loudly, “You’re so clumsy!” Mother Fox brought him a little mirror and said, “Look in the mirror. Didn’t you spill milk yesterday too?” Little Fox looked in the mirror and his face went red. “Oh yes, I did.” He went over to Little Rabbit and said, “I’m sorry, I shouldn’t have laughed at you. Let me help you wipe it up.”
sprout.ask: Why is it easy to see other people’s mistakes, and hard to see our own?
sprout.do: Take a mirror, and each person looks in it and says, “I make mistakes too, and God helps me.” Then say, “You make mistakes too, and I forgive you.”

soldier.story: King David did something very wrong and pretended nothing had happened. God sent the prophet Nathan to him with a story: a rich man with many sheep took a poor man’s one little lamb. David was angry. “That man is terrible!” Nathan looked at him and said, “You are the man!” David froze, and then he said, “I have sinned against the LORD.” He made no excuses; he honestly admitted it. And God forgave him.
ask: Why could David see another person’s wrong at first, but not his own?
Do you think “I’m sorry, but you did… too” counts as a real apology? Why?
soldier.do: As a family, play a game to tell real apologies from fake ones: Mom and Dad say a few apologies, and the children put up a hand to judge whether each is real or fake, and say why.

youth.talk: I have noticed that when I apologize I often add a “but”: “I’m sorry, but you went too far as well.” After saying it I feel I have apologized, but you feel I am only scolding you in a different way. I think that is not a real apology. When Nathan pointed it out, David said just one sentence, “I have sinned against the LORD,” without any “but.” I want to learn that.
ask: When I apologize, what makes it feel insincere to you?
When you apologize, do you want to add a “but” too? What are you thinking then?
youth.do: Parent and child each write down three “fake apologies” they often say, then rewrite them together as real apologies and swap to see them.

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for helping us see our mistakes. Give us brave hearts, so that when we do wrong we honestly say sorry and make no excuses. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

lessons.title: Zacchaeus’ Apology
lessons.theme: I believe: only those accepted by grace can truly repent and make amends

v: When Jesus came to the place, he looked up and saw him, and said to him, “Zacchaeus, hurry and come down, for today I must stay at your house.”
He hurried, came down, and received him joyfully.
When they saw it, they all murmured, saying, “He has gone in to lodge with a man who is a sinner.”
Zacchaeus stood and said to the Lord, “Behold, Lord, half of my goods I give to the poor. If I have wrongfully exacted anything of anyone, I restore four times as much.”
Jesus said to him, “Today, salvation has come to this house, because he also is a son of Abraham.

lessons.still: Imagine Jesus coming to the door of your home, looking up and calling your name, and saying, “Today I must stay at your house.” He has not yet asked you to change; he accepts you first. Quietly receive this grace.
teach: Zacchaeus was a chief tax collector who had grown rich by oppressing his own people, and in everyone’s eyes he was a sinner. As Jesus passed through Jericho, he looked up and saw him hiding in a tree, and said, “Zacchaeus, hurry and come down, for today I must stay at your house.” Jesus accepted him first, and then Zacchaeus stood up and said, “If I have wrongfully exacted anything of anyone, I restore four times as much.” Grace comes first and repentance after. Only a person who is loved has the strength to face his own wrongs.

There is something special about Zacchaeus’ apology: it was specific, and it came with action. He did not just say, “I wasn’t very good before.” He named what he had done and offered a way to make it right. A parent apologizing to a child is the same: not vaguely saying, “Mommy has a bad temper,” but specifically, “Yesterday I punished you without listening to your explanation,” and then saying how things will change.

The viewpoint has to shift: from “apologizing loses my authority” to “apologizing builds trust”; from “authority comes from always being right” to “authority comes from being honest and dependable.” Children don’t need perfect parents; they need real parents, who make mistakes, and who also admit them and change. Today, write your “I believe” declaration.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Change the belief and you change the life. When I believe “I am accepted by God,” I no longer need to prove myself by always being right. I can admit a mistake, because my worth lies not in face but in Christ. A self-emptied parent can say openly in front of his child, “This was my fault.”
q: Who is God? — Jesus accepted Zacchaeus even before he repented. Does he accept you the same way?
Who am I? — Is my authority built on “always being right,” or on being “honest and dependable”?
How should I respond? — Write your “I believe” declaration: I believe God accepted me first, so I can… ; I believe an apology will…
lessons.jesus: The crowd murmured, “He has gone in to lodge with a man who is a sinner.” Jesus did not mind being misunderstood, and insisted on going into Zacchaeus’ house. He declared, “Today, salvation has come to this house.” Jesus’ grace came not to Zacchaeus alone but to his whole household. When a parent is changed by grace, the whole home is blessed.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, thank you for coming to my home and accepting me before I had changed. I believe my worth lies not in always being right but in being loved by you. Let me, like Zacchaeus, admit specifically what I owe my children, and be willing to make it right with action. May salvation and peace come to our home. Amen.
acts: Write three “I believe” sentences: I believe God accepted me first; I believe an apology builds trust; I believe what my child needs is a real parent.
Write what you want to apologize to your child for as one specific sentence: “When…, I did…”
Think of an action to make amends, for example making up the time together that you promised and never gave.
lessons.noon: “Zacchaeus, hurry and come down, for today I must stay at your house.” — Lord, thank you for accepting me first; today, stay in our home. Amen.

fam.key: Jesus loved me first, and I am willing to change.

lamb.do: Lift your child high, then lower him gently into your arms and talk to him.
lamb.say: Jesus calls your name. Jesus loves you so much.

sprout.story: Zacchaeus was so short that he could not see Jesus, so he climbed up a big tree. Nobody liked Zacchaeus, because he often took other people’s money. But Jesus came to the tree, looked up and said, “Zacchaeus, hurry and come down, I am coming to your house today!” Zacchaeus was so happy. He jumped down and said, “Whoever’s money I took, I will give back much more!” Jesus’ love made Zacchaeus a new man.
sprout.ask: When Jesus went to Zacchaeus’ house, why did Zacchaeus want to change?
sprout.do: Play “Zacchaeus up the tree”: your child stands on a chair (with a grown-up holding him safe), Mom and Dad call his name from below, “(name), hurry and come down, Jesus loves you!” and he jumps into their arms.

soldier.story: Zacchaeus was a tax collector who often charged people too much, and everyone disliked him. But Jesus saw him, called his name, and said he would go to his house for a meal. Moved by Jesus’ love, Zacchaeus stood up and said, “I will give half of what I own to the poor, and if I cheated anyone, I will pay back four times as much!” Zacchaeus’ apology was not just words. He named what he had done wrong, and he made it right with action.
ask: How was Zacchaeus’ apology different from just saying “sorry”?
If you broke your brother’s or sister’s things, besides saying sorry, how else could you make it right?
soldier.do: Each person thinks of one time they made the family sad, and besides saying sorry, thinks of one “making-it-right action” and does it this week.

youth.talk: The story of Zacchaeus showed me something. Jesus did not scold him first; he accepted him first, and only then was Zacchaeus willing to change. I used to think I had to make your mistakes clear before you would change. But I myself began to change only after God accepted me first. I want to tell you first: whatever you have done, you are a child we accept. I would also like to apologize to you for one specific thing and make it right.
ask: Which do you think makes a person more willing to change, being accepted first or being corrected first?
Is there anything I promised you and did not do that you still remember?
youth.do: The parent finds one thing he promised the child but did not do, apologizes for it specifically this week, and sets a time to make it up.

fam.pray: Jesus, thank you for loving us as you loved Zacchaeus. Help us, when we do wrong, to say sorry and also make it right with action. Amen.

lessons.title: First Go and Be Reconciled with Your Child
lessons.theme: Six steps of a parent’s apology: do it today

v: “If therefore you are offering your gift at the altar, and there remember that your brother has anything against you,
leave your gift there before the altar, and go your way. First be reconciled to your brother, and then come and offer your gift.
I acknowledged my sin to you. I didn’t hide my iniquity. I said, I will confess my transgressions to the LORD, and you forgave the iniquity of my sin. Selah.

lessons.still: Today you are going to apologize to your child. First sit for a while before God and hand the matter over to him. Say, “Lord, I acknowledge my fault to you. Forgive me, and give me gentleness in what I say.”
teach: Jesus said that if you are offering your gift at the altar and remember that your brother has something against you, “leave your gift there before the altar, and go your way. First be reconciled to your brother, and then come and offer your gift.” Reconciliation comes before sacrifice. For parents this means: when the relationship with your child is broken, you can’t cover it with more prayer meetings and more service. You need to go home first and mend the relationship.

An apology can be made in six steps. One: go to God first, like the psalmist who said, “I acknowledged my sin to you,” and wait until you are calm. Two: choose the moment, alone with the child, crouching, looking at him. Three: say specifically what I did, without “if” and without “but.” Four: say what effect it had on the child and acknowledge his feelings. Five: say how I will change, and ask, “Will you forgive me?” Six: repair with action, and pray together.

For example: “Just now I was in a hurry and I shouted at you, and I said you were ‘slow and annoying.’ That was my fault, not yours. You must feel very sad and hurt. I’m sorry. Next time I’m in a hurry, I will take a deep breath first and tell you I need you to be a bit quicker. Will you forgive me?” Remember: don’t trade your apology for the child’s apology, and don’t hurry the child into forgiving at once. If there is violence or serious harm in your home, then beyond apologizing, also seek help from your pastor and from professionals.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Relationships matter more than tasks. Be reconciled with God first, and then you have the strength to be reconciled with people; deal with the parent’s own heart first, and then the child’s behavior. An apology lives out “life first, then relationships”: I am restored by God first, and then I go and restore my relationship with my child.
q: Who is God? — God values reconciliation above sacrifice. Does this make you rethink what true worship is?
Who am I? — Of the six steps, which is hardest for me? Why?
How should I respond? — When today, and with what specific sentence, will I apologize to which child?
lessons.jesus: Jesus, who was “existing in the form of God,” “emptied himself, taking the form of a servant,” and “humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death.” The Lord of all was willing to come down to the lowest place in order to be reconciled with us. A parent who crouches down to say sorry to a child is following this self-emptying Lord.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, to be reconciled with me you were willing to empty yourself and humble yourself. Today I want to learn your way, to lay down my face and go first to be reconciled with my child. When I open my mouth, give me words that are specific, sincere and do not pass the blame. When my child responds, give me patience, with no pressing and no demanding. Let this apology be the starting point of mending our relationship. Amen.
acts: Follow the six steps and make one complete apology to a child today.
When apologizing, avoid three words: “if,” “but” and “you too.”
After the apology, do one repair action: play with him for fifteen minutes, do the thing you promised, or pray together.
lessons.noon: “First be reconciled to your brother, and then come and offer your gift.” — Lord, today let me go home first and mend my relationship with my child. Amen.

fam.key: When we are wrong we say sorry; making up matters most.

lamb.do: If you were too loud with your child, wait until he is calm, pick him up, put your cheek to his, apologize in your softest voice, and play his favorite game with him.
lamb.say: Daddy was too loud just now and gave you a fright. I’m sorry. We’re friends again.

sprout.story: Mom was very busy cooking, and Xiaoyu kept tugging at her skirt. Mom said crossly, “You’re so annoying!” Xiaoyu hid behind the sofa. Mom turned off the stove, went over and crouched down. “Just now Mom said you were annoying, and that was wrong. You must feel very sad. I’m sorry. Next time I’m busy, I’ll tell you, ‘Wait five minutes for me.’ Will you forgive Mom?” Xiaoyu nodded and snuggled into Mom’s arms.
sprout.ask: When Mom said sorry, what things did she say?
sprout.do: Act out “Mom says sorry” with puppets: the child plays Mom, and Mom and Dad play Xiaoyu. Act out the story, then swap roles.

soldier.story: Jiahao in Melbourne was supposed to go and play ball with Dad at the weekend, but Dad canceled because of overtime. Jiahao complained, and Dad even scolded him for being “unreasonable.” The next day Dad asked him to sit down and said, “Yesterday I canceled our plan and then told you off for being unreasonable. That was my fault. You had been looking forward to it all week, so you must have been very disappointed. I’m sorry. I have already kept this Saturday free, and we will definitely go. Will you forgive me?” Jiahao said, “All right, but you have to keep your word!”
ask: Which parts of Dad’s apology made Jiahao willing to forgive?
If you were Jiahao, what would you have wanted Dad to do?
soldier.do: As a family, learn the four sentences of an apology: “I did…”, “You must feel…”, “I’m sorry. Next time I will…”, and “Will you forgive me?” Write them on a small card and stick it behind the door.

youth.talk: I want to apologize to you in a specific way, so it may sound a little formal. Please bear with me. Last month you told me something private, and I turned around and told your auntie. That was my fault. I did not keep your trust. You must have felt betrayed and very angry. I’m sorry. From now on, what you tell me I will not tell anyone without your permission. You don’t have to forgive me right now; whenever you are ready is fine.
ask: What do you think an apology needs to include for it to be sincere?
What do you need me to do so that you can slowly trust me again?
youth.do: The parent uses the six steps to apologize to the child for one specific thing, gives the child time to respond, and proves the change by action over the following week.

fam.pray: Dear Jesus, thank you for coming to make peace with us. Help our family to say sorry when we are wrong, to be willing to forgive, and to make up every day. Amen.

lessons.title: Mending After the Break
lessons.theme: Review and adjust: mending matters more than being perfect

v: Create in me a clean heart, O God. Renew a right spirit within me.
Don’t throw me from your presence, and don’t take your Holy Spirit from me.
Restore to me the joy of your salvation. Uphold me with a willing spirit.
The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit. O God, you will not despise a broken and contrite heart.

lessons.still: Look back over this week: did you apologize? How did your child respond? Ask the Holy Spirit to look with you. Whether it went well or not, first say to the Lord, “Thank you. I am still learning.”
teach: Psalm 51 was written by David after Nathan pointed out his sin. He asked God, “Create in me a clean heart, O God. Renew a right spirit within me.” And he said, “The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit. O God, you will not despise a broken and contrite heart.” What God wants is not a parent who never falls, but a parent who is willing to turn back.

In a review we need to tell two kinds of sorrow apart. Paul says, “godly sorrow produces repentance leading to salvation, which brings no regret. But the sorrow of the world produces death.” Healthy repentance makes us stand up and mend; unhealthy self-blame traps us in “I am a failure as a parent” and actually distances us from our children. God shines his light on us to heal, not to crush.

Perhaps your apology did not go smoothly this week: the child shrugged, rolled his eyes or said, “Whatever.” Don’t lose heart. Trust is like savings: each apology is a deposit, and it takes deposit after deposit to build up. A break is not the frightening thing; not mending it is. A child who has been through “quarrel, apology, making up” learns that relationships can be mended, and that will go with him into friendships, marriage and all his relationships for life.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Review, adjustment and repetition are the second half of the eight steps for changing beliefs. Parents need not be perfect, but they must keep turning back. Humility draws out humility: when children see their parents admit a fault and adjust again and again, they too will learn to be humble before God and people. This is the multiplication of life.
q: Who is God? — God does not despise a broken and contrite heart. How does this change the way you see yourself when you fail?
Who am I? — This week, am I in “healthy repentance” or in “unhealthy self-blame”?
How should I respond? — Which relationship will I keep mending next week? What action will prove it?
lessons.jesus: When Peter denied the Lord three times and the rooster crowed, “the Lord turned and looked at Peter,” and Peter went out and wept bitterly. That look was not a condemnation but a call. After the resurrection, Jesus took the first step to mend that relationship by the lake. Peter later became a pillar of the church because he had known mending after the break.
lessons.pray: God, create in me a clean heart, and renew a right spirit within me. Thank you that you do not despise my broken and contrite heart. This week I have been learning to apologize to my children, some of it smooth and some of it clumsy. Heal my children’s hearts, and keep me from sinking into self-blame. Let me turn back again and again, so that my children can see in me what mending looks like. Amen.
acts: Talk with your spouse: this week, did each of us apologize to the children? How did they respond? What did we learn?
Ask your child, “This week, was I more like Jesus? How did my apology make you feel?” Just listen, and say thank you.
Write down next week’s corrective action: which relationship you will keep mending and what action will prove it.
lessons.noon: “O God, you will not despise a broken and contrite heart.” — Lord, I come before you with this heart; renew me. Amen.

fam.key: After a quarrel, we can make up.

lamb.do: Play with blocks with your child and let the tower fall on purpose, then slowly build it up again together, and clap when it is done.
lamb.say: It fell down, never mind. We can build it again together.

sprout.story: Little Flower and Little Grass were good friends, but one day they quarreled and would not talk to each other. Grandfather Sun said, “Do you miss each other?” Little Flower said, “Yes.” Little Grass said, “Me too.” Little Flower spoke first. “I’m sorry I pushed you yesterday.” Little Grass said, “I’m sorry too. I said something unkind to you.” They held hands and danced together in the wind again. After a quarrel, we can still make up!
sprout.ask: The last time you quarreled with someone, how did you make up?
sprout.do: Draw a “making-up picture”: draw a heart in the middle, trace the cracks with a gold or yellow pen, and write beside it, “We made up!”

soldier.story: Peter had been Jesus’ boldest disciple, but one night, out of fear, he said three times, “I don’t know Jesus!” When the rooster crowed, Jesus turned and looked at him, and Peter was so sad that he wept. After Jesus rose from the dead, he prepared breakfast for Peter by the lake and asked him three times, “Do you love me?” Each time he asked, he mended Peter a little more. Peter later became a very important leader of the church.
ask: Why do you think Jesus asked Peter three times?
After you do something wrong, what kind of help lets you stand up again?
soldier.do: Hold a ten-minute family meeting: each person shares one thing about “making up this week” and one relationship they want to mend next week. Mom and Dad go first, and at the end the whole family prays together.

youth.talk: This week I tried to apologize to you, and honestly it felt awkward, and I am not sure I did it well. Maybe you feel that one apology doesn’t mean much, and I understand that. Trust can’t be mended all at once. I want you to know I won’t give up just because you didn’t forgive me straight away. I will keep correcting myself, and I hope that when you see me changing you will tell me.
ask: How did my apology this week really feel to you? Where did it feel not enough?
After a quarrel at our home, how do we usually make up? Is there a better way?
youth.do: Parent and child write “our family’s making-up agreement” together: after a quarrel, how long at most before we make up, who may speak first, and how we show that we have made up.

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you that after a quarrel we can still make up. Help our family to say sorry often, forgive often, and love each other more and more. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

39.memT: Confess your sins to one another and pray for one another, that you may be healed. The insistent prayer of a righteous person is powerfully effective.
